2. The shepherds praised God for having seen Christ; The wise men, in addition to having seen him, worshiped him. In the former, grace appears above all; in the latter a superior humility is manifested. Perhaps those shepherds, being less guilty, experienced more vividly the joy of salvation, while the wise men, burdened with many sins, more humbly begged for forgiveness. Behold, that humility recommended by divine Scripture is possessed by the Gentiles in a greater degree than by the Jews. Gentile was that centurion who, having received the Lord with all his heart, nevertheless said that he was unworthy of him entering his house, and did not want him to see his sick servant, but rather to order his recovery. In this way he kept present in his heart the one whose presence under his roof he rejected because he felt unworthy. Finally, the Lord said: I have not found so much Jeh in Israel. That Canaanite woman was also a Gentile who, hearing herself called a dog by the Lord and unworthy of having her children's bread thrown to her, demanded, because she was a dog, the crumbs, and in this way she deserved not to be one, because she did not deny being one. She also, in fact, heard from the mouth of the Lord: O woman, great is your heh. Humility had produced in her a great faith, because it had become small. 3. Thus, then, the shepherds come to see him from nearby, while the wise men come from afar to worship him. This is the humility by which the wild olive tree deserved to be grafted into the olive tree and give olives, against the laws of nature, because for gra-

cia deserved to change his nature. The whole world appeared wild and bitter because of this wild olive tree, but due to the grace of its insertion it shone with the exuberance of its fruits. So they come from the ends of the earth, saying in the words of Jeremiah: Our fathers truly worshiped false things. And they come not from a single part of the world, but, in accordance with the gospel of Luke, from the east, the west, the north and the south who are to sit at the table of the kingdom of heaven with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. In this way, the entire world, by the grace of the Trinity, is called to faith from its four parts. Number that, multiplied by 3, gives 12, the sacred number of the apostles, as prefiguring the salvation of the entire world, which consists of four parts, and its call to faith in the Trinity. Number also signified on that plate full of all kinds of animals, symbolizing all the Gentiles, which was shown to Peter; He also hung from four ropes and was lowered from heaven three times and raised again, so that the multiplication of 3 by 4 resulted in the number 12. Perhaps this is the reason why only twelve days after the birth of the Lord the wise men, the first fruits of the Gentiles, came to see and worship Christ, and they deserved not only to receive their own salvation, but also to be a sign of that of all the Gentiles. Let us therefore celebrate this day with all devotion; whom the wise men, our first fruits, adored while lying in an inn, let us adore him, now dwelling in heaven. They venerated in him as the future what we venerate.

Those who listened and were obedient, coming from here and there, found peace and put an end to the enmity. The shepherds and the wise men were the firstfruits of each other. In them the ox began to know its owner, and the donkey its master's manger. The animal with horns refers to the Jewish people, since the horns of the cross were prepared for Christ. The animal with long ears, however, to the Gentile people, as predicted: The people I did not know served me, and when they heard me, they obeyed me. Thus, the owner of the ox and the lord of the donkey lay in the manger, and gave both animals common food. He had come to be peace both for those far and near; The Israelite shepherds, as befits those who were nearby, came to him on the same day that Christ was born; They saw him and rejoiced; The Gentile wise men, however, being far away, a few days after the date of his birth, arrived today, found him and worshiped him. It was fitting, therefore, that we, the Church gathered from among the Gentiles, should unite the celebration of this day on which Christ was manifested to the firstfruits of the Gentiles, with that on which Christ was born of the Jews, and that we should preserve, through double solemnity, the memory of such a great mystery. 3. When you have the Jewish wall in mind, you should not think of the persecutors and murderers of Christ, as builders of the law and destroyers of the faith, who rejected the cornerstone and built ruin for their miserable city. Nor should we think of the multitude of Jews spread throughout the entire earth to bear witness to the divine Scriptures, which, without knowing them, they carry everywhere. In all of these Jacob is lame. In the act of hitting his thigh and leaving it dry, the multitude of his race, which was going to give up its paths, is signified. We must think, however, of the holy wall, the one that passed from them to the peace of the cornerstone; in those in whom Jacob was blessed. The same person was blessed and left lame: blessed in his sanctified descendants, and lame in the reprobate. Those who in multitude preceded and followed the donkey carrying the Savior, shouting: Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! must be thought of as included in this wall; those disciples chosen from that town and converted into apostles. It conforms to our devotion that those of us who are going to celebrate the passion, now close, of the crucified Lord, make ourselves a cross with the pleasures of the flesh, which must be tamed, according to the words of the Apostle: Those who belong to Jesus Christ crucified the flesh with its passions and concupiscence. The Christian must always remain aware of this cross throughout this life, which passes in the midst of temptations. This is not the time to pull out the nails of which it is said in the psalm: Pierce my flesh with the nails of your fear. Flesh here is equivalent to carnal lust; the nails are the precepts of justice; With them the fear of God nails the flesh to the flesh, crucifying us like a host acceptable to him. That is why the Apostle also says: I beg you, therefore, brothers, by the mercy of God, to offer your bodies as a living host, holy, pleasing to God. This is a cross in which the servant of God not only does not feel confused, but even glories, saying: Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom the world is crucified for me, and I for the world. the Christian will ardently devote himself to prayer, fasting and alms'; but this solemnity should stimulate even those who are ordinarily lazy in the matter; and those who already apply themselves diligently to such occupations must now perform them with greater intensity. Life in this world is the time of our humiliation; These days symbolize nothing else. The annual repetition of the solemnity is equivalent to a repetition of what Christ the Lord suffered for us in his only death. What took place only once in history for the renewal of our life, is celebrated every year to perpetuate its memory. Therefore, if we must be humble of heart and be filled with the affection of true piety during our entire pilgrimage that takes place in the midst of temptations, how much more so in these days, when this time of our humiliation is not only lived, but also symbolized in celebration! The humility of Christ teaches us to be humble, because when he died he gave in to the wicked; His excellency makes us exalted, because when he was resurrected he preceded the righteous. If we have died with Christ, says the Apostle, we will also live with him; If we suffer with him, we will also reign with him. With due veneration we celebrate one of these two things now thinking about the closeness of his passion; the other after Easter, thinking of his resurrection already accomplished. The Lord says: Give, and it will be given to you; forgive, and you will be forgiven. Let us fervently surrender to these two modes of almsgiving: giving and forgiving, we who ask the Lord to grant us his goods and not ask us to account for our evils. Give, he says, and it will be given to you. Is there anything more authentic and more just than someone who refuses to give, defrauds himself and receives nothing? If the farmer who goes to seek the harvest where he knows he did not sow behaves impudently, how much greater is the impudence of the one who seeks God's wealth to give him, after he did not want to listen to the poor person who asked of him! God, who does not suffer hunger, nevertheless wanted to be fed in the person of the poor. Therefore, let us not despise our needy God in the person of the poor, so that, when we feel needy, we may be satisfied in him who is rich. People in need come before us, and we also lo litatis, etiam nostrae celsitudinis tempus, etsi nondum videndo agere vacat; iam also praemeditando means delectat. for which in these days you restrain your desires for lawful things, so as not to succumb to the unlawful. Those who abstain from marriage these days should never get drunk or commit adultery. In this way, our prayer, made with humility and charity, with fasting and alms, temperance and forgiveness, practicing good and not returning evil for evil, distancing ourselves from evil and surrendering ourselves to virtue, seeks peace and achieves it. Prayer, in fact, aided by the wings of such virtues, flies and reaches more easily to heaven, where Christ, our peace, preceded us.

He fasted and prayed for us. Indeed, alms is a Greek term that means "mercy." What mercy could descend upon the unfortunate greater than that which brought down the creator of heaven from heaven and clothed the creator of earth with an earthly body? To him who from eternity remains equal to the Father, he made him equal to us through mortality, he gave the form of a servant to the lord of the world, so that bread was hungry, satiety was thirsty, strength became weak, health was wounded and life died. And all this to satisfy our hunger, water our dryness, console our weakness, extinguish iniquity and inflame charity. The creator is created, the lord serves, the redeemer is sold, he who exalts is humiliated, he who is resurrected dies: is there greater mercy? With reference to alms, we are commanded to give bread to the needy; He, in order to give himself to us, who were hungry, first gave himself to heartless people for us. We are commanded to receive the pilgrim; He came for us to his own house, and his own did not receive him. May our soul bless him, who shows himself merciful with all his iniquities; to him, who heals all her ailments, who frees her life from corruption, who crowns her in his compassion and mercy; he, who satisfies his desires with good things. Let us, therefore, exercise the duty of almsgiving, all the more generously and frequently as the day approaches when we celebrate the almsgiving given to us. Fasting, without mercy, is of no use to those who do it.

2. Let us also fast with the humility of our souls as the day approaches when the master of humility humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death on a cross. Let us imitate his crucifixion by piercing the untamed passions with the nails of continence. Let us punish our body and reduce it to servitude; And so that untamed flesh does not lead us to what is illicit, let us take away some of what is lawful to tame it. Profanity and drunkenness must always be avoided; but in these days lawful banquets must be dispensed with. At all times adultery and fornication must be execrated and avoided, but in these days marriage must be used in moderation. The flesh will obediently obey you in not going after someone else's business if it is used to dominating itself in its own business. Be careful not to change instead of reducing your pleasures. There are those who, instead of the usual wine, seek rare liquors, and, depriving themselves of grape liquor, they feel compensated with the most delicious juices of other fruits; As long as they are not meat, they diligently procure the most varied and succulent delicacies, and indulge in this time, as if it were the most appropriate, to delicacies that on another occasion it would be shameful to seek. In this way, the observance of Lent, instead of being a restraint on old passions, serves as an occasion for new delights. Watch as much as you can, brothers, so that these things do not enter, without realizing it, into your life. May fasting be linked to the economy. As we must avoid fullness of the belly, we must be alert to the incentives of gluttony. It is not about detesting any kind of food, but about restraining carnal pleasure.

Esau was not reproved for eating bull meat or fattened birds, but for immoderately craving lentils. Saint David repented for having desired water more than was right. Therefore, our body should not be repaired, or rather sustained, on fasting days with expensive and difficult to find foods, but with common and cheaper ones. 3. In these days, our prayer ascends to heaven with the help of pious alms and sparing fasts, since it is not impudent for a man to ask God for mercy if he has not denied it to another man and if the serene look of the heart of the one who asks is not disturbed by the confusing images of carnal delights. Let our prayer be chaste, lest we desire not what charity seeks, but what passion desires; Let us avoid asking for any evil for our enemies, lest, being able to harm them or take revenge on them, we show our cruelty in prayer. Just as we attain the readiness to pray through almsgiving and fasting, so our prayer itself becomes almsgiving when it rises not only for friends, but even for enemies, and abstains from anger, hatred and other pernicious vices. If we abstain from food, how much more must she abstain from poisons! Furthermore, although we regain strength by taking some foods in due time, we should never offer her the aforementioned foods. Let yours be a perpetual fast.

When the bodies of the faithful are subjected to servitude, any decrease in bodily pleasure benefits the health of the spirit. For this reason, you should avoid looking for expensive delicacies, or simply replace them with others, sometimes more exquisite, under the excuse of not eating meat. The mortification of the body and its reduction to servitude entails reducing pleasures, not exchanging them for others. What does one food or another matter if the fault lies in the immoderate desire for it? The divine voice condemned the Israelites for craving not only meat, but also some fruits and foods from the field. And Esau lost his birthright not for a pork chop, but for a stew of only lentils. I am going to omit what the hungry Lord responded to the tempter regarding the same bread, he who most certainly did not tame his flesh as if it rebelled against him, but mercifully indicated to us what we should respond to such temptations. You married people also should not throw on deaf ears, especially at this time, the Apostle's advice to temporarily abstain from prayer. It would be too impudent not to do now what is useful to do at all times. I think that it should not be too heavy a burden for married people to do in these solemn days of annual observance what widows have professed for a part of their life and what holy virgins have accepted for all of it. 2. In any case, it is almost a duty to increase alms on these dates. Is there a fairer way to spend what you save through your abstinence than by doing mercy? And is there anything more perverse than handing over to the custody of ever-present greed or to the consumption of postponed lust what was underspent due to abstinence? Consider, then, to whom you owe what you deprive yourself of, so that mercy may add to charity what temperance subtracts from pleasure. What can we say now about that work of mercy that does not involve removing anything from the pantry or the wallet, but only extracting from the heart what begins to be more harmful if it remains inside than if it comes out? I mean anger against anyone nestled in the heart. Is there anything more foolish than avoiding the external enemy and retaining another much worse one deep within? Therefore the Apostle says: Let not the sun set on your wrath: adding next: And leave no room for the devil, as if he did this who did not immediately cast out the wrath of his soul, giving the devil access through it, as if it were a door. The first thing you have to achieve is,

Therefore, do not let the setting of this sun catch you angry, so that the sun of justice does not abandon the soul itself. But, if anger has remained in anyone's chest until today, expel it at least now, as the day of the passion of the Lord is approaching, who was not angry against his murderers, for whom he shed supplications and blood when he hung on the tree. If, until these holy days, anger has resisted with great impudence in the heart of any of you, let it be cast out from there at least now, so that prayer may advance safely, without stumbles, without shocks, and may not have to remain silent under the pangs of conscience when the time comes to say: Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. Without a doubt, you must ask that something not be taken into account and that something be granted to you. Forgive, then, and you will be forgiven; Give, and it will be given to you. These are things, brothers, that you must do and meditate perpetually, even if I tell you nothing. As my voice, at the service of so many divine testimonies, also feels supported by the celebration of this day, I do not have to fear that any of you will despise me, or rather the Lord of all in my person; On the contrary, I must hope that his flock, recognizing that what was said are his words, listens to him, to be, in turn, listened to effectively.

1. The solemn time has come to exhort your charity to think more seriously about the soul and to mortify the body. These forty days are sacred to the entire globe of the earth, which as Easter approaches celebrates with devotion, worthy of being proclaimed throughout the entire world, which God reconciles to himself in Christ. If there is any enmity that should never have been born or, at least, should have died later, but that was capable of lasting in the lives of the brothers until this date, whether due to negligence, obstinacy or shame, the result not of modesty, but of pride, let it at least now cease to exist. Such feuds should never have lasted until sunset; That is why it is not too much to ask that, after repeated rises and falls, they too will someday reach their twilight, without any new emergence setting them in motion. The dumped forgets to put an end to enmities; The obstinate does not want to grant forgiveness when asked; The shameful proud disdains to ask for forgiveness. 1. Quadragesimali observatione finiendae inimicitiae. Tria vitia, quibus inimicitiae vivunt.—Solemne tempus advenit, quando de anima attentius cogitanda et corpore punishando vestram commoneam Caritatem. Hi sunt enim quadraginta dies sacratissimi toto orbe terrarum, quos propinquante Pascha universus mundus, quem Deus in Christo reconciliat sibi, praedicanda devotione concelebrat. Si quae inimicitiae, quae vel nasci non debuerunt, vel cyto mori debuerunt, et tamen usque ad hoc tempus sive neglegentia, sive pertinacia, sive non modesta, sed superba verecundia, Inter fratres perdurare potuerunt; saltem finiantur mode. Super quas sol non debuit occidere (cf. Eph 4:26), saltem post multos solis ortus et occasus, etiam ipsae suo tandem aliquando exstinguantur occasu, nec ulterius ullo renoventur exortu. Neglegens inicitias finiré obliviscitur; pertinax veniam non vult concede, cum rogatur; superbe verecundus veniam petere dedignatur, His tribus vitiis inimicitiae vivunt: sed animas in quibus non moriuntur, occidunt. milde. Whoever recognizes that he neglects harmony, wake up and shake off the torpor; He who wishes to be an executor towards his debtor, should think that he is an executor of God; He who is ashamed to ask his brother's forgiveness, overcome, through holy fear, perverse modesty, so that, these fatal enmities being extinguished, they being dead, you may live. All this is done by charity, which acts without malice. To the extent that you have charity, my brothers, exercise it by living well, and, to the extent that you lack it, obtain it through prayer. 2. In these days, our prayers must be more fervent; and so that they are helped with the pertinent support, let us also give alms with greater fervor. Add to what we already gave what we saved by fasting and abstaining from customary foods. If someone, due to some bodily need or diet, cannot abstain from anything, nor, therefore, although his alms should be more generous, add to what he usually gives to the poor what he takes from himself, due to the fact that he deprives himself of nothing, let him show his mercy by giving to the poor; If you cannot help your prayers with bodily mortification, introduce into the heart of the poor a more generous alms than can beg for him. In the sacred Scriptures we find this excellent advice, worthy of being followed: Introduce alms into the heart of the poor, and they will pray for you. 3. We also admonish those who abstain from meats not to move away from the pots in which they were cooked as submissa prudentia. Qui se concordiae recolit neglectorem, excutiat expergiscendo torporem: qui se cupit esse sui debitoris exactrem, Dei se cogitet debitorem: qui erubescit petere ut sibi frater ignoscat, vincat per bonum timorem malum divinorem: ut noxiis inimicitiis finitis, ut eis mortuis, vos vivatís. Totum hoc caritas agit, quae non agit perperam (cf. 1 Cor 13:4). Caritas, fratres mei, in quantum adest, exerceatur bene vivir; in quantum autem minus est, impetretur petendo. 2. Orationes eleemosynis adminkulandae.—Ut autem nostrae orationes congruis adminiculis adiuventur, quoniam in his diebus ferventiores eas habere debenmus; etiam eleemosynas ferventius erogemus. Ipsis [1047] adiciatur, quod nobis eiunando et a cibis solitis abstinendo detrahitur.

Quamvis eas debeat largiores habere, qui propter aliquam necessitatem corporis sui et consuetudinem alimentarum non potest abstinere, ut hoc addat pauperi, quod sibi detrahit: sed ideo pius det pauperi, quia sibi non detrahit; ut quoniam minus potest orationes suas punishmente corporis adiuvare, abundantiorem in corde pauperis includat eleemosynam, quae pro illo possit orare. De Scripturis sanctis hoc est saluberrimum amplectendumque consilium: Include, inquit, eleemosynam in corde pauperis, et haec pro te exorabit (Ecdi 29,15). 3. Abstinentia qualis suscipienda.—Admonemus etiam eos qui se a carnibus abstinent. ne vasa in quibus sunt coctae tanquam immunda

if they were unclean. Thus says the Apostle: All things are pure to the pure. What, according to sound doctrine, is done in this observance is not to avoid impurity, but to tame concupiscence. Hence, those who abstain from meat to seek other delicacies of more delicate preparation and higher prices fall into a serious error. That is not embracing abstinence, but changing the object of pleasure 1. How can we say that they give to the poor what they themselves deprive themselves of to those who give up the ordinary delicacy, but increase their expenses in buying others? Therefore, during these days, fast more frequently and, as you live more sparingly, give more generously to those in need. These dates also demand abstaining from the use of marriage. Temporarily, says the Apostle, to vacate prayer; then return to what you were before, so that Satan does not tempt you because of your incontinence. This is not arduous and difficult for a few days for the faithful married people, since the holy widows embraced it at a precise moment in their life until the end of it and the holy virgins fulfill it throughout their entire existence. But in any situation, let devotion boil and pride be repressed. Let no one rejoice in his generosity in such a way as to lose the good of humility. All the other gifts of God do not bring any benefit if the bond of charity does not exist. devitent. Sic enim loquens Apostolus ait: Omnia munda muñáis (Tit 1,15). Quod enim fit in huiusmodi observationibus sana doctrina, non fit causa immunditiae devítandae, sed concupiscentiae refrenandae. Unde et illi qui sic se a carnibus temperant, ut alias escás et difficilioris praeparationis et pretii maioris inquirant, multum errant. Non enim est hoc suscipere abstinentiam, sed mutare luxuriam. Quomodo istis dicturi sumus, ut quod sibi detrahunt dent pauperi; a quibus solitus ita cibus relinquitur, ut in alio comparing sumptus augeatur? This is ergo his diebus et crebrius ieiunantes, et vobis parcius impendentes, et egenis largius tribuntes. A coniugali quoque concubitu, hi dies postulant continentiam: Ad tempus, ait Apostolus, ut vacetis orationi: et iterum revertimini in idipsum, ne temptet vos satanás propter intemperantiam vestram (1 Cor 7,5). Non est hoc arduum atque difficile diebus paucis fidelibus coniugatis, quod a certo vitae article usque in finem sanctae viduae susceperunt, quod tota vita sanctae virgines faciunt.

Atque in his omnibus ferveat devotio, compress elatio. Nemo sic gaudeat de bono largitatis, ut bonum amittat humilitatis. Omnia vero cetera Dei dona non faciunt prodesse aliquid, nisi adsit vinculum caritatis. Here Augustine criticizes those who take abstinence from meat so far that they even distance themselves from the pots in which they are cooked, as if they too were unclean (see note 1 to sermon 208), while, on the other hand, they seek all kinds of delicacies in eating and drinking. Augustine reminds them that the practice of abstinence is not because the flesh is considered unclean, but because it is a good means of taming concupiscence. The same way of reasoning appears again in semen 210,10.

1. The solemn time has arrived that invites us to humble our souls and mortify our bodies through prayer and fasting with greater intensity than at any other time. Why does it take place when the solemnity of the Lord's passion approaches? What is the mystery that is celebrated in the number of forty days? 'Since these questions intrigue some, I have proposed to present to your charity what the Lord deigns to allow me to tell you on the matter. Their faith and piety—since we know that they are motivated not by the desire to litigate, but to know—will be of great help to us so that God grants us something to say. 2. The first question they usually ask is this: "Why did the same Lord Jesus Christ, who, having taken a human body, becoming man, manifested himself to men to give us an example of how to live and die and a proof of the resurrection, fasted not before, but after having been baptized?" Thus it is written in the Gospel: Having been baptized, he immediately came out of the water; and behold, the heavens will be SERMO

CAPOT I.—1. In Quadragesima consideradum anni tempus et dierum numerus.—Solemne tempus advenit, quod amplius quam per anni cetera spatia, nos orationibus atque ieiuniis animam humiliare, et corpus penare commoneat. Cur autem hoc propinquante solemnitate Dominicae passionis, et cur quadragesimi numeri mysterio celebretur, quoniam solet moveré nonnullos, merit de hac re quod digandum Dominus donare dignitus est, ad vestram Caritatem proferre suscipimus. Quos autem ista non ad litigandum, sed ad cognoscendum quaerere novimus, eorum fide atque pietate multum adiuvamur, ut saying impetrare possimus. [1048] 2. Quaestio: Cur eo tempore ieiunetur, ante Baptismi celebrationem. I answer.—Hoc enim solet faceré quaestionem, cur ipse Dominus Iesus Christus, qui humano corpore assumpto ad hoc utique hominibus homo factus apparuit, ut nobis et vivirdi et moriendi et resurgendi praeberet exemplum, non antequam baptizaretur, sed posteaquam baptizatus est ieiunavit. Sic enim scriptum est in Gospel: Baptizatus autem confestim ascendit de aqua; et ecce aperti sunt ei caeli,

opened, and he saw the Spirit of God descend upon him. And a voice said from heaven: "This is my beloved son, in whom I am well pleased." Then Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. And after he had fasted for forty days, he became hungry. We, on the other hand, fast with those who are to be baptized on the dates prior to their baptism, which takes place at the beginning of Easter Day, after which we suspend fasts for •fifty days. Which could be a cause for confusion if it were only permitted to administer and receive baptism on the solemnity of Easter. But since, by the grace of God, who granted us the power to be his children, it is allowed to receive it at any time of the year, remaining at the mercy of the need or will of each one 2, and, on the other hand, the annual celebration of the passion of the Lord is only allowed to be celebrated on a day that is called Easter, without a doubt the sacrament of baptism must be separated from Easter. Baptism can be received on any date; Easter is only licit to celebrate in a specific way. That is conferred to grant a new life; This is recommended to perpetuate the memory of the mysteries of religion. But the fact that a considerably greater number of candidates for baptism attend on that day is not because saving grace is more abundant on it, but because the greater joy of the festival invites it. 3. Should we not also distinguish the baptism of John,

that received then by Christ, that of Christ, which those who believe in him receive? Although Christ is better than the Christian, that baptism with which Christ was baptized is not better than the other with which the Christian is baptized; On the contrary, for the same reason, the latter, since it is Christ's, is put before the former. In fact, John baptized Christ, even though he confessed himself inferior to him; The Christian, on the other hand, is baptized by Christ, who showed himself to be superior even to John. In the same way, the circumcision of the flesh, although Christ also submitted to it, but which no Christian practices today, is inferior to the mystery of the resurrection of the Lord, by which the Christian is circumcised to put off the old life according to the flesh, according to what the Apostle says: As Christ was raised from the dead to the glory of the Father, so we too must walk in newness of life. The same thing happens with the ancient Passover, which was ordered to be celebrated by sacrificing a lamb; Not because Christ celebrated it with his disciples is it better than our Easter, in which Christ was sacrificed. He sought to give us an example of humility and devotion when upon coming he deigned to undertake even those rites in which his arrival was pre-announced. In this way he showed how much pity it is appropriate for us to accept those others in which it is announced that he has already come. Because Christ fasted immediately after receiving baptism, we are not to believe that he established a standard of observance, as if fasting necessarily had to be done after the reception of Christ's baptism.

Et cum ieiunasset quadraginta diebus et quadraginta noctibus, postea esuriit (Mt 3,16-17; 4,2). Sed quod ad illum diem longe maior baptizadorum numerus confluit, non gratia uberior salutis hic distat, sed laetitia maior festivitatis invitation. CAPOT II.—3. Baptismus Ioannis to Baptismo Christi discernendus. Here Augustine explains what the praxis of the ancient Church was regarding baptism. Although there was no problem to baptize on any date, when the need or particular reasons demanded it, it was usual, however, for the sacrament to be administered on the Easter feast; more specifically, in the Easter Vigil, to show in this way that baptism was integrated into the Paschal Mystery,

Sacramenta veteris Legis cur suscepit Christus. Quando temptatio infertur, ieiunandum.—Quid quod etiam baptismus Ioannis, quem tune Christus accepit, a baptismo ipsius Christi, quem fideles eius accipiunt, discernendus est; nec ideo ille quo baptizatus est Christus, melior est isto quo baptizatur christianus, quia christiano melior est Christus; sed ideo magis istud baptismum, quia Christi est, illi praeponitur? Ioannes enim baptizavit Christum, cum se Christo confiteretur minorem: Christus autem baptizat christianum, qui se ostendit et Ioanne maiorem. Sicut circumcisione carnis, quamvis eam et Christus accepit, et nemo christianus nunc accipit, melius est sacramentum resurrectionis Christi, quo ad expoliandam carnalem ac veterem vitam circumeiditur christianus, ut audit Apostolum dicentem: Sicut Christus resurrexit a mortuis per gloriam Patris, sic et nos in novitate vitae ambulemus (Rom 6,4). Sicut ipsum vetus Pascha, quod agni occisione celebrare praeceptum est, non ideo quia hoc cum discipulis celebravit Christus, melius est quam Pascha nostrum, quo immolatus est Christus. Pertinuit enim ad praebendum nobis humilitatis et devotionis exemplum, ut illa etiam sacramenta veniens suscipere digretur, quibus venturus ipse praenuntiabatur: ut bine osten[1049]deret quanta religione nos oportet haec suscipere sacramenta, quibus iam venisse nuntiatur. Non ergo quia Christus post acceptum Ioannis baptismum continuo ieiunavit, tanquam regulam obser-

to. With his example he showed us that we should fast, especially if we were to enter into a fierce fight with the tempter. This is the reason why Christ, who deigned to be born as a man, did not reject being tempted as a man: so that the Christian, trained by his example, can overcome the tempter. Fasting must be done, therefore, either immediately after baptism or after an indeterminate period of time, when man finds himself in this type of fight against temptation, so that the body can fulfill its militia with mortification and the soul can achieve victory with its humiliation. In the case of the Lord, the reason for the fast was not the baptism in the Jordan, but the temptation of the devil. 4. This is the reason why we fast before the solemnity of the Lord's passion and why we abandon fasting for the following fifty days3. Everyone who fasts properly either seeks to humiliate his soul, from an unfeigned faith, with the groaning of prayer and bodily mortification, or he goes from carnal pleasure to feeling hunger and thirst, because, moved by some spiritual lack, his gaze is set on the enjoyment of truth and wisdom. The Lord spoke about both types of fasting to those who asked him why his disciples did not fast. Regarding the first, which looks at the humiliation of the soul, he said: The husband's friends cannot cry while the husband is with them. But the time will come when it will be taken away from them, and then fast-

ran. Of the other who seeks to feed the mind, he said next: No one adds a patch of new cloth to an old garment, so that the tear does not become greater; Nor does anyone put new wine into old wineskins, lest the wineskins break and the wine spill out, but the new wine is poured into new wineskins, and thus both are preserved. So, since our husband has been taken from us, we, his children, must cry. The most beautiful, in appearance, of the sons of men, whose grace is manifested in his lips, when he fell into the clutches of his persecutors, he lacked beauty and decorum, and his life was cut off from the earth. It is right for us to cry if we burn with the desire to see him. Blessed are those who had the possibility of having him among them before his passion, questioning him at will and listening to him as they should. The patriarchs longed to see such days, and did not see them, before their coming. They belonged to another economy, by virtue of which they had to announce his coming, but not contemplate him once he arrived. Of them he says, speaking to the disciples: Many righteous people and prophets wanted to see what you see, and they did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and they did not hear it. In us, however, what he also says has been fulfilled: The days will come when you will want to see one of these, and you will not be able to. 5. Who does not burn in the flames of such a holy desire? Who doesn't cry in this situation? Who doesn't get tired from crying so much? Who will not say: My tears are my bread night and day,

vationis dedisse credendus est, ut post ipsius Christi Baptismum acceptum, continuo ieiunare necesse sit: sed plañe illo exemplo docuit ieiunandum esse, quando forte acriore luctamine cum temptatore confligimus. Ob hoc enim Christus, qui sicut homo dignitatus est nasci, non respuit sicut homo temptari, ut christianus magisterio eius instructus non possit a temptatore surpass. Sive ergo continuo post Baptismum, sive quolibet intervallo temporis interposito, quando simile praelium temptationis infertur homini, ieiunandum est: ut et corpus impleat de punishtíone militiam, et animus impetret de humiliatione victoriam. In illo ergo dominico exemplo illius causa ieiunii, non Iordanis tinctio, sed diaboli temptatio Fuit. CAPUT III.—4. Cur Quadragesimale ieiunium ante Pascha. Ablato sponso filiis lugendum.—Cur autem nos ante solemnitatem passionis Dominicae ieiunemus, et illa ieiuniorum relaxatio fiftieth die perficiatur, haec ratio est. Omnis qui recte ieiunat, aut animam suam in gemitu orationis et punishtíone corporis humiliat ex fide non ficta; aut ab illecebra carnali inopia aliqua spirituali veritatis et sapientiae delectatione suspensa, ad famem sitimque sentienm descendit eius intentio. De utroque ieiunii genere Dominus responderit interrogantibus cur discipuli eius non ieiunarent. Nam de illo primo, quod habet animae humiliationem: Non possunt, inquit, lugere filii sponsi, quamdiu cum eis est sponsus. Sed veniet hora when auferetur ab eis sponsus, et tune

ieiunabunt. De illo autem altero, quod habet epulas mentís, ita consequenter locutus est: Nemo assuit pannum novutn vestímento veten, ne maior scissura fiat: ñeque mittunt vinum novum in utres veteres, ne et utres rumpantur, et vinum effundatur; sed vinum novum in utres novos mittunt, et utraque servantur (Mt 9,15-17). Proinde quia iam sponsus ablatus est, utique nobis filiis illius pulchri sponsi, lugendum est. Speciosus enim forma prae filiis hominum, cuius diffusa gratia in labiis eius (cf. Ps 44,3), Inter manus persequentium non habuit speciem ñeque decorem, et ablata est de terra vita eius (cf. Is 53,2.8). Et recte lugemus, si flagramus desiderio eius. Beati quibus eum licuit ante passionem tune habere praesentem, interrogare sicut vellent, et audire sicut audire debenent. Illos dies concupierunt videre paires ante adventum eius, ñeque viderunt; quia in alia dispensatione fuerant ordinati, per quos venturus annuntiaretur, non a quibus veniens audiretur. Of his enim ad disciples loquitur they say: Multi iusti et Prophetae voluerunt videre quae vos videtis, et non viderunt; et audire quae auditis, et non audierunt (Mt 13, 17). In no[1050]bis autem íllud impletum est, quod ipse itidem dicit: Venient dies, quando desiderabitis videre unum de diebus istis, et non poteritis (Luke 17,22). CAPUT IV.—5. Cur gemendum et ieiunandum in hac vita.—Quis non sancti desiderii flamma uratur? quis non hic lugeat? quis non laboret in gemitu suo? quis non dicat: Factae sunt mihi lacrimae meae pañis die

while I am told daily: "Where is your God"? We certainly believe in the one who is already seated at the right hand of God, but while we live in this body we are pilgrims far from him, and we cannot manifest it to those who, out of doubt or denial, tell us: Where is your God? No wonder his Apostle wanted to dissolve and be with him; He did not consider remaining in the flesh as what was best for himself, but rather as a necessity for us. Where the thoughts of mortals are timid, our cautions are also uncertain, because this earthly abode oppresses the mind in its much thinking. Hence human life on earth is a temptation and that in the night of this world the lion circles around looking for someone to devour. Not the lion of the tribe of Judah, our king, but the devil, our enemy. Our king, appropriating in his one person the figures of those four animals from the Apocalypse of John, was born as a man, behaved like a lion, was sacrificed like a calf and flew like an eagle. He flew on the wings of the wind and made darkness his hidden abode. He made the darkness and the night appeared, in which all the beasts of the forest walk: the lions' cubs roaring, that is, the tempters that the devil uses to look for someone to devour, but who have no power except over those over whom they are granted, as indicated in the psalm below: Asking God for food for himself. Who will not feel filled with fear in the night of this century, so dangerous and so full of temptations? Who will not feel shaken up

in the depths of his being at the possibility of being considered worthy of being handed over to the jaws of such a cruel enemy to be devoured? Therefore, we must fast and pray. 6. And when should we do it better and with greater intensity than as the solemnity of the Lord's passion approaches? In that annual celebration, in a certain way, the memory of that night is re-sculpted in us so that it is not erased by oblivion, and the enemy, roaring and devouring, does not find us asleep; not physically, but in the spirit. The very passion of the Lord, what else did he put before our eyes, but the temptation that is this life, leaning precisely on Christ Jesus, our head? This is the reason why, as the time of his death approached, he said to Peter: Satan has desired to sift you like wheat; But I have prayed for you, Peter, so that your faith may not fail; Go and comfort your brothers. And he certainly comforted us with his apostolate, his martyrdom and his letters. In them he taught us with the comfort of prophecy, similar to a lamp that shines in the night, to maintain cautious vigilance by exhorting us to fear the night of which I am speaking. We have, he says, the word of the prophets, which is more certain, and you do well to fix your eyes on it like a lamp that shines in a dark place until the day comes, and the star rises in your hearts. 7. Therefore, keep your loins girded and your lamps lit. Let us be like men who wait for the return of their Lord from the wedding. Let us not repeat to each other: Let us eat

A little, he said, and you will not see me; another little bit, and you will see me. This is the moment of the one who said: You will be sad; The world, on the other hand, will rejoice. In other words: this life, in which we are pilgrims far from the Lord, is full of temptations. But I will see you again, he said, and your heart will be filled with joy, and your joy no one will take away from you. In any case, now we also enjoy this hope, based on the utmost fidelity of the one who has promised it, until the supreme joy of being like him comes because we will see him as he is; joy that no one will take away from us. As a pleasant and free token of that hope we have received the Holy Spirit, who works in our hearts the unspeakable groanings that are holy desires. As the prophet Isaiah says: we have conceived and given birth to the spirit of salvation. The Lord also says: a woman, when she is about to give birth, becomes sad, because her day has come; But, once he has given birth to the creature, his joy is great, because a man has come into the world. This will be the joy that no one will take away from us: the one through which we will pass through conception, the result of faith, to eternal light. Now, while the day of childbirth lasts, let us fast and pray. 8. That is what the entire body of Christ spread throughout the world does, that is, the universal Church, the being

only one who speaks in the psalm: From the ends of the earth I cried to you when my heart was in trouble. From here it is clear why Lent was instituted as a solemnity that celebrates this humiliation. The Church, which cries out from the ends of the earth when its heart is in trouble, cries out from the four parts of the world, which Scripture also mentions frequently: east and west, north and south. For all this, the decalogue of the law was promulgated, which should no longer inspire fear due to its letter, but must be fulfilled through the grace of charity. We know that 4 multiplied by 10 equals 40. But now we are still involved in the fatigue of temptation, needing forgiveness of sins. Who will perfectly fulfill that of you will have no perverse desires? Hence the need to fast and pray, but without ceasing to do good. In the end, that reward will be granted to that work that is called a denarius. As a ternary it is named after 3, a quaternary after 4, a denarius is named after 10, a number that, added to 40, expresses the reward for work. dearly beloved, in the name of Christ, to make God propitious with daily fasting, more generous alms and more fervent prayers. It is the time in which husbands must abstain from their wives, and wives from their husbands, to dedicate themselves to prayer, which they should do throughout the year on certain dates, and the more frequently, the better, since whoever desires without moderation what has been granted to him, offends the one who has granted it. An action is all the more spiritual the further the soul that performs it is removed from carnal pleasure. Moses, the minister of the law, fasted for forty days; For forty days Elijah, the greatest of the prophets, also fasted, and for forty days also the Lord, of whom the law and the prophets testified. We, who cannot endure such a long fast, spending, as they did, so many days and nights without tasting food, let us at least do what we can. There are those who during Lent claim to be more lovers of pleasure than of piety; rather than mortifying old passions, they seek new delicacies. With abundant and expensive provisions of various fruits they try to surpass the flavors and varieties of any other foods. They fear, as if they were unclean, the pots in which meat is cooked 6, and they do not fear lust and gluttony in theirs. They fast, but not to moderate their accustomed voracity with temperance, but to increase, by postponing satiating it, their immoderate appetite. Well, when the time for food arrives, they rush over the sumptuous tables like beasts over the manger. With the abundant food they bury their hearts and expand their bellies, and with strange and artificial varieties of condiments they stimulate gluttony in case abundance has it choked. Finally, it is sexus ab hac re penitus immunia membra Deo dicata servare. Puto non esse magnum, ut tota Paschali solemnitate possit coniugum castitas, quod potest tota vita virginitas. Fasting is something the Christian misses. Voluntary mortification serves as sustenance for those who have nothing. The voluntary scarcity of the rich is necessary abundance for the poor. The merciful availability for forgiveness also resides in the tamed and humble soul. Ask for forgiveness whoever committed the offense; Let him who received it grant it, so as not to fall into the hands of Satan, whose triumph is discord among Christians. This cleansing involves great gain, which consists of forgiving your fellow servant so that your master may forgive you. The heavenly teacher recommended both things to his disciples when he said to them: Forgive, and you will be forgiven; Give, and it will be given to you. Remember that servant from whom the lord once again demanded all the debt that he had forgiven him because he did not show his fellow servant, who owed him a hundred denarii, the same mercy that he received when ten thousand talents were forgiven. There is no excuse for not carrying out these types of good actions, since wanting is already power. Someone may say: "I cannot fast, otherwise my stomach hurts." You can also say: "I want to give something to a poor person, but I don't have anything"; or: "I have so little that I fear I will find myself in need if I give something." Frequently, also in these cases, men invent false excuses, because they do not find them true. But who is there who says: "I did not grant forgiveness to those who asked me because my health did not allow it or because I lacked the hand to extend"? Forgive, to be forgiven. Here the meat has nothing to do; no member of the flesh itself comes to the aid of the soul to fulfill what is asked of it. 3. Maybe it was you who offended him; You want to reconcile with him and say: "Brother, forgive me for the offense I did to you." But he doesn't want to forgive you, he doesn't want to forget the debt, he doesn't want to forgive you what you owe him. He'll figure it out when he goes to pray! He, who did not want to forgive you your offense, what will he do when he goes to recite the prayer? What will he do? Say: Our Father who art in heaven. Continue saying: Let your name be hallowed. Say again: Your kingdom come. Continue: Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven. Go ahead!: Give us today our daily bread. You have said all that; Pay attention now, lest you want to skip what comes next and change it to something else. There is no other path through which you can pass; there you find yourself detained. Say, then, and say it sincerely: Forgive us our debts. Or keep it quiet, if you have no reason to say it. But where is what the Apostle said: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth does not dwell in us? If, then, your conscience bothers you because of your fragility and the abundance of iniquity is manifested everywhere in this world, say: Forgive us our debts. But consider what follows. You who did not want to forgive your brother, you are going to say: Just as we also forgive our debtors. Or are you going to keep those words to yourself? If you keep quiet about them, you will receive nothing, and if you say them, you say a falsehood. Tell them, then; and say them so that they are true; But how can they be true, if you did not want to forgive your brother's sin? 3. Forte peccasti in illum, uis cum illo concordare, uis ei dicere: Frater, ignosce mihi, peccaui in te. Ille non uult ignoscere, non uult dimitiere debitum; quod ei deben, non uult tibi dimittere. Ipse obseruet, quando habet orare. Quando uenturus est, qui tibi noluit dimittere quod in eum forte peccasti, quando uenturus est ad orationem, quid facturus est? Dicat: Pater noster qui es in caelis. Dicat, accesat: Sanctificetur nomen tuum. Adduc dec: [162] Adueniat regnum tuum. Sequete: Fiat uoluntas tua sicut in cáelo et in terra. Adhuc ambula: Vanem nostrum cottidianum da nobis hodie. Dixisti. Quod sequitur uide ne forte uelis transcenderé et aliud dicete. Non est qua traniré possis, ibi teneris. Et ubi est illud quod idem apostolus dixit: Si dixerimus quia peccatum non habemus, nos ipsos decipimus et neritas in nobis non est (1 lo 1,8)?

Si autem mordet conscientia fragilitatis et in hoc saeculo ubique abundantia iniquitatis, dic ergo: Dimitte nobis debita nostra. Be quod sequitur uide. Noluisti enim dimittere peccatum fratri tuo et dicturus is: Sicut et nos dimittimus debitoribus nostris (Mt 6,912)? Is it not a dictator? If non is dicturus, nihil is accepturus; If autem dicturus, falsum is dicturus. Ergo dic et uerum dic. Quomodo dicturus es uerum qui fratri tuo noluisti relaxare peccatum?
Fraternal harmony and forgiveness of offenses

4. I have admonished a class of people; Now I am going to console you, whoever you are—if there is any—; to you who said to your brother: "Forgive me who has offended you"; If you said it with all your heart, with authentic humility, with unfeigned charity, just as God sees it in your heart, the place from which those words came, even if he doesn't want to forgive you, don't worry. Both of you are servants, you both have the same Lord; If you are in debt to your fellow servant and he does not want to forgive you, go to the common Lord. Let the servant demand, if he can, what the Lord has forgiven you. I say more: I have admonished anyone who does not want to forgive his brother to do the same thing that he did not want when he asks for forgiveness, lest when he prays he does not receive what he desires. And to the one who asked his brother for forgiveness for the offense committed and did not receive it, I have urged him to be sure of receiving from his Lord what he did not get from his brother. I still have something to add. You often hear people say: "Your brother offended you and he doesn't want to ask for your forgiveness." May God uproot such words from his field, that is, from your hearts! How numerous are those who, conscious of having offended their brothers, refuse to say: "Forgive me"! They were not ashamed to sin, and they are ashamed to ask for forgiveness; They did not feel shame in the face of evil, and they feel shame in the face of humility. To these, above all, my exhortation is addressed. Those of you who are in discord with your brothers and, collected within your hearts, have examined yourselves and have issued a

fair judgment recognizing that you should not have done what you did or said what you said, ask your brothers for forgiveness, do with them what the Apostle says: Forgiving each other, as God forgave you in Christ; Do it, don't be ashamed to ask for forgiveness. I say it, then, to everyone: men and women, young and old, laymen and clerics, and even to myself. Let us all hear it, let us all fear. If we have offended our brothers, if we are still given a margin of time to live, it is because death has not yet come to us; and, if we still live, we have not yet been condemned. As long as life lasts, let us do what our Father, who will be the divine judge, commands us; Let us ask forgiveness from our brothers, whom we may have offended in some way and harmed in some way. There are humble people according to the standards of this world who become arrogant if you ask for their forgiveness. Topic: The meaning of Lent. Location: Unknown. Date: In Lent.

In his passion, our Lord Jesus Christ places before our eyes the fatigues and pains of the present world; in his resurrection, the eternal and happy life of the future world. Let us tolerate the present and hope for the future. Therefore, on these dates we find ourselves in the days that signify the fatigues of the present century—the mortification of our souls with fasting and Lenten practices—; In the near future, however, we mean the days of the future century, which we have not yet reached. I said “we mean”, not “we have”. Therefore, until the day of the passion we are in a time of contrition; after the resurrection, in a time of praise. So, then, in that life, in the kingdom of God, our occupation will be this: to see, to love, to praise. Topic: The delivery of the symbol. Location: Hippo. Date: Two or three weeks before Easter.

1. It is time for you to receive the symbol, which contains, in brief, everything you believe for your eternal salvation. At the origin of the term "symbol" is a similarity; It is, therefore, a metaphorical term. The merchants establish among themselves a symbol thanks to which their group is held together by a pact of fidelity2. Your society is also a business of spiritual things, to be similar to the merchants who search for the precious stone. This is none other than charity, which will be poured into your hearts by the Holy Spirit who will be given to you. It is reached through the faith contained in this symbol, believing in God the Father almighty, invisible, immortal, king of the ages, creator of the visible and invisible and whatever sound reason and the authority of the Holy Scriptures rightly affirm about him. But do not separate the Son of God from that excellence, for affirming these things of the Father does not entail excluding them from him who said: I and the Father are one and the same thing, and from whom the Apostle affirms: Who, existing in the form of God, did not consider it a plunder to be equal to God. 1. To the extent that my age and my status as a novice allow it, to the extent that I have also learned the ministry that has been entrusted to me and as a result of the love that I profess for you, having ascended as a minister to the altar to which you are going to approach, I cannot deprive you of the favor of my word. The Apostle says: If you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that the Lord raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes for righteousness and with the mouth one confesses for salvation. The symbol builds in you what you must believe and confess in order to achieve salvation. What you are soon going to receive, commit to memory and utter verbally, is nothing new to you or something you have never heard before. In fact, in a variety of ways you often hear it both in Holy Scripture and in the sermons of the Church. Despite this, everything must be given to you together, briefly summarized and logically ordered to build your faith, facilitate recitation and not burden your memory too much. These are the things that, without changing anything, you must retain and then recite by heart. SERMO

After these introductory words, the entire symbol must be recited, without inserting any comments: I believe in God the Father almighty, etc. You know that the symbol is not usually written. Having said that, this explanation must be added: 2. What you have just heard in brief words you must not only believe, but also commit it in its entirety to memory and proclaim it verbally. But since it must be defended against those who think differently and against the slaves of the devil, who lay snares against the faith when they hinder salvation, remember that believing that God is all-powerful includes that there is absolutely no nature that has not been created by him 2, And if he punishes the sin that he did not commit, it is because it disfigures the nature that he created. All visible and invisible creatures; all those who, like the angel and man, can participate, through the rational mind, in the immutable truth; everything that has life and sensitivity, even if it lacks understanding, such as all the animals that populate the earth, the water or the air, whether they are quadrupeds, reptiles, fish or birds; everything that, without having any understanding or sensitivity, lives in some way, like plants, which deepen their roots in the earth and when they germinate they sprout and grow; everything that occupies space by its mere corpulence, such as stones and

any element of the same mass of the world that is offered to sight and touch, all these things were made by the omnipotent, uniting the medium with the lower and the higher, and arranging everything created in the appropriate place and time. He did it, but not of any material that he had not done before. He did not give shape to a foreign matter, but he created it to give it shape. Whoever says that he could do nothing out of nothing, how do you think he who is all-powerful did it? Without a doubt, he denies his omnipotence who says that God would not have been able to make the world if he had not had the means. What omnipotence is that, if the poverty is so great that, like any craftsman, he cannot see the result of his work if the material that he did not make does not come to his aid? Whoever believes that God is all-powerful must purge his mind of all opinions and errors. This so-called formless matter of things, capable of receiving any form and subject to the action of the creator, can become anything as the creator pleases 3. God did not find it coeternal with himself and made the world from it; On the contrary, he made it out of absolute nothing, like the things he made of it. It did not even exist before the things themselves, which seem to have been made from it; For this reason, the almighty already made all things from nothing from the first moment, with which he made, at the same time, that from which he made them. Therefore, the matter of heaven and earth, since these things were created in the beginning, was concretized together with them. There was nothing prior to God doing what he did in the beginning; and yet the things were done

If, then, what he did at the beginning he did out of nothing, he also has the power to do whatever he wants with everything he made, since he is omnipotent. 3. And let the wicked not believe that God is not omnipotent because they do many things against his will, since even when they do what he does not want, he will make them all what he wants. In no way do they change or overcome his will: whether man is justly condemned or mercifully freed, the will of the omnipotent is always fulfilled. The only thing the omnipotent cannot do is what he does not want. He even uses the wicked, not according to their evil, but according to his own right will. As the wicked make perverse use of their good nature, that is, of a good work of God, so he, who is good, makes right use of his good works, so that the will of the almighty is never contrary. If he did not have it in his power to obtain justice and goodness from the wicked, he would in no way allow them to be born and live. He did not make them evil, although he made them men, since he created natures, not sins, which are against nature. I said that the only thing the omnipotent cannot do is what he does not want; And so that no one should think that I have been bold in affirming that there is something that the Almighty cannot do, the blessed Apostle said: If we do not believe, he remains faithful, because he cannot deny himself. But he can't because he doesn't want to, because he can't want it either. It is impossible for justice to want to do what is unjust, or for wisdom to want what is foolish, or for truth to want what is false. All of which warns us that there are many things that the almighty God cannot do, not only what the Apostle says, namely, that he cannot deny himself. Thus, everything that God is, he is because he wants; because he wills it, it is eternal, immutable, truthful, blessed and invincible. His disciples verified this with their own eyes and hands. Neither such great goodness could mock them nor could he who is the truth deceive them. For the sake of brevity, it is immediately added that he ascended into heaven. In fact, he remained with his disciples for forty days, to prevent such a great miracle, if it later escaped their eyes, from appearing to them as a fantasy. There he is now seated at the right hand of the Father, something that we must prudently contemplate with the eyes of faith so as not to think that he is immobile in some seat, without being allowed to stand up or walk. From the fact that Saint Stephen said that he was seeing him standing, it does not follow that he saw something that is not true nor did he throw away the words of this symbol. Far be it from you to think or say this! Saying that he was sitting there, he only wanted to signify his abode in that sublime and ineffable happiness. Hence the place of residence is also called a seat, as when we ask where So-and-So is and are answered: "In his seat." Especially about the servants of God it is often said: "For so many years he settled in this or that monastery," that is, he rested, he dwelt, he lived. Not even Holy Scripture ignores this way of speaking. what you desire, that you desire with all the strength of your mind. What else does the term competent mean if not jointly asking? Quid enim aliud The authenticity of the present sermon has been denied by some authors; Others prefer to see in it a model sermon of Augustine for beginner preachers. The translation does not respond to concipitis of the Maurine text, but rather to incipitis, as the same text suggests in a note. dor. We were the ones who had debts; so many sins. He came, who owed nothing, because he was sinless, and found us oppressed by harmful usury and worthy of condemnation, and, paying what he had not taken, he mercifully freed us from the everlasting debt. We had recognized the guilt and expected the punishment; He, without becoming a partner in our guilt, became a participant in the punishment and wanted to be the remitter, at the same time, of the guilt and the punishment. He is, therefore, the one who will deliver from usury and iniquity the souls of believers and from the hearts of each one of those who say: I believe I see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living. This land must be desired not with an earthly or dead heart, but with a living and in a certain way heavenly heart. It is to her that someone, burning with his love and singing with joy, says in another psalm: You are my hope, my portion in the land of the living. Those who mortify their members on earth to obtain life turn to her; not the members that constitute the connection of this worldly body, but those others that miserably weaken the virility of the soul. They are clearly enumerated and mentioned by the vessel of election, the apostle Paul, when he says: Mortify your earthly members: fornication, uncleanness, disorder, evil desires and covetousness, which is like serving idols. See what members you must mortify in this land of the dead who wish to live in that land of the living. Become members of Christ, so that you never deprive him of them to make them members of a prostitute.

1. Christ the Lord, who hears us together with the Father, deigned to pray for us to the Father. Is there anything more certain than our happiness, if the one who grants what we ask for prays for us? Christ is, in fact, man and God; He prays as a man, and as God grants what he asks. You must be clear that he attributes everything to the Father, because it is not the Father who comes from him, but he from the Father. He assigns everything to the source from which it derives. But he is also a source born from the Father; he is the source of life. Thus, the Father fountain begot a fountain. The source begat another source, but the source that begets and the source begotten are a single source; in the same way that the God who begets and the begotten, that is, the Son born of the Father, are one God. The Father is not the Son, the Son is not the Father; The Father does not proceed from the Son, but the Son does proceed from the Father; but, nevertheless, the Father and the Son are one thing because of the one substance and they are one God because of the inseparable divinity. If the words refer to the Father and Christ: It will be difficult for them to know you, the only true God, and the one you sent, Jesus Christ, that is, to know you and Jesus Christ as the only true God, it will be difficult to demonstrate that the Holy Spirit is also true God. The Holy Spirit was not overlooked, as it is implicit. It is not only the Spirit of the Father nor only the Spirit of the Son, but the Spirit of the Father and the Son. Therefore, although his name is kept silent, when the other two are named, he is understood in them, since he is the Spirit of both. I am going to bring a phrase from Scripture that makes you understand what I am saying. The Apostle says: No one knows the things of man except the spirit of man that dwells in him. What are

the things of man? Those that man thinks as a man; there he manifests himself properly as a man, in his thoughts. Does your spirit know my thoughts, or mine yours? No one knows the things of man except the spirit of man that dwells in him. That is what the Apostle said, and added: The same thing happens with the things of God; no one knows them except the Spirit of God. How do we understand this? It is an absolute statement. If the things of God are known to no one except the Spirit of God, then does the Son of God know them? Far from us this diabolical intellection; get away from us. So the Word of God does not know the things of God? So is the Son of God ignorant of the things of God? Does he by whom everything was made know the things of God? He knows them; but who knows them except the Spirit of God? Therefore, just as when you hear: No one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God, you do not exclude the Son, in the same way, when you hear: It is important that they know you, the only true God, and him whom you sent, Jesus Christ, you must not exclude the Holy Spirit. 3. Topic: The passion of the Lord. Location: Hippo. Date: A Good Friday before 420.

1. With all solemnity we read and celebrate the passion of the one who erased our sins with his blood to joyfully revive our memory through these annual practices and make our faith radiate greater clarity through the influx of people. Solemnity asks me to speak to you, to the extent that the Lord wants to grant it to me, about his passion. Certainly, insofar as he suffered from his enemies, our Lord deigned to leave us an example of patience for our salvation, useful for this life through which we must pass; so that, persona hominis dicit, quia deus homine maior est; aut ex persona geniti dicit, in honorem eius a quo genitus est. Plus non quaeratis: nam deus deum genuit, magnus aequalem genuit. Si deus verum deum non genuit, et magnus non aequalem genuit, monstrum genuit, non verum filium. Quia vero verum filium genuit, hoc est quod ipse ille quem genuit.
OF PASSIONE DOMINI IN PARASCEVE

CAPUT I. — 1. Passionis Dominicae mysteria explicanda.—Cuius sanguine delicta nostra deleta sunt, solemniter legitur passio, solemniter celebratur; ut annua devotione memoria nostra laetius innovetur, et ipsa frequentatione populorum fides nostra clarius illustretur. Exigit ergo a nobis solemnitas, ut de passione Domini vobis sermonan, qualem donat ipse, reddamus. Et qnidem ad salutem nostram et vitae huius transigendae utilitatem, in his quae passus est ab inimicis Dominus noster, exemplum patientiae nobis praebere dignitus est; ut pro evangelica dignitate, si hoc ipse voluerit, nihil tale perpeti recusemus. Verum-

If he so wants, let us not refuse to suffer whatever is for the good of the Gospel. Since even what he suffered in this mortal flesh he suffered freely and not out of necessity, it is fair to believe that he also wanted to symbolize something in each of the events that took place and were written regarding his passion. 2. Firstly, in the fact that after being handed over for crucifixion he himself carried the cross, he left us a sample of patience and indicated in advance what anyone who wants to follow him must do. He also made the same exhortation verbally when he said: Whoever loves me, let him take up his cross and follow me. Carrying one's own cross is equivalent, in a certain way, to mastering one's own mortality. 3. By being crucified on Calvary, it meant that in his passion the forgiveness of all sins took place, of which the psalm says: My iniquities have multiplied more than the hairs of my head. 4. On his right and on his left, respectively, two other men were crucified, thereby showing that everyone must suffer, whether they are on his right or on his left. Of the former it is said: Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness' sake; of the latter, on the other hand: And even if I give my body to the flames, if I don't have love, it is of no use to me. 5. With the sign placed on the cross, on which it was written: King of the Jews, he demonstrated that not even causing him

death could the Jews achieve other than their king who with sublime power and clearly will give to each person what their works deserve. The fact that the sign was written in three languages: Hebrew, Greek and Latin, indicates that he was going to reign not only over the Jews, but also over the Gentiles. Therefore, after having said in the same psalm: He made me king over Zion, his holy mountain, that is, where the Hebrew language was spoken, he adds next, as if referring to the Greek and Latin: The Lord said to me: "You are my son, today I have begotten you; Ask me, and I will give you the towns as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession. Not because Greek and Latin are the only languages ​​spoken by the Gentiles, but because they are the ones that stand out the most; the Greek, for its literature, and the Latin, for the skill of the Romans. Although in those three languages ​​it was indicated that all the peoples were going to submit to Christ, that is not why it was also written there: "King of the Gentiles", but only: King of the Jews, so that the name already manifested the origin of the Christian race. It is written: The law will go out from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. Non quia graeca et latina solae sunt gentium linguae: sed quia ipsae máxime excellunt, graeca, propter studium litterarum; Latin, propter peritiam Romanorum. Quamvis in illis tribus linguis Christo subiuganda universitas gentium omnium monstraretur: non tamen illic scriptum est et rex Gentium, sed tantummodo Iudaeorum; ut commendaretur origo scminis, in proprietate nominis. Lex enim a Sion prodiet, dictum est, et verbum Domini ab lerusalem (Is 2,3). The princes of the Jews suggested to Pilate that he in no way write that he was the king of the Jews, but that he claimed to be so. But that doesn't mean he stops being king of the Jews. It is the root that supports the wild olive tree, not the wild olive tree the root. Although the sons of the kingdom who did not want the Son of God to be their king are cast out into outer darkness, nevertheless many will come from east and west and sit at table, not with Plato and Cicero, but with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, in the kingdom of heaven. Pilate, in fact, wrote: King of the Jews, not "King of the Greeks" or "King of the Latins", although he was to reign over the Gentiles. And what he ordered to be written remained written, without the suggestion of those who did not believe it being able to change it. Do you believe that it will be a reality for men to one day live in the company of God? Much more incredible is what has already taken place: that God has died for men. Who is Christ but the Word that existed in the beginning, the Word that existed with God and the Word that was God? This Word of God became flesh and lived among us. He would have had no place in himself to die for us if he had not taken on our mortal flesh. In this way the immortal could die and wanted to donate his life to mortals: making those of whom he had previously participated in himself in the future. For neither we had in our being where to obtain life nor did he have in his being where to suffer death. He therefore carried out an admirable trade with us based on mutual participation: the gift of dying was ours, the gift of living will be his. But the flesh that he took from us to die, he himself gave, since he is the creator; The life, however, thanks to which we will live in him and with him, he did not receive from us. Consequently, if we consider our nature, which makes us men, it did not die in its being, but in ours, since it cannot in any way die in its own nature, through which it is God. If, on the other hand, we consider that he is his creature, that he made it as God, he also died in his being, since he is also the author of the flesh in which he died. 2. And if we strive to explain what the teaching of patience is contained in this cross or how healthy it is, will we find words appropriate to the contents or time appropriate to the words? What man who believes with all truth and intensity in Christ will dare to be proud, when it is God who teaches humility not only by word, but also by his example? The usefulness of this teaching is recalled in a few words by that phrase from Holy Scripture: Before the fall the heart is exalted and before glory it is humbled. These other words affirm the same: God resists the proud, and to the humble, on the other hand, he gives his grace; and likewise: He who exalts himself will be humbled and he who humbles himself will be exalted. Therefore, in response to the Apostle's exhortation that we should not be haughty, but should have humble feelings, man must think, if possible, to what great precipice he is pushed if he does not share the humility of God and how pernicious it is for man to find difficulty in enduring what the just God wants, if God patiently suffered what the unjust enemy wanted. non corpori praeter spiritum, sed homini habenti spiritum spiritali participatione misceri. 4. I speak for the sick, the blessed for the unfortunate, the rich for the poor, the seeker for the lost, the redeemer for the sold, the shepherd for the flock and, most wonderful of all, the creator for the creature. He maintained what has always been, he delivered what had been made in him; Hidden God, visible man; giver of life by his power, subject to death by his weakness; immutable in his divinity, passible in his flesh 1; as the Apostle says: Who was delivered for our sins and rose again for our justification. You know perfectly well that this happened only once. Yet, as if it took place more than once, this solemn feast repeats from time to time what the truth proclaims through so many words of Scripture, which occurred only once. But reality and solemnity do not contradict each other, as if the latter lied and the former told the truth. What reality indicates took place only once, that same renews the solemnity so that pious hearts may celebrate it repeatedly. Reality discovers what happened as it happened; Solemnity, on the other hand, does not allow even past things to be forgotten, not by repeating them, but by celebrating them. Thus, Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed. Certainly he died only once, he who dies no more and death has no dominion over him. Therefore, according to reality, we say that Easter took place only once and that it will not happen again; According to the solemnity, however, every year we say that Easter must come. This is how I think what is written in the psalm should be understood:

1. With his resurrection, our Lord Jesus Christ made glorious the day that his death had made mournful. Therefore, solemnly bringing to memory both moments, let us remain awake remembering his death and rejoice by welcoming his resurrection. This is our festival and our annual Passover; no longer in figure, as the death of the lamb was for the ancient people, but made reality, as for a new people, by the victim who was the Savior, since Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed, and the old has passed away, and behold, everything has been renewed. We cry because the weight of our sins oppresses us and we rejoice because his grace has justified us, since he was handed over for our sins and rose again for our justification. Whether weeping at the former or rejoicing at the latter, we are full of joy. We do not let it pass unnoticed with ungrateful forgetfulness, but we celebrate with grateful memory what took place for our cause and for our benefit: both the sad event and the joyful anticipation. Let us remain awake, then, dearly beloved, since the burial of Christ lasted until this night, SERMO
