We would speak out against what faith says. Well, we must believe that we will have such bodies that allow us to be wherever and whenever we want. In fact, if, to solve the question posed by the weight of bodies, we answer that we have to live on earth, the question is reconsidered regarding the body of the Lord, the body with which he ascended to heaven. 6. You heard the gospel just read; These words sounded in our ears: Raising his hands, he blessed them. And it came to pass, as he blessed them, that he was separated from them and taken up into heaven. Who was raised to heaven? Christ the Lord. Who is Christ the Lord? The Lord Jesus. So, are you going to separate man from God, making him two persons, one divine and the other human, so that it is no longer a Trinity, but a Quaternity? You are a man consisting of soul and body; In the same way, Christ the Lord consists of the Word, soul and body. But the Word did not depart from the Father; Although he came to us, he did not abandon the Father; At the same time that he took flesh in the womb, he ruled the world. What was raised to heaven but what he took from the earth, that is, that flesh and that body? Speaking of him, he said to the disciples: Feel and see, that the spirits have neither bones nor flesh, as you see that I have. Let us believe these words, brothers; and, although we laboriously solve the problems posed by philosophers, let us retain without difficulty for faith what has been manifested to us in the Lord. Let them chatter; we create. 7. «But, they reply, an earthly body cannot be in talia corpora nos inhabitos, ut ubi velimus, quando voluerimus, ibi simus. Nam si responderus, ad solvendam de ordine ponderum quaestionem, in terra nos esse victuros; de ipso corpore Domini nobis est quaestio, cum quo ascendit in caelum. CAPUT IV.—6. Quid enim, separaturus es hominen a Deo, et facturus es aliam personara Dei, aliam hominis, ut iam non sit Trinitas, sed quaternitas? Quomodo tu [1141] homo anima es et corpus; sic Dominus Christus Verbum, anima et corpus. Sed Verbum non recessit a Patre; et ad nos venit, et Patrem non deseruit; et in utero_ carnem accepit, et mundum rexit.

the sky." What if God wants it? Respond against God and say: "God cannot do that." Do you not also affirm, pagan, whoever you are, that God is all-powerful? Notwithstanding what has been said, I also want to comment something about the difference in weight. What is above water: air. What about the air: the ether, the sky. What can we say about solid bodies, which can be picked up and manipulated? I am not referring to liquids, which slide and flow, but to manageable bodies; what are they made of? Are they earth, water, air or ether? I beg you, I said mihi: Terra terra est; Aqua aqua est; Aer aer est; Aether, id est caelum, et ignis Ule liquidus caelum est. Quattuor nempe is quasi gradatim construxerunt et aedificaverunt mundum, hoc est, ex his quattuor aedificatus est mundus. Quaere quid in imo sit, terra est; crux of super, here it is; quid super aquam, aer est; crux super aerem, caelum est, aether est. Quid corpora solida quae tenentur atque tractantur? that are from the earth. Is wood an earthly body? There is no doubt that it is terrain. It is born in the earth, it feeds on the earth and it grows on the earth. It is a solid thing, not a liquid. With all certainty you are going to answer that water has a place above the earth. In terra nascitur, in terra alitur, in terra crescit. Tractabile est, non fluxibile. Redi mecum ad illum ordinem ponderum. Terra in fundament est: ordinem sequere. Quid super terram? Aqua. Quare lignum natat super aquam? Terrenum est corpus; If you revoke ad illum ordinem ponderum, sub aqua esse debuit, non supra. Invenimus inter terram et lignum aquam mediam: subter terram, super aquam, et super aquam iterum terram, quandoquidem lignum terra est. Perdidisti illum or[1142]dinem, teñe fidem. Ergo terrena corpora inventa sunt super elementum, quod secundum est in ordine elementalum, when natant ligna, ñeque merguntur. CAPUT VIL—9. Plumbum super aquam.—Attende aliud, quod plus mireris.

Corpora ipsa gravissima, et tamen terrena, quae mox ut dimissa fuerint super aquam, continuo demerguntur, et ad ima profound perveniunt, sicut est ferrum, postremo sicut est plumbum. 10. Turn your attention and your thoughts to what I am going to tell you, if I can do it with God's help. What moves more easily, what is faster, a heavy body or a light body? Who will not answer that a light body? In fact, light bodies move more easily and are faster; The heavier ones do it with greater difficulty and slowness. You have established a certain standard; You have reflected correctly, and, in view of things, you answered that light bodies move more easily and quickly than heavier ones. "That's right," you say. So answer me now: “Why does a spider, so light in weight, move so slowly, while a heavy horse runs so fast? I'm going to talk about men. A human body is heavier the larger it is, while a small body, having less weight, is lighter. That's how it is in truth, but only if someone else carries it. If, however, the same man bids for his own body, the strong man runs, while the thin and weak man can barely walk. Put a skinny man and a robust man on the scale. The first, in its weakness, barely weighs a few pounds; The second, however, due to the robustness of his body, carries many more in his flesh. Try to lift them both: the strong one weighs a lot, the skinny one little. Stop lifting them now; now become a walker; Leave it to them to bid for their bodies alone. I see how the skinny one barely moves and how the strong and robust one runs. If this is the force of health, what is the force of immortality! 11.

Certe regulam fixisti, certe considerasti, et circumspectís Ómnibus responderi quia facilius moventur et velocius aguntur corpora leviora, quam graviora. Ita est, you say. Reply ergo mihi. Ita vero est, sed si alius portet. Si autem ipse homo corpus suum portet, validus currit, macer languore vix ambulat. CAPUT VIII.—11. Corpora spiritualia post resurrectionem, unde dicta.—Dabit ergo Deus miram facilitatem, miram levitatem. Non sine

lightness. Those bodies are precisely called spiritual. They are not called that because they are spirits instead of bodies. The ones we have now are called animal bodies 4, and yet they are not souls, but bodies. As we now call these bodies animals without being souls, in the same way they are called spiritual, even without being spirits, but bodies. Why, beloved, do we speak of a spiritual body if not because it will be at the service of whatever the spirit wants? Nothing within you will contradict yourself, nothing in you will rebel against you. There will be no place for the Apostle's groaning: The flesh has desires contrary to those of the spirit, and the spirit contrary to those of the flesh. Nor will the following exist there: I see in my members another law that opposes the law of my mind. These wars will not exist there; there will be peace, perfect peace. You will be where you want to be, but never far from God. You will be wherever you want; but wherever you go, you will have your God. You will always be with the one who makes you happy. 12. Let no one therefore be deceived; Let no one argue and rave in the midst of their assumptions. Let us believe with complete certainty that what God has promised us will take place. My brothers, when the apostles saw Christ, when they believed that he was a spirit, to convince them that he really had a body, he not only allowed them to see him with their eyes, but also to touch him with their hands. To show them this truth of faith, namely, that he had a body, he even deigned to take food; but not because he needed it, but because he wanted it that way. causa illa corpora spiritualia nuncupata sunt. Non ideo dicta sunt spiritualia, quia erunt spiritus, non corpora. Nam is ista quae moda habemus, dicuntur animalia corpora: et tamen animae non sunt, sed corpora. Quomodo nunc ist animalia dicuntur, et animae non sunt: ​​sic illa spiritualia dicuntur, sed non sunt spiritus, quia corpora erunt. Quare dicitur spirituale corpus, carissimi, nisi quia ad nutum spiritus serviet? Nihil tibi contradicet ex te, nihil in te rebellabit adversus te. Non ibi erit quod Apostolus gemit: Caro concupiscit adversus spiritum, et spiritus adversus carnem (Gal 5:17). Non ibi erit: Video aliam legem in membris meis repugnantem legi mentís meae (Rom 7,23). However, since they were still trembling with joy, he strengthened their hearts with the Holy Scriptures, saying to them: These were the words that I spoke to you while I was still with you: that everything must be fulfilled that is written about me in the law of Moses, in the projetas and in the psalms. Taking human experience as a basis, the heretics admitted that between the Father and the Son there was a chronological precedence of the first with respect to the second, a temporal diistema. The orthodox will only defend an ontological, but never chronological, priority. We have here an argument, also traditional in the Arian controversy, to show the coeternity between the Father and the Son: if Christ is the Word and Wisdom of the Father, since the Father could never exist without his Word and his Wisdom, it follows that the Son, who identifies himself with these, is eternal.

Appearance to the disciples SERMON

Theme: Appearance to the disciples (Jn 20:19-23). Location: Hippo. Date: Easter Thursday. 1. It seems that yesterday we finished reading the stories of the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ according to the truth of the four evangelists. On the first day the resurrection according to Matthew was read; the second, according to Luke; the third, according to Mark, and the fourth, that is, yesterday, according to John. But since John and Luke wrote extensively about the resurrection itself and what happened after it, their accounts could not be read in a single day; In this way, yesterday we heard one part of Juan, today another, and so on until it's over. What have we heard today? That on the same day of the resurrection, that is, Sunday, when the disciples were already gathered in the afternoon in a place with the doors closed for fear of the Jews, the Lord appeared to them in the midst of everyone. According to the evangelist's testimony, he appeared to them twice on the same day, in the morning and in the afternoon. The account of the morning appearance has already been read; Now we have just heard about the evening appearance. Primo enim die lecta est resurrectio secundum Matthaeum, alio die secundum Lucam, tertio die secundum Marcum, quarto, id est hesterno secundum Ioannem. Sed quoniam Ioannes et Lucas de ipsa resurrectione et quae contigerunt post resurrectionem, plurima scripse[1157]runt, quae non possunt una lectione recitan; et heri audimus aliquid secundum Ioannem, et hodie, et adhuc aliae lectiones restant. Hodie ergo quid audimus? Quia ipso die quo resurrexit, id est dominico die, cum sero factum esset, et essent discipuli in uno loco, et ostia clausa essent propter timorem Iudaeorum, apparuit Dominus in medio eorum. Ipso ergo die, sicut evangelista Ioannes testis est, bis apparuit discipulis suis, mane et sero. Let us see, then, what today's reading proposes to us as a theme for sermon 1. The same reading invites us and in a certain way directs us to say something about how the Lord, who rose again in the solidity of his body, so that he was not only seen, but also touched by his disciples, was able to appear to them with the doors closed. Some make so many difficulties in this regard, alleging the prejudices of their reasoning against the miracles of the Lord, that they are almost on the point of perishing. Thus they argue: «If he had a body, if he had flesh and bones, if what was raised from the tomb was the same thing that hung on the tree, how could he enter when the doors were closed? If it couldn't, they say, it didn't take place; If he could, how could he? If you understand how, it stops being a miracle, and if you don't believe it is a miracle, you are very close to also denying his resurrection from the tomb. Examine the miracles done by the Lord from the beginning and give me the explanation of each one of them. Without male contact, a maiden conceives. She explains how without a man she has conceived a maiden. Where explanation fails, there faith rises. You already have a miracle in the very conception of the Lord; hear another referring to childbirth: a maiden gives birth and remains a virgin. Already then, audimus. Non opus erat ut a me ista commemorarentur, sed ut a vobis adverterentur; propter quorumdam vero minorem intellegentiam vel maiorem neglegentiam oporttuit commemorare, ut sciatis non solum quid audistis, sed etiam de qua Scriptura vobis legitur quod audistis. 2. Ipsa quippe Iectio admonet nos, et quodammo loquitur nobis, ut aliquid dicamus, quemadmodum Dominus qui in ea soliditate corporis resurrexit, ut non solum videretur a discipulis, sed etiam tangeretur, potuerit illis apparere ostiis clausis. Before resurrecting, the Lord passed through closed doors. You ask me: "If he entered through closed doors, where are the properties of the body?" And I answer: "If he walked on the sea, where is the weight of the body?" But the Lord did all this as Lord. Did he cease to be Lord after being resurrected? Furthermore he made Peter walk on the water; what is there to say about this? What divinity was able to do in Christ, faith accomplished in Peter. But Christ did it because he could, Peter because Christ helped him. In conclusion, if you start looking for explanations for miracles with the human mind alone, I fear that you will lose faith. Do you not know that nothing is impossible with God? To anyone who tells you, "If he entered through closed doors, he had no body," twist the argument. «If it was touched, it had a body; If he ate, he had a body; and entering was the result of a miracle, not of nature. Try to give me an explanation; My question will be about what we see every day. Explain to me why the seed of a tree as large as the fig tree is so small that it can barely be seen, while the humble pumpkin produces it so large. "But, you say, it is impossible for the mass of a body to pass through a closed door." —How big was his size, I beg you? —Normal for a man. —Was it, perhaps, the same as that of a camel? -By no means. —Read the gospel, listen to it; When he wanted to show the difficulty that a rich man has in entering the kingdom of heaven, he said: It is easier for a camel to enter through the depths of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven. When the disciples heard this, thinking that it was absolutely impossible for a camel to enter through the depths of a needle, they were filled with sadness and said: If things are like this, who can be saved? If it is easier for a camel to pass through the depths of a needle than for a rich man to be saved; If a camel cannot at all pass through the hole of a needle, then no rich man can be saved. The Lord answered them: What is impossible for men is easy for God. God can make a camel go through the depths of a needle and introduce a rich man into the kingdom of heaven. Why are you making difficulties because the doors were closed? Well, together with you, the two fishings that the disciples carried out by command of the Lord, one before the passion and the other after the resurrection. In these two fishes the entire Church is symbolized, how it is now and how it will be after the resurrection of the dead. Now he has an innumerable multitude, including good and bad; but after the resurrection he will have a fixed number of only good ones. 2. Remember, then, the first catch, to see in it what the Church of the present time is like. The Lord Jesus found his disciples devoted to fishing when he first called them to follow him. So they hadn't caught anything all night. But when they saw him they heard him say to them: "Cast down the nets." —Sir, they reply; All night long we have captured nothing; but at your word we cast them.—They cast the nets by order of the almighty. What else could be done but his will? But, nevertheless, as I already said, in that very fact he deigned to symbolize for us something that it is convenient for us to know. The nets were therefore let down. The Lord had not yet suffered the passion nor had he been resurrected. The nets were cast: they caught such a quantity of fish that the two boats were filled and the nets themselves were breaking because there were so many of them. Then he said to them: Come and I will make you fishers of men. You know that the law was given to the people of God through Moses and that the most important thing it contains is the decalogue, that is, the ten commandments. The first of which refers to the worship of God; the second prescribes: Do not take the name of your God in vain; The third deals with the observance of the Sabbath, which Christians observe spiritually, while Jews violate it physically. These three commandments refer to God, and the remaining seven to men, in attention to the two most important things: You will love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul and with all your mind; and you will love your neighbor as yourself. Sed quo pertineamus? ad illa septem? Tale est ac si faceré possimus, sed quid facimus nesciamus. Ergo ad decem septem pertineamus. Topic: The miraculous fishing (Jn 21,1-14). Place; Hippo. Date: Easter Friday. 1. Jesus the Lord, who chose the weak of the world to confuse the strong and gathered his Church from all over the world, did not begin with emperors or senators, but with some fishermen. If he had first chosen men clothed with dignity, of whatever class they were, they would have dared to assign it to their merits, not to the grace of God. This secret determination of God, this decision of our Savior, is set forth by the Apostle where he says: See who you have been called, brothers—these are the words of the Apostle—; See who you have been called, for there are not many wise according to the flesh, nor many powerful nor noble; but God chose the weak things in the world to confound the things that are strong, and the unknown and contemptible things in the world, and the things that do not exist as if they did exist, to nullify the things that do exist, so that no flesh may boast in His presence. The prophet said the same thing: Every valley will be filled, and every mountain and hill made level, and the field will become a plain. Consequently, today, nobles and commoners, the wise and the ignorant, the poor and the rich, access the grace of the Lord together. SERMO

The preaching of the Gospel was a novelty; Then he found them at the fishing task, he approached them and said to them: Let down your nets. Topic: The miraculous fishing (Jn 21,1-14). Location: Hippo. Date: Easter Friday. From 412.

1. The fishing of our Liberator is our liberation. We find two catches of the Lord in the holy gospel, that is, two occasions in which the nets were lowered by his order: the first when he chose the disciples and this other after rising from the dead. That fishing symbolized the Church as it is in the present time; This other, however, after the resurrection of the Lord, symbolized the Church as it will be at the end of time. Thus, in the first one he ordered the nets to be cast, but he did not say which side; He only ordered them to lie down. The disciples did it; They were not told to throw them to the right or left. As fish symbolized men, if I had said that on the right, it would enperdit etiam gaudere debent et quia instruí tur qui nesciebat. Decem septem numera ab uno usque ad decem septem ita ut omnes addas et peruenies ad centum quinquaginta three. What are you expecting me? Number yourself uobis. SERMO
IN DIEBUS PASCHALIBUS, XXII DE EADEM LECTIONE ET DE DUABUS PISCATIONIBUS

CAPUT I.—1. Piscationes Domini iussu factae duae. In prima piscatione tria significata sunt: ​​mixtura bonorum et malorum, pressura turbarum, separationes haereticorum.—Liberatoris nostri piscatio, nostra est liberatio. Duas autem advertimus in sancto Evangelio Domini piscationes, id est, quando ad verbum ipsius missa sunt retía: unam prius, quando disciples elegit; et hanc alteram, quando a mortuis resurrexit. Illa piscatio significavit Ecclesiam, qualis es moda; ista vero post resurrectionem Domini, significavit Ecclesiam, qualisfutura est in fine saeculi. Denique in illa priori piscatione, iussit mitti retia, et non dixit in quam partem; sed tantummodo ut mitterentur, praecepit. Miserunt discipuli: non dictum est: In dexteram; non dictum est: In sinistram. Pisces enim homines significant: si ergo diceretur: In dexteram, soli boni futuri

I would tend that there would only be good ones; If left, that only bad. But since good and bad were going to be found mixed in the Church, the nets were cast indiscriminately to capture fish that symbolized the mixture of good and bad. Also in this first catch it is written that they caught so many fish that both boats, being full, sank, that is, the weight predicted sinking. Neither boat sank, but they ran that risk. Where did the danger come from? Of the quantity of fish. Symbolically, we see expressed here that discipline was going to be in danger because of the crowd that would enter the Church. In that fishing it is also added - as it is narrated - that even the nets broke due to the number of fish. What did the broken networks mean if not the schisms of the future? This fishing contains in symbol these three things: the mixture of good and bad, the oppression of the crowd and the divisions of heretics. Topic: The miraculous fishing (Jn 21,1-14). Location: Hippo. Date: Probably Easter Friday 396.

1. In many and varied ways, our Lord Jesus Christ has shown in the Holy Scriptures, through mysteries and symbolic rites, according to his custom, not only the excellency of his divinity, but also the mercy of his humanity. All with this purpose: so that he who asks may receive, he who seeks may find, and that he who knocks may be opened. What we have read today in the holy gospel requires understanding, and once understood produces spiritual joy. Your holiness be attentive to what it means for the Lord to manifest himself to the disciples in the way that the Holy Scripture attests in the evangelist's narrative. The disciples went fishing, and caught nothing all night. But the Lord appeared to them on the shore early in the morning and asked them if they had anything to eat; They answered no. Then he said to them, Cast your nets to the right and you will find. See how much the one who had apparently come to buy gave them freely: he gave them the product of the sea, created by him. that, due to their large number, they could not take out the nets. But, if you consider who its author is, this miracle ceases to cause admiration, since he had already performed greater ones. For someone who had previously raised the dead, it was no big deal to have caused those fish to be caught 1. Therefore, we must ask ourselves what the hidden meaning of the miracle is. Well, very intentionally he ordered them to cast their nets to the right and not anywhere else. Furthermore, the evangelist also took care to say the exact number of the fish and to add: And, despite there being so many, that is, so large, the nets did not break. This text reminds us of the other occasion when the Lord ordered the nets to be cast when he chose the disciples before his passion. Then there were Peter, John and James. They cast their nets, caught countless fish, and, when one boat was already full, they asked for help from a closer one, and both were filled. The fish were so many that the nets broke. But this took place before the resurrection. Why is there no number given in that fishing? Why did the nets break in that one and not in this one? Why didn't he then tell them to cast their nets to the right and now? Nothing was fortuitous, because the Lord did not do it without a precise and useful aim. Lk 5:1-7). Quare ibi numerus nullus dicitur? Quare ibi retia rumpebantur, hic non rapta sunt?

Quare ibi non dictum est, ut ad dexteram partem mitterentur retia, hic autem dixit: Mittite retia in dexteram partem? Non est utique sine causa. Non enim faciebat ist Dominus quasi frustra et inaniter. Verbum Dei est Christus, qui non solum sonis, sed etiam factis loquitur hominibus. Augustine usually gives little importance to the miracle as a wonderful fact, since he is more interested in its deep meaning. In the case of a divine subject like Jesus, there is no reason for surprise. See, e.g., sermons 75,1; 136.1; Comments on Psalms 90,11,6; Treatises on the gospel of Saint John 7,14; 49.1; 43.18. 2. We have proposed to discuss with your holiness the meaning of these differences. In fact, the nets that were cast the first time captured an uncountable number of fish, the two ships were found to be overloaded with weight, the nets were breaking, and they were not cast to the right, although it was not said that they were to the left either. The mystery enclosed in that fishing takes place in the present time. On the other hand, the other mysterious fact was carried out, not without a precise intention, after the resurrection, when he will no longer die, but will live forever, not only in divinity, in which he never died, but also in the body, in which he deigned to die for us. Therefore, it is not without value that one fishing took place before the resurrection and another after. In the first he only told them: Cast the nets, without adding whether to the right or to the left; In this one, however, he told them: Cast your nets to the right. In the first the number is not mentioned, but only the quantity, so large that the boats almost sank, something that is also said about the former; In this one, however, not only the number is indicated, but also that the fish were large. In that one, the networks broke; In this, the evangelist took care to say: And, despite being so large, the nets were not broken. Don't we already see, brothers, that the networks are the word of God, that the sea is this world and that all believers are within those networks? If by chance there is someone who doubts that this is the meaning, consider that this is what the Lord indicated in the parable that he proposed based on the miracle. Therefore he says: The kingdom of heaven is like a sweeping net cast

to the sea, which collects fish of all kinds. When it is full, they take it out and drag it to the shore, and, sitting there, they select the good ones for the baskets, while they throw the bad ones away. This is how it will happen at the end of time: the angels will come out, separate the bad from the good, and throw them into the fiery furnace; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. It is clear that casting nets into the sea is a symbol of having faith. Or is this world not a sea, in which men devour each other like fish? Or are the storms and waves of temptations that shake him small? Are the dangers in which navigators find themselves, that is, those who seek the heavenly homeland on the wood of the cross, unimportant? The analogy is extremely obvious. 3. We find this same comparison in the threshing floor at the time of threshing. There is chaff and there is wheat, but those who look at the threshing floor hardly see anything other than chaff. It takes a lot of attention to find the wheat among the chaff. Winds from all sources blow over the threshing floor; but does it not experience the force of the winds, even during threshing, before being winnowed? The wind blows, for example, from one side and carries away the straw; Then it blows in a different direction and takes them somewhere else. Whichever way he takes them, he leaves them either on the fences, on the brambles or in any other place. But the wind cannot beat the grain; He only takes the straw. But even though the wind blows from all directions and carries away chaff, is only the grain left on the threshing floor? Nothing leaves her,

but chaff, but on the threshing floor there remains chaff along with the grain. When will it all disappear? When the Lord comes with the fork in his hand, fan his threshing floor, gather the wheat into the granary and send the chaff to the unquenchable fire. Your holiness pay maximum attention to what I am going to say. Sometimes, the same winds that remove the straw from the threshing floor blow in the opposite direction, and return the straw that had remained in the hedges to the threshing floor. For example: a certain member of the Catholic Church suffered the test of some tribulation. He saw that the Donatists could help him better in his affairs from a material point of view. Someone said to him: "You will not receive help if you do not enter into communion with us." The wind blew and threw that person into the brambles. If she then happens to have another worldly matter that she could not resolve except from within the Catholic Church, not considering where she is, but where she can best resolve her affairs, as if the wind were to blow from the other side of the hedge, she is returned to the threshing floor of the Lord. 6. mere, that is, 150, in three parts, and we obtain 50. Therefore, we must focus our reflection on the number 50. 9. Is this, perhaps, the fifty days that we are celebrating? It is not without reason, my brothers, that the Church preserves the ancient tradition of singing the Hallelujah during these fifty days. Hallelujah and praise to God are the same thing. With it we are symbolically anticipated, in the midst of our fatigue, what we will do in eternal rest. In fact, when after the present work we reach that rest, the only occupation will be the praise of God, all our work will be reduced to Hallelujah. What does Hallelujah mean? Praise God. Who praises God without fainting except the angels? They do not suffer hunger or thirst, they do not get sick or die. We too have sung the Hallelujah; It was already sung this morning, and recently, when I appeared, we sang it again. A certain smell of that divine praise and that rest reaches us, but the weight of mortality is stronger. Simply repeating it tires us, and we want to replenish the strength of our limbs; If it lasts a long time, it becomes burdensome for us to praise God for the hindrance of our body. If plenitude is to consist in the uninterrupted singing of Hallelujah, it will take place only after this world and these toils. What to do then, brothers? Let's repeat it as many times as we can to deserve to sing it forever. Our food, our drink, our rest and all our joy there will be Hallelujah, that is, the praise of God. Significatur ergo nobis laborantibus actio quietis nostrae. Cum enim post istum laborem ad illam requiem veniemus, solum negotium laus Dei erit, actio nostra ibi Alleluia est. Who is Alleluia? Praise Deum. Quis laudet Deum sine defectu, nisi Angeli? Non esuriunt, non sitiunt, non aegrotant, non moriuntur. I see a large amount of manure; Also in this case I look for its place. At the same time that I saw him sad and crying, I realized that he was also praying. Sad, with moans and crying, and in prayer: it made me think of I don't know what good omen; But I'm still looking for the place. What if this one who prays and groans with great tears asks for death for his enemies? It is for that reason, but he is crying, praying and supplicating. There is only one dirty place, the fruit will be null. More serious is what we find in Scripture. When he asks for the death of his enemy, he ends up in the curse that weighs on Judas: His prayer becomes a sin. I have noticed again another who moaned, cried and prayed. I notice the manure, I look for the place. I listened to his prayer, and heard him say: I have said: “Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you. He groans for his sins; I recognize the field and am waiting for the fruit. Thank God! The manure is in a good place, it is not extra there, it is producing fruit. This is, indeed, the time of fruitful sadness; the time to grieve and be sad about our dying condition.

such, the abundance of temptations, the insinuations of sinners, the opposition of desires and the strife of concupiscence, always boiling against good thoughts. 5. The forty days before Easter symbolize this time of our misery and our groans \ if there is anyone who places such hope in their groans; The time, however, of the joy that will take place afterwards, of rest, of happiness, of eternal life and of the endless kingdom that has not yet come, is symbolized in these fifty days in which we sing the praises of God. We have two times with symbolic value: one before the resurrection of the Lord and another after; one where we are and one where we hope to be in the future. The time of sadness – the days of Lent mean nothing else – is a symbol and a reality; On the other hand, we find the time of joy, rest and kingdom, of which these days are an expression, symbolized in the Hallelujah, but we do not yet possess those praises, although you sigh now for the Hallelujah. What does Hallelujah mean? Praise the Lord. That is why in these days after the resurrection the praises of God are repeated in the Church: because after our resurrection our praise will also be perpetual. The passion of the Lord symbolizes the time when we cry now. The whippings, the chains, mockery, spitting, the crown of thorns, the wine with gall, the vinegar on the sponge, the insults, reproaches and, finally, the cross itself and the holy members hanging from it.

[CAPUT IV] Hoc tempus miseriae nostrae et gemitus nostri, si quis est qui habeat talem spem gemitus, quadraginta illi dies significant ante pascha; laetitiae vero quae posterior erit, quietis, felicitatis, vitae aeternae, regni sine fine quod nondum est, his diebus quinquaginta, quibus diebus laudes Deo dicuntur, significatur. The field was beautiful before receiving the fertilizer baskets. As a first measure, ugliness is brought to the countryside so that it reaches fertility. Without honor or beauty. Because? Ask another prophet: They counted all my bones. All the bones of the man hanging from the tree were counted. A horrible sight for a crucified man, but that ugliness engenders beauty. What beauty? That of the resurrection, since it is more beautiful than the sons of men. 6. Do you think that on the basis of his promises we can demand little from him like a debtor? God became a debtor by promising. Are you thinking about what you heard in the psalm: What will I give back to the Lord? First of all, what will I give back to the Lord? These are the words of a debtor, not a creditor. Something is

had anticipated; What will I give back to the Lord? What does it mean: What will I give you back? I will give you in return. In exchange for what? Of all the things he granted me. What did he grant you? The first: he was nothing, and he created me; He had lost me, and he looked for me; When he looked for me he found me; being captive, he redeemed me; sold, he set me free; From a servant he turned me into a brother. What will I return to the Lord? You don't have to pay him back. If you expect everything from him, what do you have to give him in return? Wait a little. I don't know what he means when he asks: What will I give back to the Lord for all the things he has given me? So much searching everywhere for something to give him instead, he found it so to speak. What did you find? I will receive the chalice of salvation. At the same time that you thought about giving back, you were still seeking to receive. Look, I beg you. If you still seek to receive, you are still a debtor. When will you give something in return? Therefore, if you are going to always be a debtor, when are you going to pay back? You will find nothing that you can give in exchange. You will have nothing else except what he has given you. 7. Look: what you said: What will I return?, is in relation to other words of yours: Every man is a liar. Whoever dares to say that he gives something back to God is a liar. We have to expect everything from him. Without it, we can obtain nothing from ourselves, except, perhaps, sin and lies, since whoever speaks a lie speaks of his own. In truth, man abounds in what is his own. He most certainly has lies in him and his heart is a treasure of lies. He lies as much as he can, he doesn't get tired. Pretend as much as you can:

in ligno membra sacra pendentia, quid nobis significat, nisi tempus quod agimus, tempus maeroris, tempus mortalitatis, tempus temptationis? Ideo foedum tempus, sed foeditas ista stercoris sit in agro, non in domo. Maeror sit de peccatis, non de cupiditatibus fraudatis. Foedum tempus, sed, si bene utatur, fertile tempus. Quid foedius agro stercorato? Pulcher fuet ager, antequam cophinum haberet stercoris. Perductus est prius ager ad foeditatem, ut comeret ad ubertatem. Foeditas ergo huius temporis signum est, sed nobis sit ista foeditas tempus fertilitatis. [OAPUT V] Et videamus cum propheta qui dicit: Vidimus eum. Qualem? Non habebat speciem ñeque decorem (Ps 53,2). Quare? Alium prophetam interrogates. Dinumeraverunt omnia ossa mea (Ps 21:18). Dinumerata sunt ossa pendentis. Foeda species, crucifixi species, sed ista foeditas pulchritudinem parturiit. Quam pulchritudinem? Resurrectionis, quia speáosus forma prae filiis hominum (Ps 44,3). 6. Laudemus ergo dominum, fratres, quia eius fidelia promissa retinemus, nondum accepimus. Parum putatis, quia promissorem tenemus, ut iam debitorem exigamus? Promissor Deus debitor factus est. Bonitate sua debitor factus est, non praerogativa nostra. Quid ei dedimus, ut eum debitorem teneamus? An forte quia audistis in psalmo: Quid retrihuam domino (Ps 115,12)? Cousin, when I said, Quid retribuam domino? verba sunt debitoris, non debitum demandingtis. Praerogatum est illi;

What retribuam do(118?)mino? Quid est, Quid retribuam? Rependam. Pro qua re? Pro omnibus quae retribuit mihi (Ps 115.12). Why retribuit tibi? Primo nihil [68] eram, et fecit me; perieram, quaesivit me; quaerens invent me; captivum redeem me; emptum liberavit me; of servo fratrem fecit me. Quid retribuam domino? There are no quid remunerations. When there are so many expectations, what will you retribuere? Be expectant. Nescio quid vult dicere, cum quaerit: Quid retribuam domino pro omnibus quae retribuit mihi? Circumspiciens undique quid retribuat, quasi invenit. Quid invent? Cdicem salutaris accipiam (Ps 115,13). Retribuere cogitabas, adhuc accipere quaerebas. Vide, pray. Si adhuc accipere quaeris, adhuc debitor eris. When retributor? Si ergo debitor semper eris, when do you repay? Non invenies quid retribuas. Nisi quod dederit, non habebis. 7. See, when you said, Quid retribuam? ad illud pertinet quod dixisti: Omnis homo mendax (Ps 115,11). Qui enim voluerit dicere, quia retribuit aliquid Deo, mendax est. Omnia ab illo speranda sunt. A nobis ipsis praeter illum nihil, nisi forte peccatum et mendacium, quia qui loquitur mendacium de suo loquitur. I will see full of suo abundat homo. Mendacium omnino ibi habet, et thesaurum mendaciorum cor suum. Mentitur quantum potest, non deficit. Fingat quicquid potest, mentitur quicquid potest. Quare? Quia quod gratis habet,

lies what he can. Because? Because what he has for free, he has from himself, without having to buy it. But when you come to the truth, if you want to be truthful, you will not be truthful about yourself. Pedro was a liar of his own making. Where was it mendacious? The Lord promises us that he will suffer, and you say: Far be it from you; this will not happen! 'Every man is a liar. Where does being a liar come from? Listen to the Lord himself: You do not taste the things of God, but those of men. When, however, was Peter truthful? You are Christ, the Son of the living God. Where did this truth come from to a lying man? See that it is a man who says: You are Christ, the Son of the living God. Who says it? Peter. Who was Peter? A man who told the truth? Indeed, every man is a liar. See, see his tongue, see the truth that flows from his tongue; How is every man a liar? Listen that every man is a liar. Quando autem venitur ad veritatem, si verax vult esse, non erit de suo. [CAPUT VI] Mendax _ Petrus de suo. Ubi mendax? Theme: Martha and Mary (Luke 10:38-42). Place: Carthage. Date: Easter time. Year 418. 1. Since the Lord wanted me to meet your charity at the moment of singing the Hallelujah, I must say a few words to you about the Hallelujah itself. I hope I am not bothering you by reminding you of what you already know, in the same way that we repeat the Hallelujah daily and it gives us satisfaction daily. laudahunt te (Ps 83.5). Lex dicit, scriptura dicit, veritas dicit. Venturi sumus ad domum Dei, quae est in caelis. Ibi non quinquaginta diebus Deum laudabimus, sed, quemadmodum scriptum est, in saecula saeculorum. Videbimus, amabimus, laudabimus; nec quod videbimus deficiet, nec quod amabimus periet, nec quod laudabimus tacebit; sempiternum totum erit, sine fine erit. Laudemus, laudemus, sed non solis voá(1186)bus, laudemus et moribus. Laudet lingua, laudet vita, ne rixetur lingua cum vita, sed habeant caritatem infinitem. Conversi ad dominum, etc.
IN DIEBUS PASCHALIBUS, XXVI OF ALLELUIA

CAPUT I.—1. Alleluia, piorum hic solatium, erit actio heatorum. Quoniamvoluít Dominus, ut Caritatem vestram in Alleluia videremus, de Alleluia vobis verbum debenmus. Non sim oneri, si commemoro quod nostis: quia et ipsum Alleluia quotidie dicimus, et quotidie delectamur. Nostis enim quia Alleluia, latine dicitur Laúdate Deum: et in hoc verb Thus, then, the sermon was preached outside of Hippo, in a place where he was occasionally found. In all probability, Carthage, where he was in May 418 to attend the council held there then against the Pelagians.

You know that Hallelujah is translated in Latin as "Praise God." In this way, singing the same thing and with identical feelings, we encourage each other to praise the Lord. Only him can man praise calmly, because he has nothing that could displease him. Also at this time of our pilgrimage we sing Hallelujah as a viaticum for our solace; Hallelujah is now a traveler's song for us. We are heading along a tiring road to the peaceful homeland, where, having laid aside all our occupations, we will have nothing left but Hallelujah. 2. This most sweet part had been chosen by Mary, who remained inactive, while learning and praising; His sister Marta, on the other hand, was busy with many things. What he did was certainly necessary, but temporary: things for the road, not yet those of the homeland; He was concerned with the trip, not yet with what he was going to possess. He had, in fact, received the Lord and all those who went with him. The Lord also had flesh; and in the same way that he deigned to take it for us, so he also deigned to suffer hunger and thirst. And because he deigned to suffer hunger and thirst, he deigned to be fed by those whom he himself had enriched. He deigned to be received in hospitality not out of necessity, but out of benevolence. Martha, then, was in charge of remedying the needs of those hungry and thirsty people; In his own house he carefully prepared what those holy men and the Holy of Holies were going to eat and drink. Beautiful work, but temporary! Should feeling hungry and thirsty last forever? When we adhiconsonantes ore et consentientes corde, exhortamur nos invicem ad laudandum Deum. Eum tantum homo securus laudat, qui non habet unde displiceat. Et in hoc quidem tempore peregrinationis nostrae ad solatium viatici dicimus Alleluia; moda nobis Alleluia canticum est viatoris: tendimus autem per viam laboriosam ad quietam patriam, ubi retractis ómnibus actionibus nostris, non remanebit nisi Alleluia. CAPUT II.—2. Mariae et Marthae diverse officia.—Istam partem suavissimam sibi Maria elegerat, quae vacabat, discebat, laudabat: Martha vero sóror eius, circa plurima fuet occupata. Equidem agebat rem necessariam, sed non permansuram; agebat rem viae, nondum patriae; agebat rem peregrinationis, nondum possessionis. Susceperat enim Dominum, et eos qui cum illo weret. Et Dominus carnero habebat: et sicut pro nobis dignities est carnem suscipere, ita dignities est esurire et sitire.

Et ex eo quod dignitus est esurire et sitire, dignities est pasci ab eis quos ipse ditavit: dignities est suscipi, non inopia, sed gratia. Agebat ergo Martha quod pertinebat ad necessitatem esurientium et sitientium: parabat conversatione sollicita, quod manducaretur et biberetur a sanctis et ab ipso Sancto sanctorum in domo eius (cf. Le 10,38-42). Magnum opus, sed transitory. Numquid esurire et sitire semper erit? When inhaerebi-

If we were to the most pure and perfect goodness, we will no longer pay tribute to any need. We will be happy, without needing anything; We will possess everything and seek nothing. What will we have, then, to not have to look for anything? I have already said it. Then you will see what you now believe. I talked about possessing everything and not looking for anything, that is, not needing anything. What will we have? What will God give to those who serve him, worship him, believe in him, put their hope in him and love him? 3. We are seeing how many things he gives in the present time to those who distrust and to those who expect nothing from him, to those who distance themselves and blaspheme against him. We are seeing how many benefits it gives them. From it comes, first of all, health: a thing so sweet that it never tires. What does a poor person lack when they are healthy? And what good is riches to the rich, if he lacks it? From him it comes, then; from him, that is, from the Lord our God, whom we worship; From the true God, in whom we believe, in whom we hope and whom we love, comes such an excellent thing: health. See, however, how, despite being so excellent, He grants it to the good and the bad, to those who blaspheme and to those who praise Him. What am I going to say? Both are men. Even the evil man is superior to any beast. God also grants health to donkeys, and dragons, and even to flies and worms; He who created everything distributes health to everyone. To omit other things, since we find nothing better than health, God gives it not only mus puríssimae illi et perfectissimae bonitoti, non erit quare serve necessitati. Beati erimus, nullo indigents; multum habentes, nihil quaerentes. Et quid est quod habebimus, ut nihil quaeramus? Dixi: quod creditis, post videbitis. Quod ergo diximus, multum habentes et nihil quaerentes, id est, nullo indigentes; quid est ipsum quod habebimus? Servientibus sibi Deus, colentibus eum, credentibus in eum, sperantibus in eum, amantibus eum quid dabit? CAPUT III.—3. Beneficia Dei in omnes et bonds et mal[íí87]los. Sanitas a Deo.—Vídemus enim quanta det in hoc tempore diffidentibus de illo, desperantibus de illo, aversis ab illo, blasphemantibus iUum; videmus quanta dona largiatur. Ab illo est enim primo sanitas: quae sic dulcís est, ut in fastidium nunquam veniat. Quando hanc habet, quid deest pauperi? Quando istam non habet, quidquid habet quid prodest diviti?

Ab illo est ergo, id est, a Domino Deo nostro quem colimus, a vero Deo in quem credimus, et in quo speramus, et quem diligimus; Ab illo is so much beef, healthy. Videte tamen, cum sit magna res sanitas, quomodo eam det et bonis et malis, et blasphematoribus suis et laudatoribus suis. Et quid dicam? Utrique homines sunt. Omni pecore melior est et malus homo. Dat sanitatem etiam iumentis et draconibus, usque ad muscas et vermiculos donat sanitatem; et salvat omnia qui creavit omnia. Ut ergo alia omittamus; quia nihil melius invenimus quam est sanitas: non solum eam dat Deus hominibus, sed et pecoribus, sicut

to men, but also to beasts, as the psalm says: You will give salvation, Lord, to men and to the donkeys, just as your mercy has multiplied, O God! Such are you, since you are God; You are such that your goodness does not remain in the heights, but rather seeks the lowest. From the angels it reaches the smallest animals. Stretching from one end to the other, wisdom comes with strength and disposes all things gently. And because his disposition of things is gentle, it is gentle for everyone's health. 4. If, then, he grants such excellent good to good and bad, to men and donkeys, what, my brothers, is what he has in store for the good? He had already said: You will give health, Lord, to men and donkeys, just as your mercy has multiplied, O God! And then he added: But the sons of men. Who are these? It seems to imply that some are the sons of men and others the men of whom he had previously said: You will give health, Lord, to men and to donkeys. Are men different from the sons of men, and the sons of men different from men? What does this distinction mean? Perhaps, that men belong to man, and the sons of men, to the Son of man; men, I repeat, to man, and the sons of men, to the Son of man. There is, in fact, a certain man who was not the son of man. The first to be created was man, but not the son of man. What came to us through man and what through the Son of man?

I remember what came to us through man, quoting the words of the Apostle: Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so it passed to all men, for all sinned in him. See what the man gave us to drink, see what we drank from that progenitor, which we could barely digest. If this came to us through man, what came to us through the Son of Man? Who did not forgive, he says, not even his own Son. If he did not spare his own Son, but gave him up for us all, how could he not give us all things with him? Furthermore: As, through the disobedience of one man, many were made sinners, so also, through the obedience of one man, many will be made righteous. So, through that sin, through Christ righteousness. Therefore all sinners belong to man, and all the righteous belong to the Son of man. Why do you wonder that the sinners, the wicked, the wicked, the despisers of God, those who turn away from him, the lovers of the world, those who embrace evil and hate the truth, that is, men belonging to man; Why are you surprised, I repeat, that they have this health, if the psalm says: You will give health, Lord, to men and to the donkeys So that men would not become emboldened by possessing bodily health, he placed the donkeys by their side. What is it that brings you joy, oh man? Isn't it something you have in common with your donkey, with your chicken, with any of your domestic animals, with birds? The health that you have, don't they all also have it?

Psalmus dicit: Homines et iumenta safes focies, Domine; sicut multiplicata este mercy tua, Deus (Ps 35,7.8). Sic enim es, quia Deus es; ut pretty yours do not remain in summis, et deserat Ínfima. Pervenit ab Angelis usque ad extreme et minute animalia. Pervenit enim a fine usque in finem pertendens fortiter sapientia, et disponit omnia suaviter (Wis 8,1): et in ipsa dispositione suavitatis eius, suavis est omnibus sanitas. CAPUT IV.—4. Deum aliquid servare bonis. Homines et filii hominum in quo differant.—Cum ergo tantum bonum det et bonis et malis, et hominibus et iumentis; quid est, fratres mei, quod servat bonis? Iam enim dixerat, Homines et iumenta safes facies, Domine; Sicut multiply this mercy of yours, Deus. Et deinde adiunxit: Filii autem hominum (Ps 35,7-8). Who sunt isti? Quasi alii sunt homines, de quibus paulo ante dixerat: Homines et iumenta safes facies, Domine; et alii filii hominum. Aliud enim sunt homines quam filii hominum, et aliud sunt filii hominum quam homines? Quid sibi ergo vult ista distinctio? Nisi forte quia homines pertinent ad hominem, filii hominum ad Filium hominis: homines, ad hominem; filii hominum, ad Filium hominis. Est enim quidam homo qui non Fuit filius hominis. Qui enim primus factus est, homo Fuit, filius hominis non Fuit. Quid ergo nobis come per

hominem, et quid nobis come per Filium hominis? Commemoro quod venit per hominem, et Apostoli verba dico: See unum hominem peccatum intravit in mundum, et per peccatum mors: et ita in omnes homines pertransiit, in quo omnes peccaverunt (Rom 5,12). Ecce quod nobis propinavit homo, ecce quod de parente bibimus, et vix digerimus. Si hoc per hominem, quid per Filium hominis? Proprio, inquit, Filio non pepercit. Si proprio Filio non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit eum; quomodo non et cum tilo omnia nobis donabit (ib., 8,32)? item: Sicut per [1188] inoboedientiam unius hominis peccatores constituti sunt multi; sic et per oboedientiam unius hominis; iusti constituentur multi (Rom 5,19). Per illum ergo peccatum, per Christum iustitia. Omnes ergo peccatores ad hominem pertinent: omnes iusti ad Filium hominis. Quid ergo miramini, quia peccatores, quia impii, quia iniqui, quia Dei contemptores, a Deo aversi, saeculi dilectores, amplectentes iniquitatem, odio habentes veritatem, hoc est, relevant homines ad hominem; quid miramini, quia habent istam sanítatem, cum audiatis Psalmum: Homines et iumenta safes facies, Domine? 5. Seek therefore what was promised to the children of men; listen to what is said next: But the sons of men will wait in the shadow of your wings. They will wait while they are traveling. But the sons of men will wait in the shadow of your wings. For we are saved in hope. Waiting in the shadow of God's wings is not for men and donkeys. Behold, hope breastfeeds us, nourishes us, strengthens us and consoles us in this busy life. Living in this hope, we sing Hallelujah. See how much joy hope brings. What will reality be like? Do you ask what it will be like? Listen to what follows: They will be drunk with the abundance of your house. This is what we hope for. We hunger and thirst for it; It is necessary to satisfy it. But man is on his way, and satiety in the homeland. When will we be satisfied? I will be satisfied when your glory is revealed. Currently the glory of our God is hidden, the glory of our Christ, and with it ours is hidden. But when Christ, your life, appears, you also will appear with him in glory. Then Hallelujah will come true; now we possess it only in hope. Hope is what sings it; love sings it now, and will sing it then too; but now hungry love sings it, and then joyful love will sing it. What then is Hallelujah, my brothers? I have already told you: it is the praise of God. Now you hear a word, and hearing it delights you, and, wrapped in delight, you praise. If you love the sprinkle so much, how you will love the fountain itself! What the burp is to him

stomach that belches, that is praise for the satisfied heart. If we praise him by simply believing in him, how will we praise him when we see him! Here is what Mary had chosen for herself; She symbolized that life, she did not yet possess it. 6. There are two lives: one that is concerned with enjoyment and another that is concerned with needs. This is tiring; that one, joyful. But go inside, do not look for joy outside; do not be puffed up because of him, lest he prevent you from entering through the narrow gate. Here is how Mary saw and heard the Lord in the flesh, as if through a veil, as you heard when the letter to the Hebrews was read. When we see him face to face there will be no veil. Mary, then, was sitting, that is, she was not doing anything else; I listened and praised him; Marta, on the other hand, was busy with a multitude of chores. The Lord says to her: Martha, Martha, you are busy with many things; only one is necessary. Only one thing really; the rest will not be necessary. Before we get to that one thing we need many others. Let that one thing keep us in tension, lest the many others relax us and distance us from it. The apostle Paul himself said of himself that he had not yet achieved it. I, he said, don't think I have reached it. Forgetting the past and in tension towards what is ahead, I pursue only one thing. In tension, not relaxed; the only thing puts you in tension, not in relaxation. Many things relax, the only thing keeps you tense. And how long does it maintain tension?

CAPUT V.—5. Pus promissa delectatio laudis Dei, quae non datur impiis.—Quaere ergo quod promissum est filiis hominum, et audi quod sequitur: Filii autem hominum sub tegmine álarum tuarum sperabunt. Interim sperabunt, quamdiu in via sunt. Filii autem hominum sub tegmine alarum tuarum sperabunt. Spe enim salvi facti sumus (ib., 8,24). Hoc non pertinet ad nomines et iumenta, sperare sub tegmine alarum Dei. Et ecce spes lactat us, nourish us, confirm us, et in this laborious vita consoletur us; in ipsa spe cantamus Alleluia. Ecce spes quantum gaudium habet. Res ipsa quid erit? Quid erit quaeris? Audi quod sequitur: Inebriabuntur ab ubertate domus tuae (Ps 35,7-9). Huius reí spes est. Sitimus, esurimus, opus est ut satiemur: sed in via fames, in patria satietas. When satiabimur? Satiabor cum manifestata fuerit gloria tua (Ps 16,15). Mode autem gloria Dei nostri, gloria Christi nostri latet: et cum illo abscondita est et nostra. Sed cum Christus apparuerit vita vestra, tune et vos cum illo apparebitis in gloria (Col 3,4). Tune erit Alleluia in re: moda autem in spe. Spes illam cantat, amor cantat moda, amor cantabit et tune: sed moda cantat amor esuriens, tune cantabit amor fruens. Quid est enim Alleluia, fratres mei? Dixi vobis: Laus Dei est. Ecce moda verbum auditis, et in audiendo delectamini, et in delectatione laudatis. Si rorem sic amatis, fontem ipsum quomodo amabitis? Quod est enim stomacho ructanti ructatio, hoc est cordi saginato laudado. Yes

enim laudamus quod credimus, quomodo laudabimus cum víderimus? Ecce quod sibi Maria elegerat: sed significat vitam illam, nondum tenebat. CAPUT VI.—6. Duae vitae in Martha et María adumbratae. Unum necessarium. Dei fruitio erit beatis bonorum omnium loco.—Duae sunt vitae: una pertinens ad delectationem, altera pertinens ad necessitatem. Unum nos extendat, ne fines distendant et abrumpant ab uno. Ipsum unum dixit apostolus Paulus, quia nondum perceperat. Ego, inquit, non me arbitror apprehendisse. Cum venerimus, colligit, non

While we live here. When we have arrived at home, instead of keeping us tense, it will relax us. What is this excellent thing that we will possess when we have no need for anything? What is it that we will possess? I had intended to say what God will give to us that he will not give to others. To tell you something that makes you understand, listen to an example of what we cannot express. aut quia habemus, aut ut habeamus?) quando ergo dicitur quia cetera subtrahuntur, et solus Deus erit quo delectemur; quasi angustatur anima, quae consuevit multis delectan; et dicit sibi anima carnalis, carni addicta, carnalibus cupididatibus implicata, visco malarum cupiditatum involutas pennas habens, ne volet ad Deum, dicit sibi: Quid mihi erit, ubi non manducabo, ubi non bibam, ubi cum uxore mea non dormiam? What mihi gaudium erit? Hoc gaudium tuum de aegritudine est, non de sanitate. Certe ipsa caro tua in hoc tempore aliquando aegrotat, aliquando sana est. Intendite, ut alíquid dicam, unde capiatis, exemplum rei quam non possum dicere. Sunt quaedam aegrotantium desideria: ardent desiderio aut alicuius fontis, aut alicuius pomi; et sic ardent, ut existence quia si sani fue[1190]rint, fruí debenant ipsis desideriis suis. Venit sanitas, et perit cupiditas. Quod desiderabat, fastidit: quia hoc in illo febris quaerebat. Et qualis est ista sanitas, in qua convalescit aegrotus? CAPUT VIII.—Sanitas ista qua dicimur sani, quid est? Sed tamen hínc capite exemplum. Quia cummula sint aegrotantium desideria, quae ista sanitas tollit; quomodo illa tollít ista sanitas, sic omnia tollit immortalitas: quia sanitas nostra immortalitas est. Recolite Apostolum, et videte quid erit: Oportet corritptibile hoc induere incorruptionem, et moríale hoc induere immortalitatem (1 Cor 15,53). Et erimus aequales Angelis Dei (cf. Mt 22:30). Numquid illi miseri sunt, qui non epulantur? Nonne ideo beatiores, quia istis non indigent? An vero quilibet dives aequabitur Angelis? Angelí I will see divites sunt. Quid dicuntur divitae?

rich that can be equal to the angels? The angels are the truly rich. What is called riches? To have the means. The angels have breadth of means, because they have the maximum facilities. When it comes to praising a rich man, you hear it said: "How great is his greatness!" He is a gentleman, he is rich, he is a potentate. How great is his greatness! To go wherever he wants he has cavalry, he has means, he has servants and luggage. This is all that the rich man has: he goes where he wants without suffering discomfort. The angel is wherever he wants, without having to say: "Unce" or "Saddle", as the rich haughtily say, gladly inflating himself by having someone to tell to unce or saddle. Unhappy! These words denote illness rather than abundance of means. Thus, we will need nothing, and that is why we will be happy. We will, indeed, be full; but full of our God, and he will be for us everything that we here deem valuable. You seek food here as something of great value to you: God will be your food. You seek the carnal embrace here: My good consists in adhering to God. You seek riches: how can you lack anything having the one who made it all? And to reassure you with the words of the Apostle, this is how he spoke of that life: So that God may be all in all. Empower yourself. Angelí habent magnas facultates, who habent magnas facilitates. Audis cum laudatur dives: Quantum magnus est, dominus est, dives est, potens est. Quantum magnum ut eat quo vult, iumenta adsunt, sumptus adsunt, servi adsunt, ministry adsunt. Omnia ista habet dives: quo vult it, laborem non patitur. Angelus ubi voluerit, ibi erit; nec dicit: Iunge; nec dicit: Sterne; quod cum superbia dicunt divites, et tumescere inde volunt, quia habent quibus dicant: Iunge et Sterne. Infelix, verba ist sunt infirmitatis, non facultatis. Non ergo indigebimus: et ideo beati erimus. Pleni enim erimus, sed Deo nostro: et omnia quae hic pro magno desideramus, ipse nobis erit. Pro magno cibum hic quaeris. Deus tibi cibus erit. Ámplexum carnis hic quaeris: Mihi autem adhaerere Deo, bonum est (Ps 72,28). Divitias hic quaeris: quomodo tibi deerunt omnia, quando illum habebis qui fecit omnia? Et ut verbis Apostoli te faciam securum, de illa vita hoc dixit: Ut sit Deus omnia in omnibus (1 Cor 15:28).

Theme: Hallelujah. Location: Hippo. Date: Eighth Sunday of Easter.

It is convenient that we pay as much praise to our creator as we can. When we praise the Lord, dear brothers, we obtain some benefit while we are in tension towards his love. We have sung the Hallelujah. Hallelujah is the new song. The new man sings the new song. I have sung it; You have also sung it, the newly baptized, those who have just been renewed by it. I am going to exhort you according to the demands of fraternal charity; but not only to us; My exhortation is also addressed to those who listen to me as brothers and children: brothers because we were born by the same mother; children, because I have begotten you for the Gospel. Live well, my beloved, so that after having received such a great sacrament you can appear before the court with impeccable conduct. Correct vices, order customs, make room for virtues; May piety, holiness, chastity, humility and sobriety be present in each of you, so that, offering such fruits to God, he may delight in you, and you in him. Theme: Hallelujah. Place: Carthage. Date: Sunday, May 5, 418. 1. It pleases the Lord our God that we are here physically present to sing, together with your charity, the Hallelujah, which, translated into our language, means "Praise the Lord." Let us praise the Lord, brothers, with our lives and with our tongues, with our hearts and with our mouths, with our voices and with our habits. God wants us to sing Hallelujah to Him so that there is no discord in those who praise Him. Let us begin, then, by agreeing with our tongue and our life, our mouth and our conscience. Let words and customs agree, I repeat, lest good words be a testimony against bad customs. Oh happy Hallelujah from heaven; where the temple of God are the angels! The concord of those who praise him is great where the joy of the singers is assured; where no law in the members opposes the law of the mind; where there is no fight against ambition that endangers the victory of charity. Let us sing, then, here, still worried, the Hallelujah, so that we can sing it there without fear. Worried here, why? IN DIEBUS PASCHALIBUS, XXVII OF ALLELUIA

1. Laudare Deum oportet vita et lingua. Concordia et securitas perfection laudantium Deum non nisi in cáelo.—Quoniam placuit Domino Deo nostro, ut hic constituti praesentía corporali, etiam cum vestra Caritate illi cantoremus Alleluia, quod latine interpretatur: Laúdate Dominum; laudemus Dominum, fratres, vita et lingua, corde et ore, vocibus et moribus. Sic enim sibi dici vult Deus Alleluia, ut non sit in laudante discordia. Concordent ergo prius in nobis ipsis lingua cum vita, os cum conscientia. Concordent, inquam, voices cum moribus, ne forte bonae voices testimoníum dicant against bad mores. O felix Alleluia in cáelo, ubi templum Dei Angelí sunt! Ibi enim concordia summa laudantium, ubi est exsultatio secura cantantium: ubi nulla lex in membris repugnat Iegi mentís; ubi non est rixa cupiditatis, in [1191] qua periclitetur victoria caritatis. Hic ergo cantemus Alleluia adhuc solliciti, ut illic possimus aliquando cantore securi. Quare hic solliciti? Non vis ut sim sollicitus, quando lego: Numquid non tentatio est vita humano super terram

on earth? How can you expect me not to be worried when I am still told: Watch and pray so that you do not fall into temptation? How do you want me not to be worried, if temptation abounds so much that even prayer itself orders us to say: Forgive us our debts, just as we forgive our debtors? If we ask daily, we are daily debtors. Do you want me to feel safe when every day I have to ask for forgiveness for sins and help in the face of difficulties? After having said: Forgive us our debts, just as we forgive our debtors because of past sins, because of the dangers of the future, I immediately add: Do not lead us into temptation. How can we say that the people are in good, if they shout with me: Deliver us from evil? However, brothers, in the midst of this evil let us sing Hallelujah to the good God who delivers us from evil. Why do you look around you looking for the evil from which it must free you? Don't go far, don't disperse your mind's gaze everywhere. Come back to yourself, examine yourself. You are still bad. Therefore, when God delivers you from yourself, then he delivers you from evil. Listen to the Apostle and understand what evil you have to be freed from. I delight, he says, in the law of God according to the inner man; but I see another law in my members that resists the law of my mind and captivates me in the law of indwelling sin. Where? That captivates me in the law of sin that resides in my members, he said. I had thought that I had you captive of I know not what unknown barbarian people; that had you captive (Iob 7,1)? Non vis ut sim sollicitus, quando mihi adhuc dicitur: Vigilate et orate, ne intretis in temptationem (Mark 14,38)? Non vis ut sim sollicitus, ubi sic abundat tentatio, ut nobis ipsa praescribat oratio, quando dicimus: Dimitte nobis debita nostra, sicut et nos dimittimus debitoribus nostris? Quotidie petitionres, quotidie debitores. Vis ut sim securus, ubi quotidie peto indulgentiam pro peccatis, adiutorium pro periculis? Cum enim dixero propter praeterita peccata: Dimitte nobis debita nostra, sicut et nos dimittimus debitoribus nostris: continuo proptetfutura pericula addo et adiungo, Ne nos inferas in tentationem (Mt 6,12.13). How is autem populus in bono, when mecum clamat: Libera nos a malo? Et tamen, fratres, in isto adhuc malo cantemus Alleluia Deo bono, qui nos liberat a malo. Quid circum inspicis unde te libetet, quando te liberat a malo? Noli longe iré, noli aciem mentís circumquaque distendere.

The land will be returned to earth and the spirit will be received into heaven; hominibus dominis. Quae est, inquit, in membris meis. He exclaims ergo cum illo: Miser ego homo, quis liberabit me? When the Apostle spoke of this corruptible and mortal body, in a certain way he touched the flesh with his voice. Then what is written will be fulfilled: “Death has been swallowed up by victory.” Sing Hallelujah. incorruptible and immortal, when all temptation has disappeared... Indeed, the body is certainly dead. Why dead? For sin. The Spirit, on the other hand, is life—these are the words of the Apostle. Because? For justice. Do we then abandon the dead body? No; But listen: If the Spirit of him who raised Christ from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies. Now the body is animal, later it will be spiritual. For the first man was made a living soul, and the last a life-giving spirit. Consequently, he will also give life to your mortal bodies because of his Spirit who dwells in you. Happy Hallelujah! In peace and without any enemy! There will be no enemy nor will the friend perish. God is praised here and there; but here they praise him full of concern, there with full security; here those who will die, there those who will live forever; here in hope, there in reality; here on a trip, there already in the homeland. Now, therefore, my brothers, let us sing it, but as a solace in work, not as a delight in rest. Sing as passers-by sing; sing, but walk; comfort your work with singing, do not love laziness: sing and walk. What does "walk" mean? Move forward, move forward in good. According to the Apostle, there are some who are getting worse. You, if you advance, you walk; but advance in goodness, in right faith, in good works: sing and walk. Don't go off the path, don't turn back, don't stand still.

Topic: Commentary on Psalm 115:11. Location: Hippo. Memory of the twenty martyrs. Date: Eighth Sunday of Easter. Between 410 and 413.

Let us therefore praise the Lord our God not only with our voice, but also with our hearts, because whoever praises Him from the heart, praises Him with the voice of the inner man. 1. Quod hebraica lingua dícitur Alleluia, latine est Laúdate dominum. Laudemus ergo dominum deum nostrum, non tantum uoce sed etiam corde, quoniam qui corde laudat, interioris hominis uoce laudat. Vox ad nomines sonus est, uox ad deum affectus est. 2. Dixit quidam in ecstasi sua, sicut legistis, sicut audistis: Omnis homo mendax (Ps 115,11). Inde fuet qui non credebat, nisi tetigisset corpus domini. Mendacium ei uidebatur quod condiscipuli eius uerum Mariano, lector, and James, deacon, suffered martyrdom in Africa; more specifically, in Lambesa, being beheaded in 258, during the persecution of Valerian, the same year in which Saint Cyprian suffered martyrdom. The account of his martyrdom was written by an eyewitness. Augustine dedicates sermon 284 to them. It refers to the council held on the first day of May in the year 418 in Carthage against the 4Pelagians. This is supposed to be sermon 284; there is no absolute certainty.

Mister. The truth that the disciples announced to him seemed like a lie to him. It wasn't enough for him to hear the truth: he wanted to touch it too. The Lord made himself present to him, according to the story that follows in the gospel that will be read later. No one who hears that Every man is a liar should remain anchored in the lie, without wanting to get out of it, as if coiling himself in vain thoughts—since he is a lying man—and saying to himself: «Will I ever leave my human condition? If while I live here I am going to be a liar, it would be better for me to lie than for the Scripture, which says: Every man is a liar. Well, if I am truthful, the Scripture becomes a liar; but since the Scripture cannot be a liar, I must be one." Chattering these things, he thinks he will find himself safe in the port of lies, so to speak, a place where he will suffer shipwreck. You wanted to rest peacefully in the port. Listen to what rock you are going to crash against: You will cause all those who speak lies to perish. It is the same Scripture of God that says: You will cause to perish all those who speak lies. Then, since every man is a liar, you are going to cause them all to perish. What have we been told? What has been indicated to us? That we are liars in what we have. If, however, we want to be truthful, let us seek refuge in the Lord. From him we receive being truthful; of us, to be liars. 3. Listen to just one short and big example: brief, for loquebantur. the speed with which it is said, and great, for its load of wisdom. Pedro was the only one to show us what I want to tell you. When the Lord said to Christ: You are Christ, the Son of the living God, what did he answer? Blessed are you, Simon, son of Juan, because it was not flesh and blood that revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. What you said is true, but not from your point of view. Where did it come from, then? My Father who is in heaven has revealed it to you. Blessed, then, because it has come to you from God; of yours you cannot be anything but miserable.' After this, when the Lord had said to him: Blessed are you, because it was not flesh and blood that revealed it to you, but my Father who is in heaven; After these words, I repeat, Christ the Lord began to announce to them his passion and death. As they went, Peter replied: Far be it from you, Lord. Every man is a liar. See how, shortly before, Peter was truthful and now he is a liar. But where does Peter's being truthful come from? Flesh and blood did not reveal it to you, but my Father who is in heaven. Where does being a liar come from? Go away, Satan, for you do not like the things of God, but those of men. Every man is a liar. To us, then, it has been said: Every man is a liar, so that we may flee from ourselves and run to God, who alone is true. magno quia sapienter adpenditur. Petrus unus otendit hoc quod uolo dici. When Christo said: “Tu es Christus, filius dei uiui” (Mt 16:16-23), what did he respond? Beatus is Simón Bar-lona, ​​quia non tibi reuelauit caro et sanguis, sed pater meus qui in caelis est. Verum dixisti, sed non tuum b. Where ergo? Vater meus qui in caelis est tibi reuelauit. Inde beatus quia de dei, non miser nisi de tuo. [342] Post haec, ubi ei dominus ait: Beatus es quia non tibi reuelauit caro et sanguis, sed pater meus qui in caelis est, post haec uerba coepit dominus Christus praenuntiare passionem et mortem suam. Ibi continued Petrus: Absit a te, domine. Omnis homo mendax. Ecce paulo ante Petrus uerax, ecce moda Petrus mendax. Sed unde Petrus uerax?
