Commentary on Psalm 117:24
Topic: Commentary on Psalm 117:24. Place: Carthage. Date: Eighth Sunday of Easter. From the year 410.

1. We have sung to God: This is the day that he made. Let us speak about it whatever the Lord grants us. Scripture, certainly prophetic, wanted to indicate something to us here. This is not an ordinary day, perceptible by the eyes of the flesh; nor of the day that has sunrise and sunset, but of another that could know beginning, but does not know the sunset. Let's see what the same psalm had said previously: The stone that the builders rejected has become the head of the corner. It has been the work of the Lord; He is the admirable stone in our eyes. And it continues: This is the day that the Lord made. Let's associate the beginning of this day with the cornerstone. Who is the cornerstone that the builders rejected but Christ the Lord, whom the Jewish doctors rejected? The Jewish doctors, knowledgeable in the law, rejected him when they said: This man who violates the Sabbath does not come from God. You have already said: This man who violates the Sabbath does not come from God. This stone that they rejected has become a corner head. How has it become a head of angle?
ALIVS SERMO QVEM DIXIT AD BASILICAM MAIOREM EADEM DIE

1. Quod cantauimus deo: Hic est dies quem fecit (Ps 117,24), hinc loquamur quod dederit dominus. Hic scriptura utique prophetica aliquid nos intellegere uoluit. Quem diem non uulgarem, non conspicuum oculis carnis! Non eum diem qui oritur et occidit sed diem (1195) qui potuit scire ortum, nescire occasum! Videamus quod supra dixerat idem psalmus: Lapidem quem reprobauerunt aedificantes, hic factus est in caput anguli. A domino factus est, iste est mirabilis in oculis nostris (lo 9,16). Et sequitur: Hic est dies quem fecit dominus. Exordium diei huius a lapide angulari sumamus. [346] Quis est lapis angularis quem reprobauerunt aedificantes nisi dominus Christus quem reprobauerunt ludaeorum doctors? Legis enim periti doctors ludaeorum reprobauerunt eum dicentes: Non est iste a deo qui soluit sabbatum (Mt 21,9). Iam dixistis: Non est iste a deo qui soluit sabbatum. Lapidem quem reprobauerunt hic factus^ est in caput anguli. Quomodo in caput anguli? Quare angularis lapis dictus

it? Why is Christ called the cornerstone? Because every angle unites two walls in opposite directions. The apostles came from the circumcision, from the Jewish people; From him also came that crowd that went before and behind the donkey that was carrying him, proclaiming the same thing that appears in this psalm: Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; from him came many churches of which the apostle Paul says: He was unknown to the churches of Judea that exist in Christ; They had only heard the following: "He who once persecuted us now announces the faith that previously devastated," and in me they magnified God. They were Jews, but they had adhered to Christ like the apostles; coming and believing in Christ, they formed a wall. Another wall remained: the church from the Gentiles. They found each other: peace in Christ, unity in Christ, who made the two one reality. Behold the day that the Lord made. Consider the day in its entirety: head and body; the head is Christ; the body, the Church. This is the day that the Lord made. 2. Remember the first formation in the world. Darkness was over the deep and the Spirit of God hovered over the waters. And God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light. And God separated the light from the darkness, and called the light day, and the darkness night. Think about the darkness of these 1 before approaching the forgiveness of sins. The darkness, then, is Christus? Quia omnis angles duos paetes de diuerso pacificat. Venerunt apostoli de circumcisione, uenerunt de gente ludaeorum, uenerunt inde et illae turbae quae praecedebant et sequebantur iumentum eius, dicentes quod in hoc ipso psalmo est: Benedictus qui uenit in nomine domini (Ps 117,26), uenerunt inde tot ecclesiae de quibus dicit apostolus Paulus: Eram ignotus faciei ecclesiis ludaeae quae sunt in Christo, tantum autem audiebant quia Ule qui aliquando nos persequebatur, nunc euangelizat fidem quam aliquando uastabat et in me magnificabant deum (Gal 1,22-24). Iudaei sed adhaerentes Christo sicut apostoli, uenientes et credentes Christo et unum parietem facientes. Restabat alius paries, ecclesia de gentibus ueniens. Inuenerunt se; pax in Christo, unitas in Christo qui fecit utraque unum (cf. Eph 2:14). Ipse est dies quem fecit dominus. Totum diem intellege caput et corpus, caput Christus, corpus ecclesia. This is dies quem fecit dominus. 2. Recolite primam mundi condicionem. Tenebrae were super abyssum et spiritus dei superferebatur super aquam.

Et dixit deus: Fiat lux et facta est lux. Et diuisit deus luzem a tenebris et luzem uocauit diem, tenebras autem uocauit noctem (Gen 1,2-5). Cogitate tenebras istorum antequam uenirent ad remissionem peccatorum. Tenebrae ergo erant Those baptized at the last Easter Vigil. During Easter week they occupied a reserved place in the church and wore white dresses. Hence Augustine can formulate the living contrast with darkness.

They were over the abyss before those sins were forgiven. But the Spirit of God hovered over the waters. They went down into the waters 2; The spirit of God hovered over the waters; The darkness of sins was expelled: these are the day that the Lord made3. To this day the Apostle says: For you were once darkness; Now, however, you are light in the Lord. Did he say, "You were darkness in the Lord"? Darkness in yourselves, light in the Lord. God called the light day because by his grace everything is done. Ellos pudieron ser tinieblas por sí mismos; but they could not have become light if the Lord had not made them. This is the day that the Lord made: the Lord made it, not the day itself. 3. Was not Thomas a man, one of the disciples, a man of the masses, to use this expression? His fellow disciples said to him: We have seen the Lord. And he replied to them: Unless I touch him and put my finger in his side, I will not believe. Do the evangelists announce it to you and you don't believe them? The world believed, and one disciple did not believe. It was said of them: Their voice went out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the earth. His words come out, they reach the ends of the earth, everyone believes; Instead, they all announce it to one and he does not believe. Aún no era día que hizo el Señor. The darkness was still in the abyss; In the depths of the human heart: there was darkness. Come he, come the head of this day, and super abyssum, antequam ista fuessent dimissa peccata. Sed ípz[348]ritus dei superferebatur super aquas. Descenderunt isti in aquis, super aquas ferebatur spiritus dei, pulsae sunt tenebrae peccatorum, isti dies quem fecit dominus. Huic diei apostolus dicit: Fuistis enim diquando tenebrae, nunc autem lux in domino (Eph 5,8). Numquid said: Fuistis tenebrae in domino? Tenebrae in uobis, lux in domino. Quia iste est dies quem fecit dominus, non ipse dies, sed dominus. 3. Numquid non homo erat Thomas, unus de discipulis quasi homo de turba? Dicebant ei condiscipuli eius: Vidimus dominum. Et dicebat ipse: Nisi teligero, nisi digitum misero in latus (1196) eius, non credapi (lo 20,25). Euangelistae tibi adnuntiant et non credis ipsis? Credidit mundus et non credit discipulus.

De ipsis dictum est: In omnem terram exiit sonus eorum et in fines orbis terrae uerba eorum (Ps 18,5). Say, suffering himself with humility and without anger, as a doctor: «Come, he said to him; Come, touch this and believe.” You said, "If I don't touch it, if I don't put my finger in, I won't believe." «Come, touch me, put your finger in, and do not be an unbeliever, but a believer. Come, put your finger in. "I knew your wounds, I saved my scar for you." By effectively putting his hand in, his faith became complete. What is the fullness of faith? Believe that Christ is not only man nor only God, but man and God. That is the fullness of faith, for the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. In this way, the disciple, after the scars and limbs of his savior were offered to him to touch, as soon as he touched him, he exclaimed: My Lord and my God! He touched the man, and he recognized God; He touched the flesh, and turned his gaze to the Word, since the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. This Word endured his flesh being suspended from a tree; This Word endured its flesh being pierced by nails; This Word endured his flesh being pierced by a spear; This Word endured his flesh being placed in the grave; This Word resurrected his flesh, he offered it to his disciples, so that they could see it, and to their hands, so that they could touch it. They touch it and exclaim: My Lord and my God! This is the day that the Lord made. dicat patiens, mitis, non iratus quia medicus: Veni, inquit, ueni, tange hoc et crede. Dixisti: Nisi tetigero, nisi digitum misero, non credam. Come, tange, mitte digitum. Et noli esse incredulus sed fidelis. Come, mitte digitum. Sciebam uulnera tua, seruaui tibi cicatricem meam. Sed plan mittens manum suam compleuit fidem. Quae est enim fidei plenitudo? Vt non credatur Christus tantum homo nec credatur Christus tantummodo deus, sed [350] homo et deus. Ipsa est fidei plenitudo, quia Verbum caro factum est et habitauit in nobis (lo 1,14). Ergo iste discipulus oblatis sibi tangendis cicatricibus et membris saluatoris sui, at ubi tetigit exclamauit: Dominus meus et deus meus. Hominem tetigit, deum cognovit et tetigit carnem, respexit ad uerbum, quia Verbum caro factum est et habitauit in nobis. Verbum hoc <passum est> carnem suam suspendí in ügno, Verbum hoc passum est in carne sua clauos figi, Verbum hoc passum est carnem suam lancea transforari, Verbum hoc passum est carnem suam in sepulchro poni, Verbum hoc resuscitauit carnem suam, obtulit aspectibus discipulorum uidendam, praebuit manibus contrectandam. Tangunt, exclamant: Dominus meus et deus meus.
This is dies quem fecit dominus.

Topic: The faith of the apostle Thomas (Jn 20:19-29). Location: Hippo. Date: Eighth Sunday of Easter. Early years.

1. Today is for us a symbol of eternal happiness. This day will pass, but the life symbolized in it will not pass in the same way. Therefore, brothers, I exhort and beg you in the name of Jesus Christ our Lord, who has forgiven our sins, who wanted his blood to be the price of our sins, who deigned to make us brothers, unworthy as we were even to be his servants, that all your gaze - that is why you are Christians and bear his name on your forehead and in your heart - be directed to that life that we have in common with the angels, where rest will be eternal, joy eternal, inexhaustible happiness; where there will be no disorder, no sadness, no death. Such a life cannot be known except by those who experience it; but they cannot experience it except those who believe. If you demand that I show you what God has promised you, it is not possible for me. However, you have heard how John's gospel ends: Blessed are those who believe without having seen. I. We co-create, and we will see it at the same time. Let us not be harsh in the face of the word of God. Would it be okay, perhaps, for Christ to come down from heaven now to show us his scars? This eighth day symbolizes, therefore, the new life that will follow the end of the world, and the seventh, the future rest of the saints on this earth. As the Scripture says, God will reign with his saints on earth, and will have here a Church of which no evil will be a part, isolated and purified from all contagion of evil; Church symbolized in those one hundred and fifty-three fish that I have already spoken of on some occasion, as I remember 2. The Church will appear here, above all, enveloped in great radiance, honor and justice. Deception, lying, or a wolf hiding under sheep's clothing will not be possible there. For, as it is written, the Lord will come and will illuminate the hidden darkness and will reveal the thoughts of the heart, and then everyone will receive praise from God. Therefore, the wicked will not be there; They will have already been separated. Then, as in an era, the clean ground, which is the multitude of the saints, will appear and will be taken to the heavenly granary of immortality. Like wheat, it is cleaned in the same place where it has been threshed, and the place where the grains suvidebimus. Non simus duri adversus verbum Dei. Numquid enim, fratres, dignum est ut Christus descendat moda de cáelo, et scars suas nobis ostendat? Ideo illi incredulo ostendere dignitus est, ut obiurgaret dubios, et instrueret credituros. 2. Octavi et septimi diei mysterium. Regnum Christi et sanctorum in terra post separationem malorum. Sabhatismus sanctorum in terra. Octavus ergo iste dies in fine saeculi novam vitam significat: septimus quietemfuturam sanctorum in hac terra. Regnabit enim Dominus in terra cum sanctis suis, sicut dicunt Scripturae, et habebit hic Ecclesiam, quo nullus malus intrabit, separatam atque purgatam ab omni contagione nequitiae; quam significant centum quinquaginta three illi pisces (cf. ib., 21,11), de quibus iam, quantum memini, aliquando tractavimus. Nam Ecclesia hic primo appeared in magna claritate et dignitate et iustitia. Non ibi libebit decipere, non lieri, non sub ovis pelle lupum latere.

Veniet enim Dominus, sicut scriptum est, et illuminabit abscondita tenebrarum et manifestabit cogitationes cordium: et tune laus erit unicuique a Deo (1 Cor 4,5). Iniqui ergo non ibi erunt: íam enim separabuntur. Tune tanquam massa purgata apparebit, veluti inarea, multitudo sanctorum, et sic mittetur in horreum caeleste immortalitatis. Sicut enim frumentum prius ubi tumbatur, ibi purgatur; et locus ubi frumenta pertulerunt tumbam, ut a palea mundarentur, decoratur dignitate massae See note 1 to sermon 248 and complementary note 30: The symbolism of the number 15} p.807.

They fried the threshing to be separated from the chaff, it is embellished with the beauty of the already clean ground. In fact, after cleaning we see on the threshing floor, on the one hand, the pile of straw and on the other, the ground of wheat. We know the purpose for which the straw is intended and how the wheat is what gives satisfaction to the farmer. On the threshing floor, the wheat appears already separated from the chaff, and after so much fatigue the sight of that heap previously hidden in the straw and invisible while the threshing lasted causes satisfaction; It is then taken to the barn, where it is kept hidden. The same thing happens in this world: you see how it is threshed in this age; but the chaff is so united to the wheat that it is difficult to distinguish it, because it has not yet been winnowed. In the same way, after the winnowing of the day of judgment, the mound of saints will appear, resplendent in their dignity, powerful in merits, having before their eyes the mercy of their liberator. Such will be the seventh day 3. The first day, so to speak, of this entire world is the time that goes from Adam to Noah; the second, from Noah to Abraham; the third, from Abraham to David; the fourth, from David to the transmigration to Babylon; the fifth, from the transmigration until the arrival of our Lord Jesus Christ. Since the coming of the Lord, therefore, the sixth day is in progress; On the sixth day we live. Therefore, purgatae. Videmus quippe inarea post ventilationem, acervum palearum ex una parte, et acervum frumenti ex alia. Quo autem palea destinata sit, novimus; et quemadmodum agricolis faciant frumenta laetitiam. Quomodo ergo apparet in area prius frumentum a palea separatum, et cum gaudium fecerit after so many labors inspecta illa congeries, quae latebat in palea, quae non videbatur, quando tumbabatur; deinde in horreum mittitur, atque in secreto servatur: sic in isto saeculo, videtis quomodo shredding haec area, sed palea frumento ita permixta est, ut difficile discernatur; quia nondum ventilata est. Sic ergo post ventilationem diei iudicii apparebit massa sanctorum, fulgens dignitate, praepotens meritis, et misericordiam liberatoris sui prae se gerens. Et ipse erit septimus dies. Quasi primus dies sit in toto saeculo tempus quod est ab Adam usque ad Noe; secundus, a Noe usque ad Abraham, et quomodo iam dividit Evangelium Matthaei, tertius ab Abraham usque ad David; quártus, to David usque ad transmigrationem in Babyloniam; quintus, a transmigratione usque ad adventum Domini nostri Iesu Christi (cf. Mt [1198] 2,17).

Ab adventu ergo Domini sextus agitur, in sixth die sumus. Et ideo quomodo formatus est homo in Genesi As will also appear in sermon 260 C (= MAI 94), it is evident that Augustine understood the seventh day as an intermediate temporal space between the end of the world and the eighth day, a symbol of new and eternal life. Like many other Fathers until the 4th century, Augustine believed in a glorious kingdom of Christ and the saints on earth, prior to the final resurrection. Unlike other authors, however, he does not mention the thousand years that this paradisiacal state would last. He refers to this primitive belief of his in The City of God (XX 7,1), to refute it below. The same in XX 21 and The Heresies 8. Read G. FOLLIET, La typologie du sabbat cbez saint Augustin. As man was created on the sixth day in the image of God, according to Genesis, so also in this time, like the sixth day of the entire century, we are renewed in baptism to receive the image of our Creator. But once this sixth day has passed, after that winnowing there will be rest, and the saints and righteous of God will keep the Sabbath. After the seventh, when the brightness of the harvest appears on the threshing floor, the brilliance and merit of the saints, we will go to that life and that rest of which it was said: No eye has seen, no ear has heard, nor has it entered into the human heart what God has prepared for those who love him. So, let's put it this way, it's back to the beginning. In fact, when these seven days have been completed, the eighth day will also be the first; After the seven ages of the present century are concluded and elapsed, we will return to that immortality and happiness from which man fell. This is why the Easter Octave ends the mystery of the newly baptized. The same number 7, multiplied by itself, gives 49; and, if you add 1, you get 50, and you return, in a certain sense, to the beginning. We celebrate the number 50 until Pentecost in a symbolic way. Number that also results from another operation: to 40 the number 10 is added, the denarius of the reward. Both methods lead to 50, which, multiplied by 3 in attention to the mystery of the Trinity, gives 150. If the number 3 is added, as a witness and indicator of the Trinity and the previous triplication, we notice that the Church is symbolized in those 153 fish. sixth die ad imaginem Dei (cf. Gen 1:26-27), sic et in isto tempore, quasi sixth die totius saeculi, renovamur in Baptism, ut recipiamus imaginem Conditoris nostri. Sextus autem dies iste cum transierit, veniet requies post íllam ventilationem, et sabbatizabunt sancti et iusti Dei. Post septimum autem, cum apparuerit in area dignitas messis, fulgor, meritumque sanctorum, ibimus in illam vitam et in illam requiem, de qua dictum: Quia oculus non vidit, nec auris audivit, nec in cor hominis ascendit, quae praeparavit Deus diligentibus se (1 Cor 2,9). Tune velut ad caput reditur. Quomodo enim cum peracti fuerint isti septem dies, octavus ipse est qui primus: sic post terminatas et peractas aetates septem saeculi transeuntis, ad illam immortalitatem beatitudinemque rediemus, de qua lapsus est homo. Et ideo octavee complent sacramenta infantium.

Hinc et ipse septenarius numerus septies multiplicatus facit quadraginta novem; et addito uno tanquam reditur ad caput, et fiunt quinquaginta: qui numerus a nobis usque ad Pentecosten in mysterio celebratur. Qui etiam secundum illam divisionem quadragesimi numeri, cui accessit tanquam merces denarius, diverse ratione idem rursus apparet. Ambae quippe rationes ad eumdem quinquagenarium numerum redeunt. Qui ter multiplicatus propter mysterium Trinitatis, facit centum quinquaginta. Addito quippe ipso ternario, tanquam teste atque Index triplicationis et Trinitatis, intellegimus Ecclesiam in illis piscibus centum quinquaginta tribus.

But now, in the meantime, until we reach that rest; in this time of fatigue, while we are in the night, while we do not see what we expect and we walk through the desert; until we reach the heavenly Jerusalem, like a land of promise flowing with milk and honey; Now then, while temptations continue unabated, let us do good. Always have medicine at hand to apply to practically everyday wounds, medicine that consists of good works of mercy. Indeed, if you want to obtain God's mercy, be merciful yourself. If you, who are a man, deny another man humanity, God will also deny you divinity, that is, the incorruption of immortality that makes us gods. God doesn't need anything from you; You, however, have need of God. He asks nothing of you to be happy; You, on the other hand, will not be able to be happy if you do not get it from him. What do you get from it? I don't know if you would dare to complain if you received from him who created everything the most excellent of created things. But he does not give you any created thing, but gives himself to you so that you can enjoy him; gives you himself the creator of everything. What thing created by him can be better and more beautiful than the one who made it? And how will he give it to you? For your merits perhaps? If you seek the result of your merits, pay attention to your sins. Listen to the sentence pronounced by God against transgressive man: You are earth, and to earth you will return. The precept had been preceded by the threat: The day you touch it you will die.

If you go after the merit of sins, what will meet you but punishment? Therefore forget your merits, lest they cause terror in your heart. Or, better yet, do not forget them, lest out of pride you reject mercy. We entrust ourselves to God, brothers, through works of mercy. Confess the Lord, because he is good, because his mercy is eternal. Confess that God is merciful and wants to forgive the sins of those who confess it. But offer him a sacrifice. Have pity on man, O man, and God will have pity on you. You and the other are two men, that is, two miserable people. God, on the other hand, is not miserable, but he is merciful. If a miserable person has no compassion for another miserable person, how can he beg for mercy from someone who will never be miserable? Pay attention to what I am going to say, brothers. If someone is cruel to a castaway, for example, his cruelty will last until he finds himself in the same situation. If he has also experienced it in himself, when he happens to see a shipwrecked man, he will remember his past life, and such misfortune, similar to his own, will move him. If participation in the same nature had not been able to bend him to mercy, participation in the same misfortune bends him. He who was once a slave, how quickly he takes pity on another slave! He who was a day laborer, how quickly he associates himself with the pain of a day laborer defrauded of his wages! Whoever once cried for the same thing, feels sorry for the man who cries bitterly for his son. So, whatever the hardness of the human heart, it is softened by sharing such pain. Yes, well, you,

Misericordiae opera commendat.—Sed interim moda, doñee veniamus ad illam requiem, isto tempore quo laboramus, et in nocte sumus, quamdiu non videmus quod speramus, et in eremo iter agimus, doñee ad Iemsalem caelestem, veluti ad terram promissionis fluentem lac et mel, veniamus: nunc ergo cum temptationes non cessant, bene operemur. Medicina semper adsit, veluti prope quotidianis adhibenda vulneribus. Est autem medicine in bonis operibus misericordiae. Si enim vis impetrare misericorde Dei, este misericors. Si tu negas homini, cum tu bomo sis, humanitatem, negabit tibi et Deus divinitatem, hoc est incorruptionem immortalitatis, qua nos facit déos. Non enim a te quidquam indiget Deus: tu autem indiges a Deo. Nihil a te ille petit, ut beatus sit: tu autem, nisi ab illo accipias, beatus esse non poteris. Quid ab illo accipis? Nescio utrum auderes conqueri si ab illo, qui omnía condidit, acciperes aliquid quod excellentissimum condidit. At ille non aliquid ex iis quae condidit; sed se ipsum tibi dat ad fruendum, se ipsum omnium conditorem. Quid enim ex iis quae facta sunt ab illo, pulchrius et melius potest esse eo qui fecit? that either you were miserable or you fear being so - while you live here you must not only fear being what you were not, but also remember what you were and think about what you are; If, then, you, I repeat, who are situated between past miseries and the fear of the future and present pain, do not feel sorry for an unfortunate man who needs your help, do you expect him to feel sorry for you whom misery never reaches? My brothers, all of you who are going to return to your homes without, from this moment on, seeing each other again, except perhaps on some other solemn feast 4, practice mercy, since sins are abundant. There is no other rest or other path to reach God, to reintegrate ourselves with him, to reconcile ourselves with the one whom we have offended at great danger to ourselves. We must come to his presence; let our works speak there in our favor, and speak in such a way as to overcome our offenses. Punishment or rest will be deserved depending on whether the sins or good works are more numerous. In the Church there are two kinds of mercy: one is such that it does not involve the expenditure of money nor fatigue; another that requires from us either the service of action or the expenditure of money. That which requires neither money nor fatigue from us lies in the soul, and consists in forgiving the one who te qui aut miser Fuisti, aut times ne miser sis (quamdiu enim hic vivis, et timere deben quod non Fuisti, et meminisse quod fueris, et cogitare quid sis): positus ergo et in memoria praeteritarum miseriarum, et in timore Futurerum, et afflictione praesentium, non misereris calamitosi hominis et egentis ope tua, et exspectas ut misereatur tibi ille, quem never tangit miseria? Et tu non das ex eo quod a Deo accepisti, et vis ut det tibi Deus ex eo quod a te non accepit? 4. Opera misericordiae overcome our offenses. Misericordia gemina.—Misericordiam, fratres mei, omnes qui ituri estis ad domos vestras, et ex hoc vix nos videbimus, nisi per aliquam solemnitatem, misericordiam operamini, quia abundant peccata. Alia requies, alia via non est, qua perveniamus ad Deum, qua redintegremur, qua reconciliemur ei, quem periculosissime offendimus. Venturi sumus in conspectum eius: loquantur ibi pro nobis opera nostra; et ita loquantur, ut superent offensiones nostras.

Quod enim amplius fuerit, hoc obtinebit, vel ad poenam, si peccata meruerint; vel ad requiem, if opera bona. offended To give this alms you have the treasure in your heart: there you communicate directly with God. You are not told: "Take out your wallet, open the chest or the barn"; nor: "Come, walk, run, hurry, intercede, speak, visit, be strong." Without moving from your spot, you threw from your heart the two things that you had against your brother: you did a work of mercy without any expense, without any fatigue, with the sole kindness, with the sole merciful thought. If we said: "Give your goods to the poor," we could be called demanding. We are certainly soft and forgiving, at least now when we tell you: “Give without losing anything; forgive so that you may be forgiven." But let us also say this: "Give, and it will be given to you." The Lord united both things in a single precept, mentioning these two types of mercy: Forgive, and you will be forgiven: the mercy of forgiveness; Give, and it will be given to you: the mercy of the generous. See if it is not more than what God gives us. You forgive a man, because it was a man who harmed another man in you; God forgives you, in whom you, man, offended God. Is offending a man the same as offending God? Therefore what he granted you is more, since you forgave an offense against a man, while he forgave the offense against God. Pay attention to another kind of mercy: that of almsgiving. You give bread, he gives you health; You give a thirsty person a glass of any drink, he gives you the drink of his wisdom. Does what you give and what you receive allow comparison? See how you have to work with interests. If you want to be usurepeccavit. Ad hanc eleemosynam impendendam thesaurus tuus in corde tuo est: ibi you explain yourself coram Deo. Non tibi [1200] dicitur: Profer sacculum, aperi arcam, resigna horreum; ñeque hoc tibi dicitur: Veni, ambula, curre, festina, intercede, loquere, visita, labora. Stans uno loco proiecisti de pectore tuo duo tenes contra fratrem tuum, fecisti misericordiam, nullo sumptu, nullo labore, sola bonitote, sola misericordiae cogitatione. Nam si dicamus: Erógate res vestras pauperibus; duri videbimur. Certe vel nunc lenes et facil sumus, quando dicimus: Impendíte unde nihil minuetis, dimittite ut dimittatur vobis. ro, I don't forbid it at all; But it lends with interest to those who do not become poorer by giving back more and whose responsibility is also to ensure that you receive better and more abundantly the same thing that you give them, whatever it may be. 5. I want to warn your charity about another thing: know that whoever personally gives something to the poor performs a double work of mercy. We must not only think about the goodness of the giver, but also the humility of the one who serves. I do not know in what way, my brothers, when the well-off reaches out his hand to the needy, the soul of the first seems to feel compassion for the common humanity and weakness. Although one gives and the other receives, those who serve and those served are united, since we are not united by misfortune, but by humility. Your wealth will be for you and your children, if it pleases God. But there is no mention of this earthly abundance, which you often notice is harmful. The treasure lies peacefully at home, but it does not let its owner rest peacefully. Fear the thief, the door-breaker, the unfaithful servant, the powerful and unscrupulous neighbor. The more you have, the greater the fear. Sunt enim homines, qui propterea vacaverunt With the arrival of Constantine and his pro-Christian policy, the civil calendar was gradually Christianized. First, Sunday was declared a holiday, prohibiting all judicial proceedings and traditional pagan entertainment. Then the great Christian holidays (Christmas, Epiphany, Easter, Pentecost) were declared non-working days, and all judicial and economic activities were also banned, in addition to pagan games. The Easter fortnight is a period of judicial holidays, which were also suspended during Lent, as well as the execution of capital sentences.
Pardons always took place on the occasion of the Easter holidays. See J. GAUDEMET, L'Église dans l'empire romain (IVe-Ve siécles) (Paris 1958) p.660-661.

Topic: The faith of the apostle Thomas (Jn 20:19-29). Location: Hippo. Date: Eighth Sunday of Easter. Starting from 409. In order not to drag on, since we have a lot to do, my sermon to those regenerated in baptism who today are going to mix with the people 1 will be brief, but rich in content. You who have been baptized and today fulfill the mystery of your octave, welcome these brief words and understand that the circumcision of the flesh, which was a figure, has been transferred to the circumcision of the heart. According to the ancient law, circumcision of the flesh took place on the eighth day, precisely in honor of Christ the Lord, who was resurrected on the eighth day of the Lord, after the seventh day or Sabbath. It was commanded that circumcision be done with stone knives: the stone was Christ. You are called infants because you have been born again, you have entered the new life and you have been reborn for eternal life, if you do not suffocate with your evil living what has been reborn in you. You are going to be restored to the people and you are going to mix with the crowd of the faithful; be careful not to SERMO

Topic: The sacraments. Location: Hippo. Date: Year 393-405.

1. My sermon is addressed to you, newborn children, little ones in Christ, new shoot of the Church, grace of the Father, fertility of the mother, pious germ, new swarm, flower of our honor and fruit of our fatigue, joy and my crown; My sermon is addressed to all of you who are firm in the Lord. I speak to you in the words of the Apostle: See that the night has passed and the day is approaching; lay aside the works of darkness and put on the armor of light; walk honestly as in the day; not in feasting and drunkenness, not in lovemaking and debauchery, not in disputes and envy; but rather put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and do not play the game of the flesh by satisfying its desires, to clothe with life whom you clothed with the sacrament. For you who have been baptized have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, male or female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus. Such is the power of the sacrament: it is a symbol of new life, which begins in the present time with the forgiveness of all past sins and will reach its fullness in the resurrection of the dead. There are those who have only clothed themselves in Christ by having received the sacrament, but are naked of him in terms of faith and customs. Let them not tell us, then: "If we already have baptism, what are you going to give us?" They do not know what they say and they do not even want to read what the Holy Scripture attests, namely, that within the Church itself, in the community of the members of Christ, there were many who were baptized in Samaria who did not receive the Holy Spirit and who remained only with baptism until the apostles arrived from Jerusalem; and that, on the contrary, Cornelius and those who were with him deserved to receive the Holy Spirit before receiving the sacrament of baptism. In this way, God made it clear that the seal of salvation is one thing and salvation itself is another; that one thing is the external form of piety and another is the force of piety. "If we already have baptism, they say, what are you going to give us?" Oh sacrilegious vanity, to think that the Church of Christ that they do not possess is nothing, so that they even think that those who join it receive nothing! Let the prophet Amos tell them: Woe to those who turn Zion into nothing! «If I already have baptism,

He says, what can I receive? You will receive the Church that you do not possess, you will receive the unity that you do not have, you will receive the peace that you lack. And, if all this seems to you to be nothing, fight, deserter, against your emperor, who tells you: He who does not gather with me scatters. The Spirit mentioned here, and which you do not have, is the author of all this. Did you know how to endure, you who separated from the Church? I hope, to which I exhort you and which I beg of you, that you preserve in its entirety what you have received, and by progressing you achieve greater goals. Today is the eighth of your birth; Today the seal of faith acquires its perfection in you, which in the ancient fathers was carried out through the circumcision of the flesh on the eighth day of carnal birth. In that human member, thanks to which the man who will have to die is born, the plundering of mortality was symbolized. Topic: Exhortation to bear witness to the truth (Acts 4:19-20). Winepress: Hippo. Date: Eighth Sunday of Easter. From the year 410. 1 • When the blessed apostles began to perform wonders and healings in the name of Christ, the Jews, filled with anger, forbade them to speak in the name of the one who had chosen them and had granted them the power to do such things. But they answered them: Judge for yourselves whether it is right before God to obey you rather than him; We cannot remain silent about what we have seen and heard. They declared themselves witnesses of Christ; Those who in our language we call witnesses are called martyrs in Greek. Thus, by saying: We cannot remain silent about what we have seen and heard, they disregarded the prohibition of some men to obtain the blessing of God. They saw and heard; and us, what? We too must be announcers. But we have seen nothing; Let us therefore preach what we have heard, since the Apostle says: Hearing comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ. Topic: The ascension of the Lord. Place: Carthage. Date: Feast of the Ascension. Year 410 or 418.

1. The resurrection of the Lord is our hope; his ascension, our glorification. Today we celebrate the solemnity of the Ascension. If, then, we properly, faithfully, devoutly, holy and piously celebrate the ascension of the Lord, let us ascend with him and have our hearts lifted up. Ascending is not equivalent to becoming arrogant. We must have our hearts lifted up, but towards the Lord. Have your heart lifted up, but not eo fons aquae salientis in vitam aeternam (lo 4,14). Securi enim praedicatis, quia non mentimini de fonte veritatis: accepistis, quod in lingua ructatis. Nana si de vestro dicere volueritis, mendaces eritis: hoc dicit ipse psalmus: ego dixi in ecstasi mea, omnis homo mendax (Ps 115,11). Quid est, omnis homo mendax? Omnis Adam mendax. Expolia te Adam, et induere Christum, et non eris mendax. Sufficiant caritati vestrae, quia fines agenda sunt. Explicit tractatus de dominico octarum sanctae Paschae. II. SERMO

The ascension of the Lord

because he said: No one ascends into heaven except he who came down from heaven, the son of man who is in heaven. It seems that these words refer only to him, as if none of us had access to him. But such words were said in attention to the unity that we form, according to which he is our head and we are his body. No one, then, but him, since we are him in that he is the son of man through us, and we are children of God through him. Thus speaks the Apostle: Just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, although they are many, are one body, so also Christ. He did not say, "So is Christ," but so also is Christ. Christ, then, is made up of many members, which are one body. He descended from heaven by mercy and no one ascends except him, since we also are in him by grace. According to this, no one descended and no one ascended except Christ. It is not about diluting the dignity of the head in the body, but rather about not separating the unity of the body from the head. It does not say "of your descendants," as if they were many, but: In your descendants who are Christ. Thus, then, he calls Christ the offspring of Abraham; and yet the same Apostle said: For you are descendants of Abraham. Therefore, if it is not a question of descendants, as if they were many, but of only one, and this is that of Abraham, who is Christ; that of Abraham, which is us, when he ascends to heaven, we are not separated from him. He who descended from heaven does not look with bad eyes on us going there, but tatio, quia dixit, nemo ascendit in caelum, nisi qui de cáelo descendit, filius hominis qui est in cáelo: de solo enim se ipso videtur dixisse, quasi hoc nemo nostrum possit accipere; sed dictum est propter unitatem, quia caput nostrum est, et nos corpus eius. Hoc ergo nemo nisi ipse, quia et nos ipse secundum id quod ipse filius hominis propter nos, et nos deí filii propter ipsum. Ita quíppe apostolus dícit: sicut enim corpus unum est, et memhra habet Fine; omnia autem corporis membra cum sint tumba, unum est corpus, ita et Christus (1 Cor 12:12). Non ait: ita Christus, sed ait: ita et Christus. Christus ergo membra plana, unum corpus. Descendit itaque de cáelo per misericordiam, nec ascendit nisi ipse, cum et nos in ipso per gratiam.

Ac per hoc non nisi Christus descendit, nec nisi Christus ascendit; non quod capitis dignitas confundatur in corpore, sed quod corporis unitas non separetur a capite. Non enim dicit ex seminihus tamquam in multis, sed tamquam in uno, in semine tuo quod est Christus (Gal 3:16). Proinde Christum dicit semen Abrahae; et tamen idem ipse apostolus, vos ergo, inquit, Abrahae semen estis (Gal 3,29). (349) Si ergo non in seminibus tamquam in multis, sed tamquam in uno: et hoc semen Abrahae, quod est Christus: et hoc semen Abrahae, quod sumus nos; cum ascendit in caelum, we abillo non separamur. Qui descendit de cáelo, non nobis [496] invidet caelum,

in a way he cries out: "Be my members if you want to join the cycle." Therefore, let us strengthen ourselves in the meantime; let us burn with all the flames of desire for it; Let us meditate on earth what we count on possessing in heaven. Then we will put off the flesh of mortality; Let us now rid ourselves of the old age of the soul: the body will be easily elevated to the heavenly heights if the weight of sins does not oppress the spirit. 3. Due to the slanderous insinuation of heretics, some are intrigued to know how the Lord descended without a body and ascended with him; It seems to them that it is in contradiction with those words: No one ascends to heaven except he who came down from heaven. How could a body that did not come down from there go up to heaven, they ask? As if he had said: "Nothing ascends to heaven but what came down from it." What he said was this: No one goes up except the one who came down. The statement refers to the person, not the person's clothing. He descended without the clothing of the body, he ascended with it; but no one ascended, except he who descended. If he incorporated us into himself as his members, so that, even with us incorporated, he remains himself, how much more reason cannot another person have in him the body that he took from the virgin! Who will say that it was not the same person who ascended a mountain, or a wall, or any other elevated place because, having descended stripped of his clothing, he ascended with them, or because, having descended unarmed, he ascended armed? ] As in this case it is said that no one ascended except he who descended, although there was sused quodammodo clamat: Mea membra estote, si asceré vultis in caelum. Et hoc ipso interim roboremur, in hoc votis omnibus aestuemus; hoc meditemur in terris, quod computamur in caelis. Tune exuturi carnem mortalitatis, nunc exuamus animi vetustatem: facile corpus levabitur in alta caelorum, si non premant spiritum sarcinae peccatorum. 3. Nam et illud nonnullos calumniantibus haereticis movet, quemadmodum dominus sine corpore descenderit, cum corpore ascenderit; velut contrarium sit illis verbis quibus ait, nemo ascendit in caelum, nisi qui de cáelo descendit. Corpus ergo, inquiunt, quod non descendit de cáelo, quomodo potuit ascendé in caelum? Quasi ille dixerit, Nihil ascendit in caelum, nisi quod de cáelo descendit; sed ait, nemo ascendit, nisi qui descendit. Hoc enim ad personam, non ad personae habitum retulit.

Descendit sine corporis indumento, ascendit cum corporis indumento: nemo tamen, nisi qui descendit, ascendit. Nam si nos sibimet tamquam sua membra ha coaptavit, ut etiam nobis coniunctis idem ipse sit; quanto magis illud corpus, quod de virgine assumpsit, aliam non potest in illo habere personam? Quis enim vel in montem, vel in murum, vel in alíquem superiorem locum dicat non eum solum qui descendit ascendisse, si, cum descendísset exutus, ascendat indutus; aut cum descendisset inermis, ascendat armatus? Quemadmodum ergo. de hoc dicitur, Nemo
The ascension of the Lord

With something that he did not have when he descended, in the same way, no one ascended to heaven except Christ, because no one except him descended from there, although he descended without a body and ascended with him, we also having to ascend not by our power, but by the union between us and with him. Indeed, they are two in one flesh; It is the great sacrament of Christ and the Church; That is why he himself says: They are no longer two, but one flesh. 4. He fasted when he was tempted, even though he needed food before his death, and he ate and drank when he was glorified, even though after his resurrection he no longer needed it. In the first case he showed our fatigue in his person; in the second, his consolation in us; on both occasions, within forty days. In fact, as recorded in the gospel, when he was tempted in the desert before the death of his flesh he had fasted for forty days; and, in turn, as Peter indicates in the Acts of the Apostles, after the resurrection of his body he spent forty days with his disciples, going in and out, eating and drinking. Under the number 40 the course of this world seems to be symbolized in those who have been called to grace by the one who did not come to annul the law, but to fulfill it 2. There are ten precepts of the law when the grace of Christ is already spread throughout the world. The world consists of four parts, and 10 multiplied by 4 gives 40, ascendit nisi qui descendit, quamvis cum ea re, cum qua non descendit, ascenderit; sic nemo in caelum nisi Christus ascendit, quia de cáelo nisi Christus nemo descendit, quamvis sine corpore descenderit, cum corpore ascenderit, ascensuris et nobis non virtute nostra, sed nostra et illius unitate. Duo quippe sunt in carne una: sacramentum magnum est in Christo et in ecclesia (Eph 5,31-32); unde et ipse dicit, iam non duo, sed una caro (Mt 19,6). (350) 4. Et ideo ieiunavit cum temptaretur, ante mortem cibo adhuc indigens; manducavit autem et bibit cum glorificaretur, post resurrectionem iam cibo non indigens. Illic enim ostendebat in se nostrum laborem, hic autem in nobis consolationem, quadraginta diebus utrumque definiens. Nam quadraginta diebus ieiunavit, cum temptaretur in eremo, sicut in gospel scriptum est, ante mortem carnis suae; et rursum quadraginta diebus cum discipulis Fuit, sicut Petrus in Actibus apostolorum loquitur, intrans et exiens, manducans et bibens [497] post resurrectionem carnis suae.

Quo numero quadragesimo huíus saeculi mean videtur excursus in his qui vocantur ad gratiam, per eum qui non venit legem solvere sed adimplere. Decem namque sunt praecepta legis, iam gratia Christi diffusa per mundum: et quadripertitus est mundus, et See additional note 10: The symbolism of the number 40 p.788.
See The Christian Combat 25,27, in addition to the sermon 265 B,2 (= BIBL. CAS. II 76).

since those who have been redeemed by the Lord were gathered from all regions: from the east and from the west, from the north and from the sea. His forty-day fast before his death was equivalent, in a way, to crying: "Abstain from worldly desires"; and eating and drinking for forty days after the resurrection of the body was equivalent to saying: I will be with you until the end of the world. Fasting, in fact, takes place in the tribulation of combat, because whoever competes in the fight abstains from everything; Food, on the other hand, is typical of the expected peace, which will not be perfect until our body, whose redemption we long for, is clothed with immortality; something that we do not boast of having already achieved, but on which we nourish ourselves in hope. We have to do one thing and another; This was shown by the Apostle when he said: Rejoicing in hope and being patient in tribulation, as if the first were symbolized in food, and the second in fasting. We must do one thing and another when we undertake the path of the Lord: fast from the vanity of the present world and strengthen ourselves with the promise of the future; in the first case, not attaching the heart, and in the second, putting their food on high. decem quadruplicata quadraginta faciunf quoniam qui redempti sunt a domino, de regionibus congregavit eos, ab oriente et occidente, et aquilone et mari (Ps 106,2-3). Ieiunans itaque quadraginta diebus ante mortem carnis, velut clamabat: Abstinete vos a desideriís huius saeculi; manducans autem et bibens quadraginta diebus post resurrectionem carnis, velut clamabat: ecce ego vobiscum sum usque ad commmationem saeculi. Ieiunium quippe est in tribulatione certaminis; quoniam qui in agone contendit, ab omnibus abstinens est (1 Cor 9:25); cibus autem in spe pacis, quae perfection non erit, nisi cum corpus nostrum, cuius expectamus redemptionem, induerit immortalitatem; quod nondum adipiscendo glotiamut, sed speraíido iam pascimur. Utrutnque apostolus simul nos agere otendit says: spe gaudentes, in tribulatione patientes (Rom 12, 12); tanquam illud esset in cibo, hoc in ieiunio. Simul enim cum viam domini carpimus, et a vanitate praesentis saeculi ieiunemus, et futuri promis'ñone reficiamur: hic non apponentes cor, illuc pascentes sursum cor.
Topic: The ascension of the Lord. Location: Unknown. Date: Feast of the Ascension. Year 413-420.

1. Many are the mysteries hidden in the divine Scriptures. The Lord has deigned to reveal some of them to our humility; others are there for us to investigate, but we do not have enough time to expose them to your holiness. I know that these days especially the church tends to be filled with people who think more about leaving than coming and who call us annoying if we ever delay anything longer.' Those same ones, if their banquets to which they rush to arrive last until the afternoon, neither get tired nor refuse attendance nor leave them with the slightest blush. However, in order not to disappoint those who come hungry, even briefly, we will not overlook the mystery contained in the fact that Jesus Christ our Lord ascended to heaven with the same body in which he was resurrected. 2. This was in view of the weakness of his disciples, since there was no lack, even within their number, of alSERMO
OF ASCENSIONE DOMINI,

1. Dicendum de mysterio ascensionis Christi.—Multa sunt divinarum Scripturarum recondita sacramenta, sive quae adhuc nos ipsi quaerenda habemus, sive quae iam humilitati nostrae Dominus reveale dignitus est: sed aperiendi haec Sanctitati vestrae tempus non sufficit. Novi enim máxime his diebus impleri ecclesiam talibus, qui citius vellent discedere, quam vinore; et onerous nos habent, si aliquando diutius colloquamur: qui tamen in prandiis suis, ad quae festinant, si teneantur usque ad vesperam, nec laborant, nec recusant, nec saltem aliquando ullo modesty discedunt. Tamen ne fraudmus eos qui esurientes veniunt, etsi breviter, non tacebimus huius rei sacramentum, quod Dominus noster Iesus Christus cum eo corpore, in quo resurrexit ascendit. 2. Christus post resurrectionem conversatur cum discipulis, ut in fide confirmentur. Ascendit in caelum, ne remaneant in carne.—Sane propter infirmitatem discipulorum suorum: non enim deerant etiam in See sermons 51,1; 68.1 (=MAI 126); Treatises on the gospel of Saint John 8,13. On the great festivals there were many who attended the liturgical acts, but moved by the solemnity of the day, not by more pious intentions. Those, of course, were always in a hurry to get out. See supplementary note 26; The auditorium, ie Agustín p.803.

Some were so tempted by the devil to disbelief that one gave more faith to fresh scars than to living members as to the resurrection in the body he knew. Thus, to strengthen them, he deigned to live in their company for forty full days after his resurrection, that is, from the very day of his passion until the present, entering and leaving, eating and drinking, as the Scripture says, and assuring them that what was presented again to their eyes after the resurrection was what had been taken from them by the cross. However, he did not want them to remain in the flesh nor for carnal love to bind them any longer. The reason why they wanted him to always be physically with them was the same reason why Peter also feared that he would suffer the passion. They saw in him a teacher, an encourager and comforter, a protector, but human, as they saw themselves; and if this did not appear to their eyes, they considered him absent, whereas he is present everywhere with his majesty. In truth, he protected them, like a hen her chicks, as he deigned to affirm; like the hen, who, due to the weakness of her chicks, also becomes weak. As you remember, there are many birds that we see give birth to chicks, but we do not see any, except the hen, become weak with their chicks. This is the reason why the Lord took it as a point of comparison: he also, in view of our weakness, deigned to make himself weak by taking the flesh. It was good for them, therefore, to be elevated a little and to begin to think of him in spiritual categories: as the Word of the Father, God illo numero, quos diabolus infidelitate tentaret, ita ut quídam discipulus eius in ipsa specie in qua noverat, non tamen magis fidem haberet vivostibus membris, quam recentibus cicatricibus (cf. lo 20,25): ergo ad eorum confirmationem digntus est post resurrectionem vivere cum illis quadraginta diebus integris, ab ipso die passionis suae usque in hodiernum diem, intrans et exiens, manducara et bibens, sicut dicit Scriptura (cf. Acts 1,3-4); confirmans hoc redditum esse oculis eorum post resurrectionem, quod ablatum erat per cruzem. Verumtamen non illos voluit in carne remanere, nec carnal dilectione diutius retiñere. Eo enim animo volebant eum esse semper carnaliter secum, quo animo etiam Petrus timebat eum pati.

Videbant enim secum magistrum, comfortatorem et [1213] consolatorem et protectorem hominem, quales videbant se ipsos. Si tal aliquid non viderent, absentem credebant; cum ubique ille maiestate sit praesens. Tuebatur autem eos revera, quemadmodum ipse dicere dignitus est, tanquam gallina pullos suos (cf. Mt 23:37). Sicut enim gallina propter infirmítatem puflorum et ipsa infirmatur. Si enim remember, before oculos we sunt so many birds, quae pullos faciunt; non videmus aliquam avem infirman cum pullis, nisi gallinam: et ideo de illa Dominus similitudinem duxit; quia propter infirmítatem nostram et ipse susceptione carnis infirman dignitus est. Oportebat autem ut erigerentur aliquantum, et iam inciperent eum spiritualiter cogitare, tanquam
The ascension of the Lord

together with God, by whom all things were made, to which the flesh they contemplated was an impediment. It was beneficial for them to strengthen their faith by living with him for forty days; But it was even more beneficial to them that he was hidden from their eyes and that the one who on earth had lived with them as a brother, helped them from heaven as Lord and that they learned to consider him as God. This was indicated by the evangelist John; You just have to notice it and understand it. In effect, the Lord says: Let not your heart be troubled. If you loved me, he says, you would be glad that I am going to the Father, because the Father is greater than me. And in another text he says: I and the Father are one and the same. He vindicates for himself so much equality, not the fruit of plunder, but equality of nature, that to a certain disciple who said to him: Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us, he replied: Philip, I have been with you for so long, and you still do not know the Father? Whoever saw me, also saw the Father. What does it mean: Who saw me? If you mean seeing it with the eyes of the flesh, those who crucified Him also saw it. What does it mean, then: Who saw me, but who understood what I am, who saw me with the eyes of the heart? In fact, just as there are interior ears—those that the Lord sought when he said: He who has ears, let him hear, even though there is no deaf person there—so there is also an interior look of the heart. If anyone had seen the Lord with her, he would have seen the Father, since he is just like him. 3. Listen to the Apostle, who wants us to consider the Verbum Patris, Deum apud Deum, per quem facta sunt omnia: et non eos sinebat caro, quam videbant. Proderat ergo illis confirm in fide per conversationem eius secum quadraginta diebus: sed plus proderat eis, ut se ab oculis eorum subtraheret; et qui in terra tanquam frater conversatus fuet, de cáelo tanquam Dominus subveniret; discerentque illum cogitare secundum Deum. Hoc enim evangelist Ioannes sonuit: si quis advertat, si quis intellegat. Ait enim Dominus: Non turbe tur cor vestrum. Si me diligeretis, inquit, gauderetis, quia vado ad Patrem; quoniam Vater maior me est (lo 14,1.28). Et alio loco, dicit: Ego et Pater unum sumus (ib., 10,30). Tantamque sibi aequalitatem vindicat, non rapiña, sed natura, ut hoc diceret carem disciple digoti sibi: Domine, ostende nobis Patrem, et sujficit nobis; et ille: Philippe, tanta tempore vobiscum sum, et Patrem nescitis? Qui me vidit, viiit et Patrem (ib., 14,8.9). Quid est: Who vidit me?

Si secundum oculos carnis, viderunt et qui crucifixerunt. Quid est ergo: Qui me vidit, nisi: qui intellexit, qui oculo cordis vidit? Quomodo enim sunt aures interiors, quas quaerebat Dominus, cum diceret: Qui habet aures, auditat (Mt 11:15), cum ante illum nuílus surdus staret: sic est etiam aspectus interior cordis, quo si quis viderat Dominum, viderat Patrem; quia aequalis est Patri. 3. Pilius Dei natura aequalis Patri, Misericordia ad mortem usque infirmatus.—Audi Apostolum volentem nobis commendare Misericordiam

mercy of the Lord, who became weak for us to gather us under his wings like chicks and to teach the disciples that if anyone, having overcome the common weakness, has risen to a certain robustness, he too should have compassion for the weakness of others, considering that Christ descended from his heavenly strength to our weakness. The Apostle tells them: Have the same feelings that Christ Jesus had. Deign, he said, to imitate the Son of God in his compassion towards the little ones. Which, existing in the form of God. By saying: existing in the form of God, he showed that he was equal to God. It is not a lesser form than the one whose form it is, for if it is a lesser form, it is no longer a form. However, so that no one would doubt, he added and put the word capable of stopping the mouths of the sacrilegious. Who, existing in the form of God, said, did not consider it a plunder to be equal to God. What do these words of the Apostle mean, dearly beloved brothers: He did not judge a robbery? Which is the same by nature. For whom was being equal to God an object of plunder? For the first man, to whom it was said: Try it, and you will be like gods. He wanted to achieve equality through plunder, and in punishment he lost immortality. He, on the other hand, for whom it was not a robbery, did not consider it a robbery to be equal to God. Therefore, if we do not have to talk about plunder, we have to talk about nature, total unity and utmost equality. But what did he do? He emptied himself, he says, by taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men and found as a man in outward bearing; He humbled himself and became obedient to death, even death on a cross. It was little to mention the death, quia propter nos infirmatus est, ut sub alis suis pullos colligeret, docens alios etiam disciples, ut et ipsi compaterentur infirmitati infirmorum, qui ad aliquam firmitatem de infirmitate communi ascendissent; cum ille de caelesti firmitate ad infirmitatem nostram descenderit; ait illis: Hoc sentite in vobis, quoá et in Christo lesu. Dignamini, inquit, imitan Filium Dei per compassionem cum parvulis. Qui cum in forma Dei esset. Iam saying, in forma Dei esset, aequalem otendit Deo. Non enim forma minor est quam ille cuius forma est. If enim minor est, form non est. Tamen ne aliquis dubitaret, adiecit, et posuit ipsum Verbum, unde ora sacrilegis clauderet: Qui cum in forma Dei esset, inquit, non rapinam arbitratus est esse aequalis Deo. Quid est, fratres carissimi, quod ait Apostolus: Non rapinam arbitratus est?

Quia natura[1214]liter aequalis. Cui ergo erat plunder aequalitas Dei? Primo homini, cui dictum est, Taste yourself, et eritis sicut dii (Gen 3,5). Voluit per rapinam tende se ad aequalitatem, et per poenam losdidit immortalitatem. Ille enim cui rapiña non erat, non rapinam arbitratus est esse aequalis Deo. Yes ergo non plunder; natura, integra societas et summa ipsa comparatio. Sed quid fecit? Semetipsum, ait, exinanivit, formam servi accipiens; in similarityinem hominum factus, et habitu inventus ut homo: humiliavit se, factus oboediens usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis (Phil 2,5-8).

te, and that's why he mentioned what kind of death. Why this too? Because there are many who are willing to die, many who say: "I am not afraid of dying, but I would like to die in my bed, surrounded by my children, grandchildren and the tears of my wife." Certainly, it seems that these do not refuse death; but, when choosing the type of death, they feel tormented by a certain fear. Christ, on the other hand, chose the kind of death, but he chose the worst of all 2. As all men choose for themselves the best of deaths, so he chose the worst of all, the most execrable for all the Jews. He, who is to come to judge the living and the dead, was not afraid to die because of false witnesses, by the sentence of a judge; He was not afraid to die in the ignominy of the cross, to free all believers from any other ignominy. Therefore, he became obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross. Yet he is equal to God by nature; strong in the vigor of his majesty, and weak out of compassion for humanity; strong to create everything, and weak to recreate it again. 4. Pay attention to what John says: If you loved me, you would be glad that I was going to the Father, because the Father is greater than me. How then is it equal, according to what the Apostle says? The Lord himself says: The Father and I are one. And in another place: Whoever saw me, also saw the Father. How does it say here: Because the Father is greater than I? These words, brothers, as the Lord intends to insinuate to me, are, in a certain way, Parum erat dicere mortem, et genus mortis otendit. Quare et genus mortis? Quia multi ad mortem sunt parati; multi enim dicunt: Non timeo mori, sed vellem in lectulo meo morí, circumdatus filiis, nepotibus, lacrimis uxoris. Mortem quidem videntur isti non recusare, sed electing genus mortis, from timore puniuntur. Ille autem elegit genus mortis, sed quod est deterius omnibus. Quomodo sibi eligunt nomines melius genus mortis, sic ipse deterius elegit, hoc quod exsecrabile erat omnibus Iudaeis. Non enim timuit mori per false tests, per sententiam iudicis, qui veniet iudicare vivos et mortuos: non timuit mori per ignominiam crucis, ut omnes credentes ab omni ignominia liberaet. Ergo factus oboediens usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis: tamen naturaliter aequalis Deo; fortis in virtute maestatis, infirmus compassione humanitatis: fortis, ut faceret omnia; infirmus, ut reficeret omnia. 4. Christus abire vult, ut absenté carne divinitas ipsius cogitetur.

Filius Dei in se non minor per incarnationem.—Qaoá ergo ait Ioannes attendite: Si diligeretis me, gauderetis, quia vado ad Patrem; quoniam Pater maior me est. Quomodo aequalis, sicut dicit Apostolus? Sicut ipse Dominus: Ego et Pater unum sumus. Et alio loco: Qui me vidit, vidit et Patrem. How did I do, Quia Pater maior is me? Vox ista, fratres, The same in the sermon 68,11 (= MAI 126); Comments on Psalms 140:20; Treatises on the gospel of Saint John 12,6; 36.4.

way, words of reproach and consolation. They were anchored in man, and were unable to think of him as God. They would think of him as God when he disappeared from their presence and from their eyes as a man, so that, having eliminated the usual familiarity with the flesh, they would learn to think of his divinity at least in the absence of the flesh. Consequently, this is what he says to them: —If you loved me, you would be glad that I am going to the Father. -As? —So that, when I have gone to the Father, you can think that I am equal to the Father 3. Therefore, therefore, he is greater than me. While you see me in the flesh, the Father is greater than me. See if you have understood it.—They didn't know how to think about him other than his condition as a man. I am going to repeat this more calmly in attention of our more dull brothers of intelligence; Those who have already understood it should endure the slowness of others and imitate the Lord Himself, who, existing in the form of God, humbled Himself, becoming obedient to the point of death. If you loved me. What does this mean? If you loved me, you would be glad that I am going to the Father. If you loved me: what is this but a way of saying that you do not love me? What do you love, then? The flesh that you see, and that you do not want to leave your eyes. If, on the contrary, you loved me. What does this mean to me? In the beginning there was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God, according to John himself. If you loved me in my capacity as creator of everything, you would be glad that I am going to the Father. Because? Because the Father is greater than me. Still, while you continue to see me in the

earth, the Father is greater than me. I will leave your presence; I will remove from your eyes the mortal flesh that I assumed in attention to your mortality; You will begin to not see this dress that I took out of humility. But it must be taken up to heaven so that you may learn that you must wait. He did not leave on earth the tunic that he wanted to wear here 4, because if he had abandoned it here below, everyone would have lost hope in the resurrection of the body. Even now, after having raised it to heaven, there are those who doubt the resurrection of the body. If God manifested it in his own person, is he going to deny it to man? God took her out of compassion; man, however, by nature. And yet, he let it be seen, strengthened them and lifted it to heaven. Made impossible by the ascension to look with the eyes of the flesh, they no longer saw him as a man. If there was something in his heart moved by carnal desires, he must have been saddened. However, they came together in unity and began to pray. After ten days, he had to send them the Holy Spirit, so that he would fill them with spiritual love, annihilating carnal desires. In this way he made them understand that Christ was the Word of God, God together with God, by whom all things were made. But this intelligence could not take possession of them as long as carnal love had not been removed from their eyes. Therefore he said: If you loved me, you would be glad that I am going to the Father, because the Father is greater than I. He is greater than me, insofar as I am a man, and equal, insofar as I am God;

Topic: The ascension of the Lord. Location: Unknown. Date: Feast of the ascension of 412.

1. We are going to turn the solemnity of this date into a wake-up call for those who know its meaning, and an instruction for those who are negligent in this regard. Today we solemnly celebrate the ascension of the Lord to heaven. In fact, the Lord, our Savior, after putting off his body and taking it up again when he rose from the dead, manifested himself alive to his disciples, who, upon seeing him die, had lost all hope. Then he allowed them to see him with their eyes and touch him with their hands, raising their faith and showing them the reality of the body. It was little for human fragility and trembling weakness for such a great miracle to be shown to them for a single day, then disappearing from their eyes; For this reason – as we have heard in the reading of the Acts of the Apostles – he lived with them on earth for forty days, entering and leaving, eating and drinking; not because he felt the need, but to demonstrate the truth of his body. After exactly forty days, seeing him and following him with their eyes, he ascended to heaven. This is what we celebrate today 2. After, full of amazement, they saw him ascend SERMO

Therefore, I confess to you that I am still investigating why the Lord gave the Holy Spirit twice; I want to reach greater certainty. May the Lord help me through your prayers so that I do not keep from you what he deigns to grant me. So, I ignore it. However, I will not remain silent not only about what I know, but about what I think, because I still do not have it as certain, as I do when Jesus gave the Spirit. If my opinion is true, may the Lord confirm it; If there is something else with greater rings of truth, may the Lord grant it to us. I am of the opinion—mere opinion—that the Holy Spirit was given twice to teach us the two precepts of charity. Indeed, there are two precepts and only one love: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul; and: You will love your neighbor as yourself. In these two precepts the entire law and the prophets are summarized. There is only one love and two are the precepts: one is the Spirit and two are the gifts of the same. One was not given before and another after, since there is not one love that loves one's neighbor and another that loves God. These are not, therefore, different loves. We love God with the same love with which we love our neighbor. But since God is one thing and neighbor another, although they are loved with the same love, that does not mean that what is loved is a single thing. Although

Topic: Commentary on Psalm 140.5. Place: Carthage. Date: Pentecost Vigil. May 23, 397. 1. Among other divine words heard when singing the psalm, I like to discuss and comment in a special way, with the help of the Lord, that phrase that sounds like this: The righteous will correct me and rebuke me with mercy, but the oil of the sinner will not anoint my head. There were those who believed that the oil of the sinner was the oil of man, since every man is a liar. The oil of Christ, however, since he had no sin, is not the oil of the sinner, even if it is administered by a sinner. Three aspects are presented to the mind for consideration: who gives, to whom he gives, for whom he gives 2; Let us not fear, then, the oil of the sinner, since the intermediary minister does not intercept the grace of the donor.
IN VIGILIIS PENTECOSTÉS DE VERSU PSALMI 140.5: EMENDABIT ME TUSTÚS, ETC. AGAINST DONATISTS

1. Psalmi versus male intellectus a Donatistis.—inter alia divina eloquia, quae, cum Psalmus cantoretur, audivimus, placet adiuvante Domino istam potissircmm discusse et pertractare sententiam, qua dictum est: Emendabit me iustus in misericordia, et argüet me; oleum autem peccatoris non impinguet caput meum (Ps 140.5). Nonnulli enim crediderunt oleum peccatoris, oleum esse hominis; quia omnis homo mendax (Ps 115,11). Oleum autem Christi, quia nullum habuit omnino peccatum, etsi per peccatorem ministretur, non est oleum peccatoris. Cum tres consideringi animo occurrant: a quo datur, cui datur, per quem datur; non timeamus oleum peccatoris, quia non intercipit medius minister benefícium largitoris. The Donatists used this text to defend their thesis of the invalidity of baptism administered by a sinner. The relationship was easy to establish based on the anointing that took place at baptism. See Reply to the letter of Parmenian II 10,20-22; III 2,4. It appears before in San Cipriano (Letter 70,2.2). Augustine saves the situation by denying that the administrator of the sacrament anoints with his own oil; he is nothing more than a steward of the oil of God, grace. Of the three elements mentioned here, Augustine insists, above all, on "who gives", in opposition to the Donatists, who emphasized, above all, on "for whom he gives."

2. Indeed, we now celebrate the solemnity of the coming of the Holy Spirit. On the day of Pentecost that has already begun, one hundred and twenty people were gathered in a place, among them the apostles, the mother of the Lord and others of both sexes, in prayer and waiting for the promise of Christ, that is, the arrival of the Holy Spirit. His hope and expectation were not in vain, since the promise of the one who had committed himself was not fallacious. What he was waiting for arrived, and he found the vessels that were going to welcome him clean. Divided tongues appeared to them, like those of fire, which rested on each of them, and they began to speak in Lencas as the spirit granted them to speak. Each one spoke all languages, prefiguring the Church, which was going to be present in all languages. A single man was a sign of unity: the totality of the languages ​​in a single man symbolized all the peoples gathered in unity. Those who were full of the Spirit spoke and those who were empty of it marveled. And what is worthy of greater reproach, they combined accusation with admiration. They said: Those are drunk and full of wine. What a foolish and slanderous accusation! A drunk man does not learn a foreign language, but rather loses his own. Through the mouths of the ignorant and slanderers the truth speaks. Indeed, they were already full of the new wine, because they had become new wineskins. The old wineskins were filled with admiration for the new ones, and, indulging in slander, they were neither renewed nor filled. Be per nomines, inquiunt, ibatur. Numquid ideo erat Donator and ministrator are the two terms that Augustine uses to define the part of God and that of man in the donation of grace that takes place in the sacraments. The minister of the sacrament is nothing more than what his name indicates: a servant, never the owner. See Treatises on the Gospel of Saint John 13:16; 5.7; 6.6. Whether through a righteous person or a sinner, it is always God who gives his grace. This reaches people per hominem, but never de homine. The minister is the channel through which it passes, not the source from which it comes (Reply to Varmenimo's letter II 15,33).

The Holy Spirit descended on the eunuch. Perhaps someone who wants to argue can tell me that this is not about the deacon he had baptized in Samaria, but about Philip the apostle, since among the apostles there is one named Philip, and he who is properly called "the evangelist" is one of the seven deacons. But he thinks what he wants; I will resolve the issue quickly. Let us keep it doubtful whether it was the apostle or the deacon, something that Scripture is silent about. In any case, it is written that, as soon as he came out of the water, the Holy Spirit came upon the eunuch, without indicating that anyone laid hands on him. Perhaps this itself is not enough, since he can reply: "With absolute certainty, someone laid hands on him, but the Scripture kept him silent." 6. What do you say then? «The following: on the first hundred and twenty, since the Holy Spirit then came for the first time, he descended without the laying on of hands; but, from then on, it no longer came upon anyone except by its imposition." You have forgotten centurion Cornelius. Read carefully

tion and judge wisely. Cornelius was a centurion, as we read in the same book of the Acts of the Apostles, where the coming of the Holy Spirit is also proclaimed. An angel was sent to him, who announced that his alms had been pleasing to God, and his prayers had been heard, and that, therefore, he should send for Peter, who was in Joppa, to the house of a tanner named Simon. Then there was a lively discussion between Jews and Gentiles, that is, between believers who came from Judaism and those from Gentiles, whether the uncircumcised should be admitted to the Gospel. There was great doubt about this when Cornelio sent for him. Meanwhile, Pedro received a warning. The matter of the kingdom of heaven is dealt with in one place and in another by someone who is everywhere. While what was said was happening in Cornelius's house, Peter became hungry in Joppa, and while food was being prepared for him he went up to pray, and his soul was transported from earth to heaven, not to take him out of his way, but so that he could see. A large plate that came down from heaven reaches him, like a heavenly delicacy for him, hungry. This dish, suspended from four ropes, contained all kinds of animals, pure and impure. A voice from above knocked at their hungry doors: Peter, get up; kill and eat. He looked carefully, saw the impure animals on the plate, which he was not used to touching, and responded to the voice: Far be it from me, Lord! Vulgar and impure food has never entered my mouth. The voice replied: Do not call impure what God has purified. Here Peter was not offered carnal food, but rather it was announced to him that Cornelius was pure. This happens

It was fired three times, and the plate returned to heaven. The mystery is clear. The plate is the orb of the earth. The four ropes that hold it are the four cardinal points, which Scripture mentions when it says: From the east and from the west, from the north and from the sea. Animals are all people. In the triple descent the Trinity is intimated to us. Peter is the Church; Peter hungry, the Church longing for the faith of the Gentiles. The voice of heaven, the holy gospel. Kill and eat: put to death what they are and transform them into what you are. As soon as Peter showed his disagreement with the order, he was told that some soldiers sent by Cornelius wanted to see him. The Holy Spirit said to Peter: Go with them; I have sent them. Peter set out, no longer doubting the meaning of the vision. As we read, he announces himself to Cornelius, goes out to meet him, humbly prostrates himself before him, and rises up even more humbly. They arrive at his house, where many others are gathered. They tell Pedro why they went looking for him and thank him for coming. In this way, opening his mouth, he began to evangelize to the uncircumcised the grace of Jesus Christ the Lord, on which the discussion centered. Accompanying Peter were some believers of Judaism who might feel disturbed by the baptism of an uncircumcised person; Then Peter precisely said: You know, brothers, how abominable it must be for a Jew to approach or associate with a Gentile; but God has shown me that no one should call a man vulgar or impure. He, hungry, looked at the plate.

7. Where are those who said—in consideration of what I am going to say I have recounted all of the above—where are those who said that the Holy Spirit can be communicated by a man? At Peter's announcement, Cornelius and all those who were with him, that is, Gentiles, believed; and immediately, before being baptized, they were filled with the Holy Spirit.
