1. Today's solemnity brings to mind the greatness of the Lord God and his grace, which he has poured out on us. This is precisely why the solemnity is celebrated: so that what happened only once is not erased from memory. Solemnitas comes from solet in anno, that is, solemnity indicates what usually happens each year; In the same way, we speak of the perenniality of a river, because it does not dry up in the summer, but rather flows all year round. Perenne means per annum (throughout the year), as solemn means solet in anno (usually celebrated once a year). Today we celebrate the arrival of the Holy Spirit. In fact, the Lord sent the promised Holy Spirit from heaven already on earth. In this way he had promised to send it from the sanum facit virga obiurgantis; grande caput facit oleum peccatoris, hoc est, assentatio adulatoris. Si caput grande fecisti, cave pondus capitis, ne in praecipitium perducaris. Haec, quantum existimo, pro tempore de hac una Psafini sententia sufficienter locuti sumus, Domino adiuvante, et corda vestra in secreto aedificante.
IN DIE PENTECOST, I

CAPUT I.—1. Solemnitas adventus Spiritus sancti.—Hodierni diei solemnitas, Domini Dei magni et magnae gratiae, quae superfusa est super nos remembranceem facit. Ideo enim solemnitas celebratur, ne quod semel factum est, de memoria deleátur. Solemnitas enim ab eo quod solet in anno, nomen ac[1230]cepit: quomodo perennítas fluminis dicitur, quia non siccatur aestate, sed per totum annum fluit: ideo perenne, id est, per annum; sic et solemne, quod solet in anno celebrati. Celebramus hodie adventum Spiritus sancti. Dominus enim Spiritum sanctum de cáelo misit, quem in terra promisit. Et quia sic promiserat de cáelo esse

Heaven: He cannot come until I go; but once I am gone, I will send it to you. That is why he suffered, died, rose again and ascended; All that was left was to keep the promise. It was what his disciples expected, one hundred and twenty people, as it is written; that is, ten times the number of the apostles. In fact, he chose twelve and sent the Spirit on one hundred and twenty. While waiting for this promise, they were gathered in a house praying, since they already desired the same things with the same faith as with prayer and spiritual longing. They were new wineskins waiting for the new wine from heaven that arrived. That great cluster had already been trampled and glorified. We read, in fact, in the gospel: The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified. 2. You have already heard what his response was: a great miracle. Each of those present had learned only one language. The Holy Spirit came, they were filled with it, and they began to speak in the different languages ​​of all the peoples that they neither knew nor had learned. The one who had come showed them to them; He entered into them, and filled them to overflowing. And this then was the sign: everyone who received the Spirit, as soon as he felt filled with it, spoke in everyone's languages. And this is not just the one hundred and twenty. The same Scriptures teach us that later other men believed, who were baptized, received the Holy Spirit and spoke in the languages ​​of all peoples. Those present were frightened, some admiring each other, others mocking, to the point of saying: Those

The carnal man does not understand the things of the spirit. The flesh is oldness, the grace is new. The more man is renewed for the better, the more he understands, because he tastes what is true. The must was bubbling, and from that bubbling the languages ​​of the people flowed.

In fact, the fact that that tiny Church spoke the languages ​​of all men, what did it mean if not that this great Church speaks the languages ​​of all men from sunrise to sunset? Now what was then a promise is fulfilled. We hear the promise and see its fulfillment. Listen, daughter; look. To the queen herself it was said: Listen, daughter; look: hear the promise, see it fulfilled. Your God has not deceived you, your husband has not deceived you, he has not deceived you who gave his own blood as a dowry, he has not deceived you who made you beautiful from being ugly, and a virgin from a harlot. You have received a promise that is yourself; promise received when you consisted of few and fulfilled now that you possess so many. 4. Let no one say, then: "I have received the Holy Spirit; Why don't I speak the languages ​​of all peoples? If you want to possess the Holy Spirit, pay attention, my brothers. Our spirit, thanks to which every man lives, is called soul, and you see what the function of the soul is with respect to the body. Give strength to all members; She sees with her eyes, hears with her ears, smells with her nostrils, speaks with her tongue, acts with her hands and walks with her feet; It is present in all the members at the same time to keep them alive; it gives life to everyone and each one their function. The eye does not hear, nor does the ear or the tongue see, nor does the ear or the eye speak; but, nevertheless, they live: the ear lives, the language lives: the functions are diverse, but the same life. This is the Church of God: in some

saints perform miracles, in others he proclaims the truth, in others he preserves virginity, in others marital chastity; in some one thing and in others another; Each one performs their own function, but they all live the same life. What the soul is with respect to the body of man, that is the same thing the Holy Spirit is with respect to the body of Christ, which is the Church. The Holy Spirit works in the Church the same as the soul does in all the members of a single body. But see what you must guard against, what you must fulfill and what you must fear. It happens that in a human body, better, a human body, a member must be amputated: the hand, a finger, a foot. Does the soul go after the severed limb? While he was in the body he lived; Once cut, he lost his life. In the same way, the Christian man is Catholic while he lives in the body; Becoming a heretic is equivalent to being amputated, and the soul does not follow an amputated limb. Therefore, if you want to receive the life of the Holy Spirit, preserve charity, love the truth and desire unity to reach eternity. Amen.

Topic: The Spirit and the unity of the Church. Location: Unknown. Date: Feast of Pentecost. Between 405 and 410. 1. The coming of the Holy Spirit has clothed this day with solemnity for us, the fiftieth after the resurrection, made up of seven weeks. If you count the seven weeks, you will find only forty-nine, but the unity is added to intimate the unity. What did the very coming of the Holy Spirit consist of? What did he do? How did he show his presence? What was used to express it? They all spoke in the languages ​​of all the peoples. One hundred and twenty people were gathered in one place, a sacred number that results from multiplying the number of the apostles by ten. How did it happen then? Did each of those on whom the Holy Spirit came speak one of the languages, some one and others another, as if distributing among them those of all the peoples? The reality was different: each man, a single man, spoke the languages ​​of all the peoples. A single man spoke those of all peoples: here the unity of the Church is symbolized in the languages ​​of all nations. Here we are also intimated with the unity of the Catholic Church spread throughout the world. 2. Therefore, whoever has the Holy Spirit is within SERMO
IN ME PENTECOST, II

1. Spiritus sanetus dotto linguarum unitatem Ecclesiae catholicae commendat.—Propter adventum Spiritus [1232] sancti hodiernus dies solemnis est nobis, a resurrectione Domini quinquagesimus, septem septimanis multiplicatus. Sed computantes septem septimanas, quadraginta novem invenietis: unus additur, ut nobis unitas commendetur. Quid ipse adventus Spiritus sancti, quid egit? Praesentiam suam unde docuit? where monstravit? Linguis omnium gentium locuti sunt omnes. Erant autem in uno loco centum vigínti: per decem duodenarius. Apostolomm numerus sacratus mysterio est decuplatus. Quid ergo, singuli in quos venit Spiritus sanctus, singulis linguis omnium gentium sunt locuti, illi alia lingua, et illi alia, et quasi diviserunt inter se linguas omnium gentium? Non sic: sed unusquisque homo, unus homo linguis omnium gentium locobatur. Loquebatur unus homo linguis omnium gentium: unitas Ecclesiae in linguis omnium gentium. Ecce et hic unitas Ecclesiae catholicae commendatur toto orbe diffusae. 2. Spiritus sanctus extra Ecclesiam non habetur.—Qui ergo habet

the Church that speaks the languages ​​of all. Whoever is outside of it lacks the Holy Spirit. For this reason, the Holy Spirit deigned to manifest himself in the languages ​​of all peoples, so that they may understand that it is the Spirit who maintains the unity of the Church, who speaks in all languages. One body, says the apostle Paul; one body and one Spirit. Consider our members. The body consists of many members, and one soul gives strength to all of them. See that, thanks to the human soul by which I am a man, I keep all the members united. I command the members to move, I apply the eyes to see, the ears to hear, the tongue to speak, the hands to act and the feet to walk. The functions of the members are different, but a single spirit unifies everything. There are many orders, many actions, but only one who gives orders and only one who is obeyed. What our spirit or our soul is with respect to our members, the same is the • Holy Spirit with respect to the members of Christ, to the body of Christ which is the Church. For this reason, the Apostle, when mentioning a single body, so that we would not think of a dead one, said: A single body. But I beg you: is this body alive? Yes, live. Where do you receive life from? Of a single spirit. And only one spirit. Focus, therefore, brothers, your attention on our body and the crimes of those who break away from the Church. Each of our members performs their functions while we are alive, while we remain healthy; Spiritum sanctum, in Ecclesia est, quae loquitur omnium linguis. Quicumque praeter hanc Ecclesiam est, non habet Spiritum sanctum. Ideo enirn Spiritus sanctus in omnium linguis gentium se demonstrare dignitus est, ut Ule se intellegat habere Spiritum sanctum, qui in unitate Ecclesiae continetur, quae linguis ómnibus loquitur. Unum corpus, Paulus dicit Apostolus: unum corpus, et unus spiritus (Eph 4,4). Membra nostra attendite. Multis membris constitutum est corpus, et vegetat membra omnia unus spiritus. Ecce humano spiritu, quo sum ego ipse homo, membra omnia colligo: impero membris ut moveantur, intendo oculos ad videndum, aures ad audiendum, linguam ad loquendum, manus ad operandum, pedes, ad ambulandum. Officia membrorum dispartita sunt, sed unus spiritus continet omnia. Fine iubentur, fine fiunt: unus iubet, uni servitur.

Quod est spiritus noster, id es anima nostra, ad membra nostra; hoc Spiritus sanctus ad membra Christi, ad corpus Christi, quod est Ecclesia. Ideo Apostolus, cum corpus unum nominasset, ne intellegeremus mortuum corpus: Unum, inquit, corpus. Sed rogo te, vivit hoc corpus? Vivit. Where? Of one spirit. Et unus spiritus. Attendite ergo, fratres, in our corpore, et dolete eos qui de Ecclesia praeciduntur. In membris nostris, quamdiu vivimus, cum sani sumus, implent omnia S.Ag. 24

If one suffers from any cause, all the members suffer with him. However, since it is in the body, it can feel pain, but it cannot breathe out. What is it, then, to expire but to lose the spirit? And now, if a member separates from the body, does the soul follow? The member in question is recognized: it is a finger, a hand, an arm, an ear; outside the body it has only form, but not life.' The same thing happens to the man separated from the Church. You look for the sacrament in him, and you find it; you seek baptism, and you find it; you look for symbol 2, and you find it. It is the exterior; But if the spirit does not invigorate you internally, you boast externally of the rite in vain. 3. Dearly beloved, God insists a lot on unity. Let us think that, at the beginning of creation, when he made all things, the stars in the firmament, and the herbs and trees on the earth, God said: Let the earth produce, and the trees and everything green appeared; He said: Let the waters produce fish and birds, and so it was done; Let the earth produce the living soul of all the domestic animals and wild beasts, and so it came to pass. Did God make all the others from a single bird? from a single fish, a single horse and a single beast the remaining fish, horses and wild beasts? Did not the earth produce abundant things at the same time and fill many spaces with numerous shoots? But he came to the creation of man and created only one, and from that one, the entire genus membra officia sua. Si unum membrum dolet alicunde, compatiuntur omnia membra. Tamen quia ín corpore est, doleré potest, exspirare non potest. Quid est enim exspirare, nisi spiritum amittere? Iam vero si membrum praecidatur de corpore, numquid sequitur spiritus? Et tamen membrum agnoscitur quid est; digitus est, manus est, brachium est, auris est: praeter corpus habet formam, sed non habet vitam. Sic et homo ab Ecclesia separatas. Quaeris ab illo sacramentum, invenis; quaeris Baptismum, invenís; quaeris symbolum, invenis. Forma est: nisi intus [1233] spiritu vegetaris, frustra foris de forma gloriaris. 3. Si ergo unitati non accesseritis, segregantes vosmetipsos, animals eritis, Spiritum non habentes. Si autem ficte accesseritis, Spiritus sanctus disciplinae effugiet fictum (Wis 1,5). Tune ergo vos sanctum Spiritum habere cognoscite, quando mentem vestram per_ sinceram caritatem unitati consenseritis haerere. Haec eis responderamus dicetibus: Quid accepturi sumus? nosque ipsos, fratres, exemplum illis bonorum operum praebeamus, nec quia stamus superientes, nec de iacentibus desperantes. SERMO

Cur Spiritus sanctus non posset vinore, nisi abeunte Christo. Humanitas Christi, in qua humano affectu haerebant, oculis discipulorum auferri debuit. Petra super quam aedificata Ecclesia, ipse est Christus. Ubi primum illud admoneo Caritatem vestram, ut aliquantum vosconsidere non pigeat, quare dictum sít ab ipso Domino: Non potest ille vinore, nisi ego abiero. Quasi aliquid, ut secundum carnalem sensum loquamur, quasi aliquid in supernis Dominus Christus servaret, et inde descendens hoc quod servabat, sancto Spiritui commendasset, et ideo ad nos vinore non posset, nisi ille rediisset qui commendatum reciperet; aut quasi nos utrumque ferré non valeremus, nec utriusque possemus tolerare

tolerate the presence of each other; or as if one excluded the other, or as if, when they come to us, they suffer hardships instead of expanding ourselves. What does it mean, then: He cannot come without me leaving? It is better for you, he said, that I go away; Well, if I do not go, the Paraclete will not come to you. Let your charity listen to what these words mean, as I have understood or believe I have understood, or as I have received as a gift from them. I speak what I believe. I think that the disciples were focused on the human form of Jesus, and as men, human affection had them captured in the man. He, on the other hand, wanted their love to be rather divine, to transform them in this way, from carnal, into spiritual, something that man only achieves through the gift of the Holy Spirit. Something like this tells them: «I send you a gift that transforms you into spiritual ones, that is, the gift of the Holy Spirit. But you cannot become spiritual if you do not stop being carnal. But you will cease to be carnal if my carnal form disappears from your eyes so that the form of God is embedded in your hearts. This human form, that is, this form of a servant, by which the Lord emptied himself, taking the form of a servant; This human form had captivated the affection of the servant Peter when he feared that the one he loved so much would die. He loved Jesus Christ the Lord, but as a man to another man, as a carnal man to another carnal man, and not as a spiritual man to the majesty. How do we prove it? Well, the Lord having asked his disciples praesentiam. Quasi vero alter ab alter separetur; aut quando ad nos veniunt, ipsi anxieties patiantur, ac non potius nos dilatemur. Quid sibi ergo vult: Non potest Ule vinore, nisi ego abiero? Expedit enim, inquit, vobis ut ego eam. Nam si non tero, Paracletus non veniet ad vos (lo 16, 7). Hoc ergo quid sit, quantum vel capimus, vel aestimamus, vel ipso donor percipimus, vel quae credimus loquimur, breviter accipiat Caritas vestra. Videtur mihi, quod discipuli circa formam humanom Domini Christi fuerant occupati, et tanquam nomines in homine humane tenebantur affectu. Volebat autem eos affectum potius habere divinum, atque ita de carnalibus faceré spirituales: quod non fit homo nisi dono Spiritus sancti. Hoc ergo ait: Mitto vobis donum, quo efficiamini spirituales; donum scilicet Spiritus sancti. Spirituales autem fieri non poteritis, nisi carnales esse destiteritis.

Clearly, Christ, the Son of the living God, the good of the good, God of God, the living of the living, the source of life and true life, had come to lose to death, not to perish by death. Yet Peter, being a man and, as I remembered, full of human affection toward the flesh of Christ, said: Have mercy on you, Lord. Far be it from you that this comes to pass! And the Lord refutes such words with the just and appropriate response. As he gave him the deserved praise for the previous confession, so he gives the deserved correction to this fear. Stand down, Satan, he tells him. Where is that: Blessed are you, Simon, son of John? He distinguishes his words when he praises him and when he corrects him; distinguishes the causes of confession and fear. That of confession: Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. The cause of fear: For you do not like the things of God, but those of men. Are we not going to want, then, for such people to be told: It is better for you that I go away. Well, if I don't go, won't the Paraclete come to you? Until this human form is removed from your carnal gaze, you will never be able to understand, feel or think anything divine. Let what has been said be sufficient. Hence the convenience of fulfilling his promise regarding the Holy Spirit after the resurrection and ascension of Jesus Christ the Lord. Referring to the Holy Spirit himself, Jesus had exclaimed and said: Whoever thirsts, let him come to me and drink, and rivers of living water will flow from his bosom. Next, speaking in his own person, the same evangelist John says: This he said about the Spirit that those who believed in him would receive. Well still

3. As the holy books teach us, the Lord spent with his disciples forty days after his resurrection, appearing to them so that no one would think that the truth of the resurrection of the body was a fiction, entering where they were and leaving, eating and drinking. But after forty days, which we celebrated exactly ten ago, in his presence he ascended to heaven, promising that he would return just as he left. Which means he will be a judge in the same human form in which he was judged. He wanted to send the Spirit on a day other than that of his ascension; not after two or three days, but after ten. This question compels us to investigate and ask ourselves about some mysteries hidden in numbers. The forty days result from multiplying 10 by 4. In this number, it seems to me, a mystery is entrusted to us. I speak as a man to men, and we are rightly called expositors of the Scriptures, not affirmers of our own opinions. This number 40, which contains four times the 10, means, as it seems to me, this century that we now live and go through, and in which we find ourselves involved by the passage of time, la inestaquem accepturi Erant ii qui in eum credituri Erant. Nondum enim erat Spiritus datus, quia lesus nondum fuet glorificatus (lo 7,37-39). Glorificatus est ergo Dominus noster Iesus Christus resurrectione et ascensione, et misit Spiritum sanctum. 3. Throughout this time and this world, both divided into four parts, the law of God is preached, like the number 10. Hence, above all, the decalogue is entrusted to us, since the law is contained in ten precepts, because it seems that this number contains a certain perfection. The one who counts reaches it in ascending order, and then starts again with 1 to reach 10 again and return to 13, whether it is hundreds, thousands or higher figures: by adding tens, the infinite jungle of numbers is formed. While we live in this century, we are taught to abstain from worldly desires; This is what the forty-day fast, known to everyone as Lent, means. Indeed, the law without grace is a letter that kills. For, if a law had been given, he says, that could give life, justice would proceed entirely from the law. Vero the Scripture closed everything under sin, so that the promise could be given to believers through Jesus Christ. Therefore, the letter kills; The Spirit, however, vivifies; not so that you fulfill other precepts other than those ordered in the letter; but the letter alone makes you guilty, while grace frees from sin and grants the fulfillment of the letter. Consequently, through grace the remission of all sins and the faith that acts through charity become a reality. Do not think, then, that because we have said: The letter kills, the letter has been condemned. It only means that the letter makes the guilty. Once you have received the precept, if you lack the help of grace, you will immediately notice not only that you do not comply with the law, but that you are also guilty of its transgression. For where there is no law, there is no transgression either. When saying: The letter kills; The Spirit, on the other hand, gives life, nothing is said against the law, as if it were condemned and the spirit was praised; What is said is that the letter kills, but the letter alone, without grace. I am telling your charity something that you too can easily consider and see: that charity fulfills the law. The fear of punishment makes man comply, but still as if he were a slave. In fact, if you do good because you fear suffering evil or if you avoid doing evil because you fear suffering another evil, if someone guaranteed you impunity, you would instantly commit iniquity. If you were told: “Be calm; you will suffer no harm, do this”, you would do it. Only the fear of punishment would turn you back, not the love of justice. Charity had not yet acted on you. Consider, then, how charity works. Let us love the one we fear so that we fear him with a chaste love. The chaste woman also fears her husband. But distinguish between fear and fear. The chaste wife fears that her absent husband will abandon her; The adulterous wife fears being surprised by the arrival of her husband. Charity, then, fulfills the law, since perfect love expels fear; that is,

servile fear, which comes from sin, for the chaste fear of the Lord remains forever and ever. If, then, charity fulfills the law, where does that charity come from? Remember, pay attention, and see that charity is a gift of the Holy Spirit, because the love of God has been spread in our hearts through the Holy Spirit that has been given to us. With all reason, then, the Lord Jesus Christ sent the Holy Spirit once the ten days were completed, a number that also symbolizes the perfection of the law, since it is freely granted to us to fulfill the law by someone who did not come to repeal it, but to fulfill it. 5. He said, "God sanctified the light." Let the firmament be made, and it was made, and God saw that it was good; Nor was it said here that the firmament had been sanctified. And so as not to waste time on obvious things, let the same be said of the other works, including those of the sixth day, with the creation of man in the image of God; They are all mentioned, but none of them are said to have been sanctified. But, arriving at the seventh day, in which nothing was created, but the rest of God is referred to, God sanctified it. The first sanctification is linked to the seventh day; Having examined all the texts of Scripture, it is found there for the first time. Where God's rest is mentioned, our own rest is also hinted at. Indeed, God's work was not such that it required rest, nor did he sanctify that day on which it is permissible not to work as gratifying himself with a day of vacation after work. The Feast of Pentecost
Theme: The Feast of Pentecost. Location: Unknown. Date: Feast of Pentecost. Before 405.

Shine for us, brothers, the pleasant day in which the holy Church appears full of brilliance before the eyes of the faithful, and of fervor in the hearts. We celebrate, in fact, the day on which Jesus Christ the Lord, after being resurrected and glorified by his ascension, sent the Holy Spirit. Thus it is written in the gospel: If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink; Rivers of living water will flow from the bosom of those who believe in me. And the evangelist explained it below with these words: He said this referring to the Holy Spirit that those who believed in him were going to receive. In fact, the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified. It only remained that, once Jesus had been glorified after having risen from the dead and having ascended to heaven, the Holy Spirit would be given, being sent by the one who had promised it. And so it happened. The Lord ascended to heaven after having spent forty days with his disciples after his resurrection, and on fifty days after his resurrection he sent the Holy Spirit, as it is written: Suddenly there was a noise from heaven, like a strong wind blowing, and divided tongues, like fire, appeared before them and settled down SERMO

Hoc quod videtis in altari Dei, etiam transacta nocte vidistis: sed quid esset, quid sibi vellet, quam magnae rei sacramentum contineret, nondum audistis. In fact, the prophet says: If you do not believe, you will not understand. Now you can say to me: «You command us to believe it; Explain it to us so that we understand it. The following thought may, in fact, arise in anyone's mind: "We know where Jesus Christ our Lord took flesh from: from the virgin Mary. Being small, he took the breast, was fed, grew, reached maturity, was persecuted by the Jews, hung on a tree, died on the tree and was taken down from the tree; He was buried, resurrected on the third day and when he wanted, he ascended to heaven, taking his body there; from there he must come to judge the living and the dead, and there he is now seated at the right hand of the Father: how is this bread his body and how is this cup, or what it contains, his blood? We call these things, my brothers, sacraments, because in them it is one thing that is seen and another that is understood. 2. What is seen has a corporeal form; what is understood has spiritual fruit. Therefore, if you want to understand the body of Christ, listen to the Apostle, who says to the faithful: You are the body of Christ and his members. Consequently, if you are the body and members of Christ, on the Lord's table is the mystery that is yourselves and you receive the mystery that is you. To what you are you respond with the Amen, and with your response you sign it 3. Infans lactatus est, nuttitus est, crevit, ad iuvenilem aetatem perductus est, a Iudaeis persecutionem passus est, ligno suspensus est, in ligno interfectus est, de ligno depositus est, sepultus est, tertia die resurrexit, quo die voluit, in caelum ascendit; illuc levavit corpus suum; inde est venturus ut iudicet vivos et mortuos; ibi est moda sedens ad dexteram Patris: quomodo [1247] est pañis corpus eius? et calix, vel quod habet calix, quomodo est sanguis eius? Ista, fratres, ideo dicuntur Sacramenta, quia in eis aliud videtur, aliud intellegitur. Quod videtur, speciem habet corporalem, quod intellegitur, fructum habet spiritualem. Corpus ergo Christi si vis intellegere, Apostolum audi dicentem fidelibus: Vos autem estis corpus Christi, et membra (1 Cor 12:27).

Si ergo vos estis corpus Christi et membra, mysterium vestrum in mensa Dominica positum est: mysterium vestrum accipitis. Ad id quod estis, Amen responderis, et responder subscribitis. Audis enim: Corpus Christi; and you respond, Amen. This membrane corporis Christi, ut verum sit Amen. Quare ergo Definition of sacrament that has become classic. Only in Augustine it has a greater breadth than it is ordinarily given, since, for him, the "sacraments" cannot be reduced to the seven of later theology. For him, all Scripture is full of these sacraments or mysteries, and so is the liturgy of the Church. The humble beginning of the Church

Be a member of the body of Christ so that the Amen is authentic. Why precisely in bread? Let us not contribute anything personal to this matter, and let us listen again to the Apostle, who, speaking of the same sacrament, says: Being many, we are one bread, one body. Understand it and be filled with joy: unity, truth, piety, charity. One bread: who is this one bread? Many of us are one body. Remember that bread is not made from one grain, but from many. When you received exorcisms, you were as if ground; when you were baptized, as if you were sprinkled; When you received the fire of the Holy Spirit you were as if cooked. Be what you see and receive what you are. That is what the Apostle said about bread. What we have to understand regarding the chalice, even without saying it expressly, he showed it sufficiently. For this visible type of bread to exist, many grains have been brought together into a single mass, as if the same thing happened that the Holy Scripture says about the faithful: They had one soul and one heart towards God. [1] The survival of rhetoric.—Augustine was a student and teacher of rhetoric (Confessions II 3,5; III 3,6; IV 1,1; V 7,13; 8,14; 13,23). At the time of his conversion he decided to abandon the professorship he held in Milan (ibid., IX 2,4). But although it can be said that he abandoned the profession of rhetor, it cannot be said in any way that he abandoned rhetoric, which had penetrated very deeply into his spirit, as in so many others of antiquity, since it was the queen subject, the one that formed the spirits (see H. I. MAUROU, Storia dell'eáucazione nelVantichita [Rome 31971] p.266.375). An example, among many others that could be chosen in his sermons, is the beginning of 187, where he develops a little more broadly what is common to almost all Christmas sermons. We do not want to focus only on the parallelisms, so successful, or on the antitheses or other literary figures, but on the development of the Saint's ideas, which allow us to perceive the influence that the school has left on him. In the aforementioned text we see how he resorts to the "attributes" of the person (CICERONE, The Invention I 24,34-36; QUINTILIAN, The Oratory Formation V 10,23). Thus we see that he already insists on the cognatio or kinship: born of the Father, son of David, seed of Abraham, all titles of glory, such as being born of a virgin mother, proof of his majesty (serm.184,1); already in the form of his birth (see QUINTILLIAN, The Formation... V 10,23): double and each one more admirable: without father and without mother, of father and without mother respectively: one of father without mother and another of mother without father; a new, unusual, unprecedented nativity, unique in the world, without example (serm.184,3; see Rhetoric to Herennius I 7). In her birth, a virgin conceives, gives birth and remains a virgin. Another of the points on which Augustine usually dwells is on what the rhetors called the aetas, the age; His was a birth without time, without beginning; There was no time when it did not exist; endless; a birth without a temporal day; before all times, at the opportune moment; everlasting like the Father, born of his immortality. Also his facta, his facts: creator of all the heavens, organizer of them, creator of the sun, maker of heaven and earth; moreover, maker of his own mother. And not only its past actions, but also its present ones: it contains the world, it clothes us with immortality. His wisdom: ineffably wise, etc.

Augustine knew how to take advantage of the resources that his rhetorical training gave him to maintain the attention of his listeners, on the one hand, and to make an authentic encomium of the Lord - do not forget that sermon 187 begins by expressing his desire to proclaim the praise of the Lord -, reviewing the different aspects that the rhetors indicated should be exploited for this purpose. See Pío by Luis VIZCAÍNO, The acts of Jesus in the preaching of Saint Augustine. Classical rhetoric at the service of patristic exegesis. Augustinian study (Valladolid 1933) p.125-126. [2] The human word and the divine Word.—Augustine's recourse to the human word to explain, in a certain way, some data of faith about the divine Word, the Word, is very frequent in his sermons:
(= GUELF. 22). Also the

Trinity XV 11,20. The procedure is always identical: from the analysis of the human word we move on to the Word of God, not without reinforcing the conclusions, based precisely on the infinite distance that separates one from the other: "If this is what the human word is like, what will the Word of God be like?" (serm.293 D,3). What is the human word like? Augustine bases his analysis on the distinction between the interior word and the exterior word, or, what is the same, between the idea and the voice and the sound, which includes what the philosophical tradition, and also the Christian one, expressed in the Greek language through the terms logos endiáthetos and logas prophorikós. The interior word does not belong to any language (serm.225,3; 288,3); It is in the mind or in the heart, the terms being synonymous to express interiority. To get out of here, or, in other words, to reach others, he uses voice or sound; These are like the vehicle by which the inner word is transported from the interior of one person to that of another. Through sound the inner word, which is silent, becomes audible (serm. 225,3). According to this, the inner word is always prior to the sound. Furthermore, this word, pronounced, that is, on the vehicle of sound, reaches the interlocutor, but without moving away from the person who pronounces it (serm.237,4; 288,3-4; 293 D,3; 119,7). It is a going out while staying inside. “It is in my heart and in your ears” (serm.265 F,3). That word is not divisible: it reaches everyone as a whole and to each one in particular (serm.237,4). Just because one takes ownership of it does not mean that the neighbor is left with nothing (serm.187,2). It reaches everyone in its entirety and, furthermore, at the same time. On the other hand, while the inner word endures, the sound does not (serm.293 B,2). Augustine uses this image to explain: —The incarnation, that is, that the Word of God has come to us while remaining with the Father; who has entered the mother's womb without having left the Father's. In this context, meat is the vehicle used to go out into the world. As the interior word takes sound to become audible, so the Word of God took flesh to become visible (serm.225,3; 223 A,2). Christ is, therefore, Word and voice at the same time (serm.293 D,3). —The reciprocal relationship between Jesus and Tuan the Baptist. Jesus is the Word, John the voice (serm.228,3; 289,3; 293 A,5; 293 D,3). John is the voice through which Jesus becomes audible.

The voice is added to the Word and the Word is made known (serm.289,3). The fact that the voice dies, while the Word remains, explains the phrase: It is fitting that he increase and I decrease (Jn 3:30). —Prophecy: what the sound of our mouth is with respect to the inner word, that is every preacher with respect to the Word. Just as the inner word can be manifested through various external voices, so also the Word through many messengers: the patriarchs and the prophets, until the Word came in his own voice, in his flesh as his own vehicle (serm.288,4). —Contemplation: the ideal will consist of the voices disappearing as a means to get closer to seeing Christ. The closer we come to the contemplation of Wisdom, the less we need voices. The need for the voice decreases as the direct approach to the Word occurs (serm.288,3-4). It will come at a time when

let us see the Word as the angels see it without the intermediary of the voice (serm.293 A,5). That will take place in eternal life. —In summary, Augustine has taken over a traditional theme in Christian theology. But while the apologists applied it to the Trinitarian moment, with the consequent subordinationism, Augustine knew how to focus it on the incarnation, thus avoiding the pitfalls that his predecessors ended up in, although he fell into others; For example, by identifying the voice and the flesh in the image, since the voice disappears, the flesh of Christ should disappear, something that Augustine was not willing to accept. See G. BAVAUD, Un theme augustinien: le mystére de l'incarnation a la lamiere de la distinction entre le Verbe interieur et le Yerbe proferé: Revue des études augustiniennes 9 (1963) 95-101. [3] Marriage and virginity.—The literature on marriage and virginity from the pens of the Fathers of the Church was abundant. Limiting ourselves to the Latin world in which Saint Augustine lived and was inspired, Tertullian, Saint Cyprian, Saint Jerome and Saint Ambrose, that is, his great teachers, wrote profusely on the subject. Marriage and virginity can be talked about separately or in their mutual relationships, which is what interests us here. Then it was a topical issue, especially since Elvídio, a denier of the perpetual virginity of Mary, and Joviniano, who equated virginity and marriage, entered the scene. In this context Augustine writes, and explains why in his work The Holy Virginity he dedicates abundant pages to talking about marriage. The Bishop of Hippo summarizes his thoughts in the lapidary phrase that gave rise to this note: "Conjugal fertility is good, but virginal integrity is better" (serm.184,4). Here we have the key to Augustine's thought: affirming the superiority of virginity does not mean, in any way, denying the moral value of marriage. Virginity does not owe its excellency to an alleged evil of marriage (Holy Virginity 18,18; 19,19). Virginity is superior in itself by divine right (ibid., 1,1). Always at the level of states, since Agustín is very cautious when speaking at the level of people. It means an overwhelming victory over concupiscence by abstaining from even what is licit where marriage is limited to not exceeding what is permitted (serm.161,11). Marriage, on the other hand, is a good that only fits our present situation.

Augustine linked it excessively to the idea of ​​procreation; When death disappears, procreation and, therefore, marriage will cease to have meaning (Questions about the Gospels II 49). Virginity, on the other hand, has lasting and eternal value, being the definitive form of chastity when the other two disappear: conjugal chastity and that of the state of widowhood. Furthermore, elaborating on the above, marriage will not exist when bodies are spiritualized and will have no place in heaven (Holy Virginity 13,13). But virginity is not superior as pure physical integrity. What makes it stand out are the reasons for it. A virginity lived only for its usefulness for the present life would be supreme idiocy (ibid., 13,13; 22,22). Virginal chastity only has value if it is lived for the kingdom of heaven, as Scripture indicates: Mt 19:10-12; 1 Cor 7,32-34; Rev 14,1-4 (ibid., 23-23; 24,24). This eschatological aspect cannot be forgotten, since it will be precisely in heaven where the hierarchy between states is clearly seen; according to the Apostle (1 Cor 7:26), the rewards will be different, because the merits have been different; each star will shine with its own brilliance (ibid., 14,14). Virginity is superior because it lacks the negative of marriage.

[4] The Church, virgin and mother.—Although Augustine normally associates both realities, for convenience we are going to treat the two topics separately. The Church, virgin. Augustine considers the topic very frequently in his
sermons: 64 A,3 ( = M A I

105.6; 138.8-9; 188.4; 191.3-4; 192.2; 195.2; 213.8 ( = GUELF. 1); 223.1; 260 C,7 ( = MAI 94); 264.4; 267.3; 281.1; 341.5, to which many other texts from outside the sermons should be added. The Saint usually speaks of the virginity of the Church, above all, in relation to 2 Cor 11:2-3; sometimes, in combination with Mt 25,1-13. The virginity of the Church is not different, nor, therefore, separable from that of the faithful. Since there are few who have bodily virginity (serm. 93,4; 341,5; Commentaries on Psalms 90,11,9; 147,10; Treatises on the Gospel of Saint John 13,12), it is evident that this is not the only virginity of the Church. Augustine usually speaks of the virginity of the soul (serm.93,3-4), of the heart (Comments on Psalms 39,1; 49,4; 90,11,9; 147,10; serm.93,4) or of the virginity of conscience (serm. 192,2). This virginity is defined as virginity in faith. But we must not think only of the deposit of faith; Well, in a nuptial context like the present, faith would mean fidelity to one man, trust in his promise and love for him alone; that is, to Christ in the case of the Church. «What is the virginity of the mind? An integral faith, a solid hope and a sincere charity» (Treaties...13,12). It is clear, then, that the virginity of the Church consists of that triple integrity of faith, hope and charity; Without this, the corporal would be of no use (ibid.). If the virginity of the Church is not separable from that of the faithful, it follows that when a Christian loses his spiritual virginity, he also suffers the virginity of the Church. The warning not to allow oneself to be corrupted is addressed by Augustine both to the individual soul (serm.241,5) and to the Church itself (serm.213,8). The seducer or corrupter is the devil (2 Cor 11:2-3). He, who is the serpent of paradise, tries to violate the virginity of the heart, not that of the flesh (against those who thought he had lain with Eve; see n.4 to serm.213). "As the adulterous man rejoices in his wickedness when he violates the flesh, so the devil rejoices when he violates the mind" (Comments...39,1). To do this, he presents himself as a lion, in times of persecution; already as a dragon or serpent, in times of peace (ibid.; also 90,11,9). He acts like a snake using the herees. In this regard, Augustine speaks of the Donatist heresy (Comments...39,1), Pelagian (serm.299,12), Arian (serm.341,5), and also of paganism (serm.361,4).

In these cases he does not use persecution, but rather doctrine, appealing to pride, sensuality and error, all things that destroy the virginity of the mind (serm.93,4; 72 A,8; 361,5; Comments...39,1; Treatises...13,12). In this context the fornication of the soul that Augustine speaks of is integrated. By faith, a man gives himself to God as to his husband, and receives from him the ring of the Holy Spirit. God becomes the husband of the soul (serm.137,9). Whoever dethrones him to appoint anyone else becomes an adulterer. While he usually calls idolatry and polytheism fornication (serm.15,3), he considers Christians adulterers, on the other hand.

[5] The crying of children.—Agustín was a fine observer. Already in the Confessions (X 35,54) this vain and curious concupiscence was accused, palliated with the name of knowledge and science: what is called-

We are curious. It was not lost on him that children all cry when they are born. Then he begins to reflect on it. Since man is capable of laughter and crying, why does he enter this life accompanied by crying and not laughter, which is only seen a few days later? (serm.167,1; Comments on Psalms 125,10; The City of God XXI 14). Augustine gives this cry a prophetic value. Every man, at birth, encounters his misfortune (serm.189,3), which this cry proclaims. By crying, the child becomes a prophet of his own calamity, since, evidently, tears are indicators of misery. The child has not yet spoken, says the Saint, and is already a prophet of his future sufferings and fears (serm.167,1). In the city of God (XXI 14), the crying of children at birth becomes proof of the truth of the words of Job 7,1 (according to the LXX): Is not life on earth a continuous test? Indeed, the child can enter this world laughing, and he entered crying, announcing in his own way, without realizing it, the evils that await him. This cry, furthermore, testifies to the fundamental equality between the poor and the rich (serm.61,9). A man like Augustine, provided with a deep sense of God's providence and justice, could not help but give theological meaning to the event. The occasion was provided by the Pelagian controversy. When it came to defending the existence of original sin, he found, in this observation common to all, proof that for him there was no way around it. That every child needs a liberator from birth is undoubtedly attested to by the haste of Mother Church in taking him to baptism; but that same cry also attests to it: «As far as it can, his weak nature manifests it, even without the use of reason; It does not begin with laughter, but with crying. Recognize his misery, give him help” (serm.293, 10).

And already at the end of his life, in controversy with Julian of Eclana, he once again extracts from the crying of children the same proof of original sin as the only way to save the justice of God: «In fact, if you consider with a healthy mind the miseries of human life, which begin with the crying of children and end with the moans of the dying, you would see clearly that neither you nor I, but Adam, is at the origin and is the cause of them; but, closing your eyes, you shout that God is just and that there is no original sin; You would see how those two statements of yours are contrary..." (Incomplete Work against Julián II 104; I 50). [6] The fertility of virginity.—The superiority of the state of virginity over that of marriage lies, according to Augustine, in the fact that the former lacks the negative of the latter, the servitude to concupiscence, and possesses, on the other hand, what is positive about it, fertility. Virginity is also fruitful. As in Mary virginity was not an obstacle to fertility, so it is not in them either. But, unlike Mary, her fertility is not carnal, but spiritual. "Do not consider yourselves sterile because you have remained virgins," Augustine tells them in sermon 191,4. A first fruit of this spiritual fruitfulness is precisely the pious integrity of the flesh (ibid.). Not being able to be mothers according to the flesh should not be a reason for sadness for them. Like Mary, they are also mothers of Christ. Not being able to conceive him in the flesh, like her, they conceive him in the heart and consecrate their virginity to him (ha holy virginity 11,11). What they admire in the flesh of Mary they must realize within their own soul: they must conceive and give birth to Christ. How? «Whoever believes in his heart toward righteousness conceives Christ; whoever confesses it with an eye toward salvation, gives birth to it” (serm.191,4). Virgins participate in the most eminent degree of motherhood

of the Church (see complementary note 4: The Church, virgin and mother p.783). Like every Christian, even without being able to give birth to Christ, they are also his mother, according to Mt 12:50, as long as they do the will of the Father. "In fact, every pious soul is his mother who, fulfilling the will of the Father, with most fruitful charity, generates spiritual children and gives birth to them until Christ is formed in them" (Holy Virginity 5,5; also serm.192,2). In the virgin, not the womb with the offspring must be fruitful, but the soul with the virtues; Thus the fertility of the spirit will be exuberant, always preserving the virginity of the flesh (serm.191,4). [7] A rhetorical scheme: the "posse" and the "velle".—To prove the existence of any fact, classical rhetoric had already established some procedures, which are specified in the questions an voluerit, an potuerit, an fecerit, that is, if the alleged subject wanted and could, to conclude in whether he did it or not. Therefore, the voluntas, the will, must be investigated, which includes two more precise questions: the consilium, as a determination or intentionality that justifies the work in the case of being able to do it, and the cui bono, for the benefit of whom?, since interests can be a good conduit to reach the executor of an action. The potestas must also be investigated, that is, the power or capacity to carry it out, and the faculties, that is, whether the means to do so are available. It will not always be necessary to answer each of these questions. The concrete situation will indicate what really needs to be proven, whether the will or the power, since one or the other can be easily assumed or be so evident that they do not need proof (see H. LAUSBERG, Manual of literary rhetoric. Fundamentals of a science of literature [Madrid 1966] § 99 150-165). When Augustine addresses the acts of Jesus, he does so knowing that many of them are denied by the enemies of the Christian faith, particularly the pagans, Jews, and Manichaeans. They usually give the reason that such events are impossible, in addition to being incredible and unworthy of God. The question is therefore frequent: "How could they have taken place?" This is what happens with respect to the incarnation (serm.119,6; 126,5; 186,2; 187,2; 225,3), to the virgin birth (serm.191,1), to the resurrection (serm. 116,2), to the Easter appearances (serm.247,2), to the ascension (serm.242, 7).

According to the cases, Augustine will show that they were possible (see supplementary note 29: The outline of the sermon p.806), that is, the potestas; or that they were loved, that is, the voluntas. The latter happens, for example, regarding the incarnation: "Who can properly value the fact that God wanted to be born as a man for men?" (serm.215,3). Or regarding the virgin birth: «The birth of a virgin causes us admiration, and we try to persuade the unbelievers of this new way of being born... This power is worthy of admiration; But more must be admired the mercy, (by which) whoever could be born like this, wanted to be born like this” (serm.192,1). We have, therefore, both the power and the will. But we must note the translation carried out by Agustín. While such unbelievers insisted on power, on possibility, he passes the problem by wanting. The problem is not in that one, but in this one. The demonstration of the fact must not be based on the demonstration of power, since, in the case of God, that is assured, but on that of will. We find this way of acting identical in Tertullian, who writes: "Let us consider whether he wanted to be born, because, if he wanted, he could and was born" (The Flesh of Christ 3,1, also regarding the birth of Christ). We have the same procedure, with reference to death, in sermons 362,12 and 265,2. So, to anyone who, even indirectly, asks

for the posse, the power, to believe in the existence of a fact of Jesus, the Saint responds that, since it is God, the problem lies, rather, in the velle, the will. Once the existence of that will has been proven, nothing prevents us from believing in the truth of the fact itself. See P. de Luis VIZCAÍNO, The acts of Jesus in the preaching of Saint Augustine. [8] Conception by faith.—That Mary conceived Christ by faith is an idea that Augustine constantly repeats in his sermons and writings (serm.72 A,7 [ = DENIS 251; 196,1; 214,6; 215,4; 229 P,4 [ = LAMBOT 3 ]; 233,4; 246,5; 291,5; 275 C,7 [ = M A I 95]; Reply to Faustus XXIX 4; The Trinity XIII 18,23; Treatises on the Gospel of Saint John 4,10; The precise meaning of the expression is not easy to ascertain. What does Augustine mean when he states that the conception of Christ was the result of the mother's faith? (serm.229 P,4). Two possibilities can be thought of: either that faith is what really causes conception, or that it is the precondition for conception to occur. Taking into account that faith is opposed to concupiscence in this context (serm.214,6; 229 P,4; 246,5) or to libido (Manual...34,10; The Trinity concupiscence in the conception of man. Now, concupiscence is not in itself what engenders; It is rather a precondition, the spring that sets direct causes into operation. Although the comparison cannot be extended to all individuals, it may be enough for us to try to understand the meaning of Mary's faith in the conception of Christ. Faith was the condition that made it possible. The faith present in the soul was what allowed Christ to appear in its womb (serm.196,1). This is, we believe, what is meant by Augustine's statement that Mary had conceived Christ before in her spirit than in her womb (serm.72 A,7; 215,4). This idea is so dear to Augustine because of the Mariological, and above all Christological, repercussions that it entails. As for Mariology, it shows, above all, its relationship with pneumatology.

In fact, the idea is frequently expressed in relation to the text of Luke 1,35 (serm.215,4; 233,4; 291,5). Also to confirm his theory that the generative members in the saints were not subjected to clumsy movements (Reply to Faust XXIX 4). Regarding Christology, more than one aspect must also be highlighted. On the one hand, Augustine uses this to explain the text of Is 53,8b: Who will narrate his generation?, when he applies it to human birth (serm.196,1; see n.2 to serm.184). Secondly, to explain the text of Jn 20:17, where Jesus expresses himself clearly distinguishing himself from other men when speaking about my God and your God (serm.246,5). But, above all, Augustine uses this thought to explain why Christ is equal to men and at the same time different, but with a precise intention: to show how he has not contracted original sin despite coming from the race of Adam (serm.229 P,4; 246,5; The Trinity XIII 18,23; Treatises...4,10; Manual...34,10). [9] Flight from persecution.—One of the moral problems raised by the time of persecution was whether a Christian could or should flee to avoid death. If we except the rigorist Tertullian, who in his work Flight in Persecution defends that flight is morally inadmissible, since

Persecution is willed, not only permitted, by God to test the righteous and increase their merits, and, consequently, flight would be equivalent to denying the will of God; If we also except other practical rigorists who denounced themselves as Christians, knowing that this would bring them death, the rest of the Christian tradition has generally admitted the moral legality and even the convenience of flight, which finds its support in the doctrine and behavior of Jesus and the apostles (Mt 2:13-15; 10:17-23; Jn 8:59; 11:53-54; Acts 8,4; 9,23-24). The two best-known examples, but not the only ones, were Saint Cyprian and Saint Athanasius: both fled from persecution, and both also had to justify their behavior with separate writings, since not everyone saw it favorably. Of Saint Athanasius we preserve the work Apology for his escape. Better known to Augustine was the case of Saint Cyprian. From some of his letters (14,1; 59,6) and also from the Life of Cyprian (7), we know that, faced with the multiplication of cries "Cyprian to the lion" from the mouths of the pagans, he chose to flee to an unknown place, advised by his colleagues and friends, thinking that his presence in Carthage would bring more harm than good to the Christians. Letter 20 is a justification of the Saint in the face of the accusation that came to him from the clergy of Rome, who had seen how their bishop Fabian had lost his life in the same persecution. Augustine also admits the legality of flight (serm.133,7; 202,2; Comments on the Psalms 141,11; Reply to the letter of Petiliano II 19,43). But the statement must be qualified when it refers to pastors. This has been expressed in Comments...141,11 and note 228. It is this last text that best expresses the Saint's opinion, because it directly addresses the issue at the request of his friend and also bishop Honorato, who asked him for advice on how to behave in the face of the imminent arrival of the barbarians. Augustine's position can be summarized in these words: it is lawful for shepherds to flee, as long as the flock of Christ is not left unattended. His words: «Let the servants of Christ, ministers of his word and his sacraments, do what he commanded or permitted. Flee from city to city when you are personally sought by persecutors, while the Church is cared for by others who do not suffer persecution...

But, when danger is common to bishops, clerics and laymen, those who need others cannot be abandoned by them. Either everyone seeks refuge..., or those who need to stay should not be abandoned by those who provide them with the necessary ecclesial services. Either they all live together or they all suffer together whatever the Father of the family decides” (n.2). If the evils that are coming are such that flight is advised, "those who demand our presence must first flee, and thus they will free us from the need to stay. Nobody says that ministers should stay when they no longer have anyone to serve” (n.5). In short, the pastor can flee "when there is no one left in Christ's flock to care for, or when there is, but the indispensable service is already covered by another who does not have the same reasons for fleeing" (n.6). [10] The symbolism of the number 40.—To our current mentality, the way the Fathers had of interpreting numbers is, to say the least, shocking. The Pythagorean philosophical tradition had already given them a value that transcended mere quantitative information. In Scripture, on the other hand, they are frequently given symbolic value. The two traditions, the secular and the biblical, come together in Augustine, who has a special predilection for unraveling the mystery, the ratio, of any

figure: The number 40 is one whose meaning is most frequently explained by Augustine. This is due, on the one hand, to the repeated frequency with which it appears in the biblical text: 40 days of the flood, 40 years in the desert, 40 days of fasting of Moses, Elijah and Jesus himself (serm.205,1; 210,9; 252,10.12; 264,5; Treatises on the gospel of Saint John 17,4; Commentaries on the psalms 110,1; etc.), and, on the other hand, to its presence in the liturgical calendar with the 40 days of Lent and the 40 days that follow the resurrection until the ascension of the Lord. The interpretive scheme is based on the breakdown of the number into two multiples, always the same: 10 and 4; 40 results from multiplying 10 by 4. The next step is to decipher the meaning of each of them. The 10: although in some text it says that it symbolizes the fullness of wisdom (serm.264,5) and in another it is derived from the sum of 7 (creation) plus 3 (Trinity) (serm.252,10), the normal thing is that it refers to the law (serm.205,1; 210,9; 363 A,4 [ = MAI 98]; Treatises on the Gospel of Saint John 17:6). The 4: according to the Saint, it relates to the four seasons of the year (serm.252,10; 264,5), to the four cardinal points (serm.252,10; 264,5), to the four winds (serm.252,10), to the four gospels (serm.205,1; Treatises...17,6); but, above all, to the four parts of the world (serm.210,9; 263 A,4; 264,5; Treatises...17,6; Comments...110,1). Of the two multiples, 10 usually gives the number 40 the ascetic tone, and 4 the note of universality, which sometimes derives from biological theories (man would be formed in the womb in the space of forty days: serm.205,1). Hence it follows that the number 40 means this time, in which it is necessary to abstain from temporal things (serm. 252,10); the time of misery and groaning in which we find ourselves (serm.254, 3); the passing of this world (serm.264,5); the passage through this life (serm. 263 A,4); the totality of this life (serm.205,1); the tiring present time (serm.252,10). The meaning is derived not only from the value assigned to the numbers, but also from the context in which the number 40 appears: almost always in the context of fasting and Lent, since fasting is associated in the Bible with that figure: Moses, Elijah and Jesus fasted for forty days. Hence, in addition to meaning the totality of the present life, it carries with it an invitation to restrain worldly appetites (serm.263 Á,4; 264,5; Comments...110,1), not to adhere to this world.

When, on the other hand, the comment is not associated with fasting, but with the forty days after the resurrection that Jesus spent with his disciples, always within this symbolism of totality, it means that Jesus will be with us until the end of time (serm.263 A,4); the necessity of faith in the incarnation while we live here (serm.264,5); the object of our waiting (serm.254,3). If the 10 (denarium reward of Mt 20) is added to this present time of fatigue, effort and waiting, we have the meaning of eternal life, symbolized in the number 50 (serm.252,12; Treatises...17,4). In this case, the number 40 indicates the perfection of good works, the complete fulfillment of the law, which makes one worthy of the prize or reward of the denarius. [11] Lenten fasting.—Fasting is, along with prayer and almsgiving, the constant element in the preaching of Saint Augustine during Lent (serm.205,2; 206,1; 207,1; 208,1; 209,2; 210,2). During it, fasting was daily, except on Sundays and Holy Thursday. Then it was interrupted for the fifty days that followed Easter, that is, until Pentecost (serm.210,4; ctas.36,8,18; 55,15,28). throughout

of the year it was customary to fast on Wednesdays, in remembrance of the day on which the Jews made the decision to kill Jesus, and on Fridays, in remembrance of his death (ct.36,13,30). Regarding the Sabbath, there were different customs: while some fasted to commemorate the humiliation of the Lord, who lay in the tomb on Saturday, others did not, associating their rest in the tomb with God's rest in creation on the seventh day (act.36, 13,31). In addition to these days, Augustine tried to convert the date of the New Year into a day of penance and, therefore, fasting, in order to compensate for the licentious life of the pagans (see n.3 to serm.198). When justifying fasting, Augustine will resort to the example of Moses, Elijah and Jesus (serm.205,1; 210,9; Treatises on the Gospel of Saint John 17,4; Commentaries on the Psalms 110,1), who fasted forty days, symbolizing that in this life one must abstain from all worldly delights (see supplementary note 10: The symbolism of the number 40 p.788). Through him the Christian raises his own cross, on which he must crucify the old man, and from which he must hang so as not to sink his feet into the mud of the earth (serm.205,1). In imitation of Jesus, fasting is also done to combat temptations (serm.210,3). The fast consisted of a single meal a day at the ninth hour, that is, around three in the afternoon (acta.54,6,9), eliminating the one at noon. With fasting was linked abstinence from meat and wine and renunciation of attendance at public baths. Augustine also associates sexual abstinence with fasting in all Lenten sermons (serm.205,2; 206,3; 207,2; 208,1; 209,3; 210,4). The reasons for fasting that Christians had were very different from those that a Manichean might have, for example. Augustine insists that the deprivation of some foods does not in any way mean that those foods are bad.

At the same time he constantly reminds his listeners that fasting does not consist of the pure materiality of abstaining from certain foods (serm.207,2); he attacks with finesse and irony those who, in their desire to get away from meat on those days, even distance themselves from the pots in which it is cooked (serm.209,3; 210,10), and those who deprive themselves, yes, of meat and wine, but to look for other more exquisite foods and liquors, or even fast in order to later eat with greater appetite; In this way, Lenten observances, instead of being a brake on old passions, serve as an occasion for new delights (serm.207,2); Abstinence is not embraced, but the object of pleasure is changed (serm.209,3; 210,11); men become deliciosi instead of religiosi (serm.210,11). Augustine was no fan of fasting; He knows how to make concessions with those who would find it difficult to fast for any reason, but he warns them that they can change fasting for almsgiving, since that is one of the reasons for fasting: to help those in need with what we deprive ourselves of. And he who cannot give alms of money because he is poor, can and should give alms from the heart: forgiveness. Fasting and almsgiving are the two wings of prayer so that it can reach God (serm.206,3; 207,3). As there is double alms, that which is done with money and that of the heart, that is, forgiveness, so there is also a double fast: the corporal and the spiritual, the most important without a doubt, which consists of abstaining from arguments and discord (serm.205,3), in always abstaining from hatred and always feeding on love (serm.207,3). [12] The Fathers and usury.—Writings against usury or lending at interest are abundant in patristic literature prior to Augustine. With greater or lesser extent, the following have written about her: Clement of Alexandria (The Pedagogue 1,10; Tapestries 2,19), Saint Athanasius (Exposition of Psalm 14,2-5), Saint Basil (Homily on Psalm 14; cta.188), Saint

Gregory Niseno (Homily IV on Ecclesiastes; Against usurers), Saint Gregory of Nazianzus (Discourse 16:18) and Saint John Chrysostom (Homily 14 on Genesis; Homilies 56 and 61 on Matthew), in the Greek language. In Latin language: Tertullian (Against Marcion 4,17), Saint Cyprian (Book of Testimonies to Quirinus I I I 48), Commodiano (Instructions 65), Lactantius (Divine Institutions 6,18; Epitome 64), Saint Hilary (Commentary on Psalm 14,15), Saint Ambrose (Tobias; cta.19) and Saint Jerome (Commentary on Ezekiel 6,18). Common to all of them, without exception, is the condemnation of usurious practices. The reasons given are the following: a) They oppose Scripture, particularly the Old Testament, whose legislation in this regard they consider continues to have value. This is how we find it in Clement of Alexandria (Ez 18,8), Tertullian (Ez 18,8), Saint Cyprian (Ez 18,8; Dt 23,20 and Ps 15,5), Saint Basil (Ez 22,12; Dt 23,19; Jer 9,6; Ps 54,12 and Mt 5,42), Saint Ambrose (Ez 22,24; Dt 23,20; Lev 25,33; b) It is incompatible with Christian love. This way of arguing, that is, of considering usury in connection with its effects on the poor, is even more frequent than the previous one. Charging interest means living off the needs of the poor (Lactantius); Money having been created to alleviate poverty and not to increase it, the practice of usury, instead of helping the poor, increases their need (Hilary, Cappadocians, Ambrose, John Chrysostom); It brings evils and is shameful both for the one who lends at interest and for the one who receives the loan (Gregorio Niseno and Juan Chrysóstomo). The rich become inhuman (Basilio, Ambrose), c) Only animated things produce fruit; Consequently, usury as a fruit of money is unnatural (Basilio, Gregory Niseno, Ambrose, taking an idea from Aristotle). To understand the force of the patristic condemnation of usury, we must take into account that it was a practice permitted by civil law and that it was also condemned even when it was lent not to the poor, but to wealthy people. Likewise, not only the interest charged in money was condemned, but any type and in any form that attempted to receive something more than what was lent (Basilio, Ambrosio). Augustine is no less radical; His position fits perfectly into this entire tradition.

He speaks especially against usury in Commentaries on Psalms 36,111,6; 128.6; account154.25; Baptism against the Donatists IV 9 and the Serm. 38.8 and 86.5. His argument rests on the identification of the poor with Christ; Asking for interest means stealing from Christ (and Saint Ambrose). Despite being permitted by law, the usurer is little different from a thief, as Saint Gregory Nisene, Saint John Chrysostom and Saint Ambrose had previously proclaimed. If the prohibition is general, it is even more so for clerics (Comments...128,6). Its gravity is such that it excludes one from the kingdom of heaven (Baptism against the Donatists IV 9, based on Ps 15:5 and the little work The Apostates 6, by Saint Cyprian). See R. P. MALONEY, The teaching of the Fathers on Usury: An historical Study on the Development of Christian Think: Vigiliae Christianae 27 (1973) 241-265. [13] Meaning of "otium".—The Latin term otium has in its use, by Augustine, some nuances that are useful to highlight. Although in some text he refers to it as inactivity (The City of God I I I 9: warlike inactivity), the Saint's conception takes other directions: otium, leisure, is not, normally, a lack of activity for him, but rather a specific activity. In fact, if he sometimes contrasts otium with negotium
