Additional notes

(cta.48,1-2; 10,2; The city of God XIX 19), in other texts he considers the otium as a subspecies of the negotium or activity (Comments...110,1; 147,3; serm.221 A). When contrasted with otium, negotium refers, at a profane level, to entering public administration or devoting oneself to other worldly activities, particularly lucrative ones, and, at an ecclesiastical level, to assuming responsibilities in the pastoral ministry (cta.10,2; ha city of God XIX 19). In cta.48, Augustine contrasts his business activity as a shepherd with the otius of the monks, whose "activities" he lists in number 3 of the same, showing that this otium should never be understood as doing nothing. Otium is not inaction, but rather a search or discovery of the truth (The City of God XIX 19); It is the occupation in studies that lead to good and, ultimately, to God (Treatise on the Gospel of Saint John 57,5), which becomes contemplation of God (The City of God XIX 19). Thus, he can speak of otiosum negotium or "idle activity." Eternal life will be the place of perfect otium. Which does not prevent Augustine from asking what our activity will be there, to answer: «Praising God: loving him and praising him; praise him with love and love him with praise” (Comments on Psalms 147,3; also serm.211 A). It will be an otium full of only sweetness, without any discomfort or fatigue (ibid.). All of this synthesized in the Hallelujah, the negotium otiosorum, the activity of the "idle" (Comments...110,1). Obviously, the previous philosophical tradition weighs heavily in this entire conception, which reaches Augustine fundamentally through Cicero, but not only through him (see G. FOLLIET, Deifican in otio: Recherches Augustiniennes 2,225-236). But he has known how to adapt it to what is specifically Christian. [14] The delivery of the symbol and the Lord's Prayer.—A moment of special importance in the path of preparation for baptism on the Easter Vigil was the traditio symboli and the traditio orationis, that is, the delivery of the symbol of faith and the prayer of the Lord's Prayer so that the candidates for the reception of the sacrament, the competent ones, could learn them. This first rite was followed by a second, that of the redditio symboli and the redditio orationis, that is, the recitation, by heart and before the Christian community, of both texts. These were the moments that the bishop took advantage of to do a catechesis on them.

From these catechesis on the symbol we preserve sermons 212, 213, 214, 215, 216; on the Lord's Prayer, sermons 56, 57, 58 and 59. Regarding the precise calendar of events, not all authors have the same opinion. P. Verbraken (Les sermons CCXV et LVI de sainl Augustin: Revue Bénédictine 68 [1958] 5-40) proposes the following order: the traditio symboli took place on the Saturday of the fourth week of Lent (third before Easter), and on the following Saturday the first redditio, together with the traditio orationis; On the Saturday before Palm Sunday, a second redditio symboli took place, and on Easter night, the third and solemn one. S. Póque, on the other hand, proposes the following calendar, which seems more accurate to us: fifteen days before Easter the traditio symboli took place; eight days before, the first redditio symboli and the traditio orationis; at the Easter Vigil, the solemne redditio symboli (Sermons pour la Vaque; SC 116 [Paris 1966] p.59ff). The order in which both deliveries occurred was not accidental, but was based on theological reasons, which Augustine took care to explain in his sermons to his listeners. At the base was a text from the letter to the Romans (10:13-15): How are they going to call on him in whom they have not

believed? "You did not receive, says Augustine, first the prayer and then the symbol, but first the symbol, so that you would know in whom you were to believe, and then the prayer, so that you would know whom to invoke" (serm.56,1; also 57,1; 58,1; 59,1). Those being baptized, as already indicated, had to learn both texts by heart. Augustine placed more emphasis on the symbol, because it offered greater difficulty, since it was longer, and then because, while the prayer would be heard daily in the Eucharistic celebration, the symbol would not (serm.58,12-13). For this reason, he invites them to repeat it constantly, even when going to bed and getting up, so that they do not forget (serm.58,13; 215,1). They had to learn it by just hearing it recited, since they were prevented from writing it. This measure had not been taken on a whim or for practical reasons; It was a way to symbolize what was written by the prophet Jeremiah (31,33): This is my alliance that I will establish with them after these days, says the Lord. I will give my law to their minds and write it on their hearts. «To mean that, says Agustín, the symbol is learned by hearing it. It is not written on tablets or on any other material, but only on the heart” (serm.212,2; 214,1). [15] The formless matter.—We find the understanding of creation that Saint Augustine exposes in sermon 214 more fully developed in other texts. Due to their importance, we highlight Confessions In the first of them it is evident in the term "Principle", which Augustine, following Jn 8:25, refers to the Word; in the second, in the expression God said, which reveals the Word of the Father. Consequently, Augustine speaks of two successive moments of creation, with logical rather than chronological succession (serm.214, 2). Referring to the first, the Saint speaks of simultaneous creation; with reference to the second, of a per ordinem process. The first moment results in formless matter; the second, the things, the formed beings. The formless matter. It is the first stage of creation. Augustine finds it described in those words of Gen 1:2: The earth was invisible and imperfect and darkness rested on the face of the abyss. The first chapters of Book XII of the Confessions are dedicated to the description of this matter.

If it is under darkness it is because it lacks light; then it is formless, then it is formless; It was, therefore, "a certain formlessness without any form", but that did not mean it was absolutely nothing (XII 3,3). If it is said that it was "earth", it is because it must be expressed in some way and because the earth is precisely the last grade in the ladder of beings with form (species) (ibid., 4,4). That formless matter is something that remains halfway between form and nothingness; It is neither something formed nor pure nothingness, but something that can be called "almost nothingness." If we could talk about "nothing something" and "it is not", he would call it that. It was already a something, insofar as it was capable of receiving visible and composed forms (XII 6,6; 8,8). Referring to it, he says that God made almost nothing out of nothing, from which, in turn, he would make everything that we as men contemplate and admire. From it, then, comes everything we see with its own forms. The formed beings. It is the second stage of creation. It is carried out by the Word as a Word, not as a Principle, as in the previous one. In fact, if this second action of the Word did not exist on both spiritual and corporeal creatures, they would remain in disrepair.

jance and immoderation. So that this would not happen, the Word called them to their unity, and thus they acquired the form to be good (XIII 2,2). In this way, in response to the call (vocatio), conversion (conversio) occurs, which causes the formation or acquisition of form (formatio), or illumination, consisting of becoming similar to the Word, enabling one to live according to Wisdom (XIII 2,3). This second moment is meant in the expression "Let there be light" and the work of the remaining "days" of creation (XIII 3,4; Literal Commentary on Genesis I 4,9). Both moments of creation are recorded in this other Augustinian text: «Through conversion and formation, the creature imitates, in its own way, the Word of God... But it does not imitate the form of the Word if, separating itself from the creator, it remains formless and imperfect. Therefore, when it is said: In the Beginning God made heaven and earth, the Son is not mentioned as a Word, but as a Principle, since reference is made to the beginning of the creature, even in a state of formlessness and imperfection. In the words: God said: 'Let there be', mention is made of the Son as Word, so that if his condition of Principle refers to the beginning of the creature, still imperfect, that exists through him, his condition of Word insinuates the perfection of the creature, called to him to receive the form, adhering to the creator and imitating, according to his ability, the Form united to the Father ever and immutably, from whom he instantly receives the being that he is" (Literal Commentary of the Genesis I 4,9). [16] A Lenten exorcism.—"At the time of the scrutiny, it is true, and when the same inducer of flight and desertion [the devil] is rebuked with the force of the tremendous Trinity, you were not clothed in sackcloth; but, nevertheless, your feet were mystically firm in it” (serm.216,10). The present text makes mention of a Lenten exorcism that is also known to us from the writings of Quodvultdeus (Sermon 1 on the symbol to the catechumens 2,1 [PL 40,637] and another Sermon on the symbol to the catechumens [ I V ] 1,1 [PL 40,660], once attributed to Augustine, among whose works they appear in the appendix). The rite, which consisted of standing on a goat skin, is unknown in the ancient Roman, Milanese and Gallic liturgies. However, it is known in Spain, as witnessed by Saint Ildefonso of Toledo (The Knowledge of Baptism 109).

It also existed in the East; specifically, in the Antiochene liturgy, as attested by two catechesis by Theodore of Mopsuestia on baptism, the first as a remote preparation and the second immediately before the administration of the sacrament, which suggests that it took place twice: the first, at the beginning of the catechumenate, and the second, in the Easter vigil, this repetition being the difference between the African and Spanish praxis and the Antiochene. The meaning of the rite is explained by Augustine below: «Vices and goatskins must be trampled; we must tear the rags taken from sinister goats” (serm.216,11). For Augustine, then, the goatskin is a symbol of the sins and vices that catechumens abjure. The symbols of sin must be mystically torn, since these skins are reminiscent of the goats, which must be on the left on the day of judgment. Standing on one's skin means trampling on old sins or, what is the same, turning away from vices (see The City of God XV 4; The Concordance of the Evangelists I I 4-13). The ritual has the same meaning in the other two explicit non-African testimonies. For San Ildefonso of Toledo it is a sign of penitence, and for Teodoro de Mopsuestia, a rite that should bring to mind one's own

sins. See J. QUASTEN, Ein Taufexorcismus bei Augustinus: Revue des études augustiniennes (1956) 101-108, whom we have summarized. [17] The mother of all vigils.—Referring to the Easter Vigil, Augustine says that it is the most sacred and holy of vigils (serm.223 B), that it occupies the first place among all those instituted for the worship of God (serm.223 D [ = WILMART 4]), that it is the vigil par excellence, and that it stands out so much that it can claim as its own the name that is common to all the others. (serm.221,2 [ = GUELF. 5]), and also that she is the mother of all holy vigils (serm.219). From all the texts mentioned, it is evident that more vigils were held and that they were known to the faithful of Hippo. It is worth asking, then, what those other vigils were. From the texts the following can be deduced: Possibly there was a vigil eight days before the great Easter vigil. This seems to be deduced from the following text: «In eight days you will have to proclaim in public what you have received [the symbol] today. Your parents, those who welcome you, will teach you, so that you are prepared, how you are to remain vigil until the rooster crows, for the prayer that you celebrate here” (serm.213,11 [ = GUELF. 1]). With all certainty, there was the vigil of Pentecost, the occasion on which Augustine delivered sermons 29, 29 A (= DENIS 9) and 266. It is also probable that the vigil of the feast of Saint Cyprian was celebrated. Perhaps it can be deduced from sermon 311,5, when Augustine speaks of how at the place of martyrdom they sang and danced all night. The same seems to be deduced from the indications in the manuscripts of the Commentaries on Psalms 32, I I, s.l.; 85, I I and sermon 308 A (= DENIS 11), which took place, according to such indications, on the vigil of the holy martyr Cyprian. The same must be said of sermon 360, although in this case it is the vigil of the feast of Saint Maximian. Finally, there is the practice of vigil as a private exercise of devotion practiced by the faithful. This is how the following text can be understood: «In the night well into the night I have gone forward and cried out: 'I have waited for your word' (Ps 118:147).

If you refer these words to the individual faithful and take them in their proper sense, it often happens that during such nocturnal hours the love for the Lord watches over, and, after the strong impulse exercised by the taste of prayer, the moment of prayer is not waited for, but is anticipated, which is usually after the crowing of the rooster" (Comments on Psalms 118, XXIX, 4). We know, therefore, other vigils different from the great Easter vigil from the texts of Augustine. But the statement cannot be made with certainty for Hippo. In fact, the sermons preached on the eve of Pentecost and on the feast of Saint Cyprian took place in Carthage and inform us only about the praxis of that city, not about that of Hippo. As for the feast of Saint Maximian, the place is unknown. For Hippo, then, only the Easter Vigil and the probable one referred to in sermon 213,11 remain with certainty. But we are talking only about what we know, not about what really existed. The texts with which we began this note clearly indicate that the faithful of Hippo knew of other vigils. See F. W. THIELE, Die Theologie der “Vigilia” nach den Sermones des hl. Augustinus zur Ostervigil (Hildesheim 1979) p.11-14. [18] «Ventase and «sollemnitas».—The celebration of Easter has a sacramental dimension, in Augustinian terminology, which distinguishes it from other celebrations. He expresses this through the distinction between veritas and sollemnitas. An event can be remembered or it can be celebrated. What is characteristic of the sollemnitas is precisely that ce-

lebration, which is more than a mere memory; It is also participation. The event itself, the sale, took place only once and forever; But that does not prevent it from being updated, or rather, from being acted out again, the subject benefiting from what the event itself means. Where this reality is best expressed is in letter 55,1,2. A certain Jenaro had asked him why the anniversary of the Lord's passion was not celebrated on a fixed date, like the day of his birth. Augustine answers him by distinguishing the sacramental celebration (in sacramento) of the Lord's passion from the non-sacramental celebration (non in sacramento). Since this sacrament was not celebrated, it was only a matter of recalling the fact that he was born, it was only necessary to indicate the day of the year on which it took place. A sacramental celebration occurs when the celebration is such that the existence of a hidden meaning that must be received holyly is noted. Thus, when we celebrate Easter, we do not limit ourselves to remembering the event of the death and resurrection of the Lord, but we act out the other things that the "sacrament" entails. The Apostle says that Christ was handed over for our sins and was resurrected for our justification (Rom 4:25); Accordingly, in the passion and resurrection of the Lord the passage from death to life was consecrated, the transition from this mortal life to the immortal, which is what is celebrated at Easter. Thus, the Easter sollemnitas must mean a sacramental reality or, what is the same, not only remember the death and resurrection of the Lord, the event, but also its mystical or salvific aspect: what Jesus acted, the Christian must now act. Easter must be the moment in which the renewal of the inner man takes place through the passage from death to life, which begins already in baptism, as participation in the death and resurrection of Christ. This transition is now made through faith, hope and love, awaiting the renewal of the external man, the resurrection of the body, of which the resurrection of Christ is proof and I anticipate. [19] Theology of the Easter Vigil.—The Easter Vigil is the mother of all vigils (serm.219), the most sacred and holy (serm.223 B [ = GUELF. 4]), which deserved the name vigil without further appellation (serm.221,2 [ = GUELF. 5 ]; see complementary note 17: The mother of all vigils vigils p.795).

Augustine has dedicated a good number of sermons, generally short, to explaining his theology (serm.219, 220, 221, 223 A-K). There are many reasons why Christians stay awake. According to Augustinian texts, vigil has an ascetic value, an eschatological value and a mystical-sacramental value. ascetic value. The Christian watches to avoid falling into temptation, in accordance with the words of the Lord to his disciples in Gethsemane: Watch and pray so that you do not enter into temptation (Mt 26:41). Augustine refers to it in sermons 223 B,2 and 223 E, l (= WILMART 5). He also watches to imitate Saint Paul, who, according to 2 Cor 11,27, had to spend a lot of time in vigils (serm.223 B, l; 221,2; 219,1). The fight against the powers of evil also has great importance, according to Eph 6:12 (serm.219, 222, 223 E). Eschatological value. We all await the rest of eternal life, in which neither death nor sleep, its image, will have a place; realities typical of mortals, since angels do not sleep, but live an endless life (serm.221,2). Thus, then, the Christian watches to manifest that desire for eternal life; Shorten sleep time to live longer.

Whoever attends the vigil, undoubtedly already practices the life of angels. The members that still need to sleep imitate, while the moment arrives, his head, already awake forever, keeping vigil themselves, since they have to do it like him and they have to reign with him in eternal vigil, in which there will be no sleep. Therefore, Christ is awakened, depriving himself of sleep for a little time in honor of him who is no longer dominated by sleep (serm.223 G [ = WILMART 7]). Mystical-sacramental value. Agustín dedicates great space to the theme of light and new life. The Christian who remains awake becomes a witness of the passage from darkness to light, from night to day, from death to life; a step that is taken in the soul, but of which waiting during the night for the arrival of the new day is an image. Always under the protection of biblical texts: Psalm 138,3 (serm.219); 17.29 (serm.221.1); 2 Cor 4,6 (serm.223 D,2); Col 1,12 (serm.222); Rom 13,12 (serm.221,4); Eph 5,8 (serm.219,1; 222). [20] Concubinage.—Sermon 224 is not the only Augustinian text in which we discover how some Christians of that time valued prostitution and concubinage differently from a moral point of view. While they considered it contrary to Christian morality to join a prostitute, they considered it normal to live with a concubine. This is evident from the response of Augustine's fictional interlocutor in sermon 224: "She is not a prostitute, she is my concubine." In sermon 392,2, Augustine will insist with increasing emphasis that it is not lawful for a Christian to live with a concubine: «It is not lawful for you to have concubines. Even if you do not yet have a wife, you are not allowed to have concubines that you think about abandoning when you get married. From these texts, a double situation can be deduced: 1) That of those who, before contracting a legal marriage, live with a concubine, whom they will abandon at the appropriate time. 2) That of those who, despite being married, live in common law. This situation is perfectly understood from Roman legislation. According to Roman law, when marriage was not possible due to certain circumstances, some forms of cohabitation between a man and a woman other than marriage itself were permitted.

One of them was concubinage. This is the name given to the stable marital union, without the purpose of marriage, between free people, whose union was not punished by law. Such a union was not a marriage either because of legal impossibility or simply because the interested parties did not want to. It was not indissoluble nor did it require fidelity between the parties. However, it required certain conditions: no one be married in a legitimate marriage, since in that case adultery would occur. The same degrees of kinship that prevented marriage also prevented concubinage.

born, so as not to fall into incest. Free consent on both sides was also necessary, without violence or corruption. They had to be nubile women. Lastly, it had to be with only one person. Outwardly, it had all the appearance of marriage; when the law did not prevent it, it only differed from it by intention. Only inner determination distinguished the wife from the concubine. The practice of concubinage must have existed in Rome at all times, but the law dealt with it only since Augustus. In the Julia Law on adultery, it is the only non-marital union that is not punished as statutory rape. Then it became very common, especially among personnel with unequal status and widows with children who did not want a second marriage. The woman did not participate in the dignity of the partner nor did propter nuptiae donation exist. Children born from concubinage were considered natural, taking the name and status of the mother, without the father having power (potestas) over them. Under the Christian emperors it was not well regarded, although it persisted until Emperor Leo the Philosopher repealed the laws in this regard, for the East, in the year 887. Constantine and Zeno had provided many facilities for concubinages to become legitimate marriages, following a praxis that the Church itself had already begun. See J. GUILLEN, Urbs Roma. Life and customs of the Romans. I. Private life (Salamanca 1977) p.156-158. [22] "Form" and "virtus."—The text of 2 Tim 3:5: Those who have the outward form of godliness, but deny its power, appears constantly in the pages of Augustinian preaching; many times in direct quotation and, even more, in simple references. Augustine uses the text in his sacramental theology to distinguish two different planes: the exterior and the interior; the exterior, which is the work of the minister of the sacrament, and the interior, which is the work of the Holy Spirit. The form is the external appearance, what is seen, the ritual; strength (virtus) is inner efficacy, the life it confers, grace, charity. Agustín is not uniform in the way he expresses himself. Sometimes, most frequently, it is served forma-virtus; but on other occasions he resorts to different expressions, but with the same fundamental content: species-virtus (Treaties on the Gospel of Saint John 61,2; The Christian Cambate 30,32), sacramentum-virtus sacramenti (Treaties...26,12), forma visibilis-invisibilis gratia (cta. 105,3,12). Augustine's use of this sacramental theology has two levels, one general and one specific. Let's start with the first one. Leaving aside its use, but in the opposite sense, to explain the sacrament of the altar, in which the external form of the elements is identical before and after sanctification (consecration), while the virtus is different after it (serm.229 A, l [ = GUELF. 7]), Augustine uses the distinction between forma and virtus to show that the sacraments are useless if they are not received properly or lived as they should. In these cases the sacrament is received, but not its effectiveness (virtus). Scripture gives you two clear examples; the first, referring to baptism, and the second, to the Eucharist.

Simon Magus was baptized, but he did not abandon his old way of thinking; Consequently, having received the sacrament did not prevent him from hearing from the mouth of Saint Peter: You have no part or lot in this faith (Acts 8:21, as Augustine read). He resorts to the example twice in the sermons (260 A,2 [ = DE NIS 8 ]; 229 U). Likewise, Judas also received the body of Christ at the Last Supper, but for his condemnation (Treaties...26,11). All those who have received the sacraments are counted among the members of the People of God, but not all fall under his mercy. You can be in the era of Christ, but be chaff, not grain (Comments on Psalms 47:8); you can have the baptism of Christ, but not the faith and love of Christ; to have the sacrament of holiness, and not to be counted among the saints. It is not enough, therefore, to have the form of piety, the visible sacrament; You must also possess its virtus, its strength, which is charity (serm.229 U; 229 V; 260 A,2; etc.). Specifically, Augustine applies the same thing to heretics. To the Luciferians (The Christian Combat 30,32), and above all, with the greatest frequency, to the Donatists. While these defended that baptism administered outside of their Church was invalid, and that, therefore, in case of return to it it had to be reiterated, Augustine admits the validity and, consequently, the non-iterability, of all baptism, even that administered by heretics. But he distinguishes between forma and virtus: heretics have

nen the first, but not the second; that is, they have the sacrament, but not its saving fruit (serm.260 A,2; 272). When applying the text to the Donatists, he also tends to rely on Jds 1,19: Those who separate themselves are animal men who do not have the Spirit (serm.8,18; 268,2). Since they do not possess the Spirit because they have separated, they do not obtain the fruit of the sacrament, life. Along with the example of the soldier who does not lose the king's seal even if he has deserted (serm.260 A,2), the Saint constantly uses two comparisons: an amputated limb and a pruned branch: both have the same external shape as before when they were attached to the body or the vine; The external form changes nothing, but they lack life because they are separated from its source, the root (serm.71,32; 268,2; Treatises...13,16; Treatises on the first letter of Saint John 2,9; The Christian combat 30,32). Thus, the Donatist who asked him why he should enter the Catholic Church, if it were accepted that the Donatist baptism itself was valid and, therefore, nothing else could be given to him, Augustine would always respond in the name of the Church: «You already possess the baptism of Christ; come to receive the Spirit of Christ” (serm.71,32; 269,3; Treatises on the Gospel of Saint John 13,16). The form, that is, the sacrament, is good and holy; but, if the Spirit does not invigorate it internally, the boasting of the external rite is vain (serm.268,2). The form alone is not enough without the force of piety, that is, without the root of charity (Treatise on the first letter of Saint John 2,9), which can only be obtained and maintained within the bond of peace (serm.71,32; 260 A,2). It is not enough to belong to the communio sacramentorum; You must also be part of the societas sanctorum (see n.5 to serm.214). [23] Merchant Christ.—One of the most frequent images in Augustinian sermons is that of Christus mercator, merchant Christ. Christ is presented as the merchant who travels to distant lands to exchange goods. He came from heaven, from his region, the region of the angels (serm.229 E, l [ = GUELF. 9 ]; 231,5; 233,4), to this our region; He came from God to our land, to our miseries (serm.229 H, l [ = GUELF. 12 ]; 231,5), which means that he came from the region of life to the region of death, from the place of happiness to that of fatigue (serm.229 E, l).

But he came by another path different from ours: he came from a virgin by the Holy Spirit, without carnal embrace, without lust (serm.233,4). He came to teach us what we did not know (serm.229 H, l), to bring us his goods (serm.229 E, l), and, in return, he took our evils. Man knew two things: being born and dying; birth, as the beginning of fatigue, and death, as a journey into the unknown (serm.229 E, l; 229 H, l; 233,4). He took what was known here, what was usual in this land, and, instead, he left us the great novelty. Who, in fact, knew about resurrection and living forever? (serm.229 H, l). That was what brought us, establishing an admirable trade, consisting of mutual participation: man had nowhere to get life and he had nowhere to suffer death. Where to die was ours and where to live was his. Truly, where to find death in the Word?... The Word had nowhere to die, man nowhere to live. «I took from you where to die for you, take from me where to live with me. Let's make a commercial contract: I give to you and you give to me. I receive death from you, you receive life from me. Wake up, see what I give you and what I receive. Being exalted in heaven, I have received humility on earth from you. I am your Lord, and I have received from you the form of a servant. I am your health, and I have received your wounds from you. I am your life, and I have received death from you, Being the Word,

I became flesh so I could die. Next to the Father he had no flesh; I took it from your dough to give you a gift... I received from you the flesh in which to die for you; receive from me the life-giving spirit to live with me. To finish, I have died in yours, you live in mine» (serm.375 13,5 [ = DENIS 5 ]; 265 D,7 [ = MORIN 17]). The increase was clearly favorable to men; what was given and what was received were not equal for yet another reason: the flesh that he took from us was his gift, while the life, thanks to which we live with him and in him, he did not take from us (serm.218 C, l [ = GUELF. 3]).

Christ is an honest and honest merchant. He didn't hide anything. What he bought he paid for and left it in writing. "Thank God, he did not deceive us" (Tracts on the Gospel of Saint John 13:14). This commercial trip was made under the sign of friendship, of which sitting at the table is proof. He did not disdain to sit down to eat with the man and partake of what abounded in his miserable pantry. And, in turn, he invited him to his own table, a splendid table: that of heaven, that of the angels, in which he himself is the bread. He did not despise the misery of the poor, but promised him his wealth. «I invite you to the region of the angels, to friendship with the Father and the Holy Spirit, to the eternal dinner, to be my brothers, to myself; I invite you into my life. Don't you want to believe it? Receive my death as a pledge” (serm.231,5). With his coming, this good merchant confirmed to us the goodness of what we all seek: a happy life. But he made it very clear to us that it is not a product of this region, but of his, and that it is not here, therefore, where we should look for it, but there" (serm.231,5; 233,4). [24] Christ the Physician.—One of the images that Augustine most frequently uses to explain the work of Christ is that of the physician. Christ is the great doctor who came from heaven (serm.23 A [ = MAI 16]; 142,2 [=WILMART 11]; 175,1; 340 A,5 [ = GUELF. 32]), the humble doctor (serm.341 A, l [ = MAI 22]). The sick person who caused his coming was the human race, which lay stretched out all over the earth (serm.155,10; 171,2; 175,1; 340 A,5 [ = GUELF. 32]; 345,7 [=FEANGIPANE 3 ]; 346 A,8 [ = CAILLAU II 19]). In fact, when he came here, he found no one healthy (serm.155,10). Since the sick man could not go to the doctor, in his kindness, he came personally (serm.142,2; 88,7). He had already sent his assistants, the prophets, who cured some, but they foresaw that the sick man was going to get noticeably worse, and announced the arrival of the doctor (serm.345,7; 346 A,8; 340 A,5). Indeed it arrived when the world was already declining and evils abounded (serm.345,7). The patient believed that the worsening of his condition was caused by the arrival of the doctor, unaware that the opposite was true, that is, that it was his worsening that caused the doctor to come (serm.345,7; 346 A,8). The illness was so serious that it prevented the sick person from going to the doctor in person (serm.142,2).

The danger in which the human race found itself, victim of all vices, water that flowed from the fountain of pride, was extremely serious (serm.340 A,5). The patient was the victim of such madness that it even led him to kill the doctor (serm.174,6; 175,1-3). He gave the sick person a bitter but healthy medicine (serm.229 E,3 [ = GUELF. 9 ]; 306 C,7 [ = MOMN 15]); Furthermore, from his blood he made a medicine that would heal his insane murderer (serm.174,6; 175, 2-3); Furthermore, he himself took the medicine that he did not need, to encourage the sick person to do so (serm.142,6). [26] Augustine's audience.—The audience of an ancient Christian preacher was, from a religious point of view, more diverse than we can imagine from our present situation. Not only Christians came, already baptized or simply catechumens (at least to the liturgy of the Word), but also members of the other cultural and religious currents of the world of that time, drawn by the most different motivations, not excluding artistic ones, especially if men of recognized fame sat in the chair. In Augustine's Africa nothing different happened from what happened in Antioch or Constantinople with Saint John Chrysostom or in Milan with Saint Ambrose. We must not forget that Augustine himself felt compelled to listen to the preaching of the Bishop of Milan because of the fame he had as an orator (Confessions V 13,23). Later, he himself would have among his listeners strangers to the Catholic faith. In sermon 296,14 (= BIBL. CAS. I 133) he refers to a Donatist expelled from the Church due to the fervor of some, a fervor that the Saint disapproves; in 265 D, he (= MORIN 17) says: «Abusing your patience, I am going to address them [the Manichaeans] for a little time; Thinking about the possibility that they are hidden among you, you should not miss the opportunity that this reading provides.» And in 237.4: "Just in case there are any bad weeds in this field, I even address those whom I do not see." Evidently, they were a minimal part, not discernible.

The vast majority of Augustine's listeners were, logically, Catholics. Their influx to the Church is difficult to measure. Certainly, on great solemnities the sacred precinct was filled to the brim; but, Agustín comments, they were the same ones who filled the theaters on the remaining days: «So many thieves! How many drunks and detractors! How many there are that fill the amphitheatres! Aren't they the same ones who fill churches and amphitheatres? And often, with their uproar, they seek in churches the same thing that they used to seek in theaters! And many times also, if something of a spiritual nature is said or commanded, they resist, they rebel, going after the flesh and opposing the Holy Spirit" (serm.252,4; also serm.51,1; 361,4). Evidently, these occasional visitors were in a hurry to leave: «I know that these days especially the church tends to be filled with people who think more about leaving than coming, and they call us annoying if we ever linger any longer. Those same ones, if their banquets, to which they rush to arrive, last until the afternoon, neither get tired, nor refuse attendance, nor do they leave them with the slightest blush" (serm.264,1). That's why I often had to send them away with a brief sermon and leave the comment for another day.

[25] The argument of the "praeiudicium."—Among the evidence that the orator could resort to according to the precepts of classical rhetoric is that of the praeiudicium, that is, the sentence handed down in a previous case with the same characteristics (QUINTILIAN, Oratorical Training V 2,1). Augustine will also resort to the praeiudicium to prove the fact of the resurrection in the flesh of Jesus against the Manichaeans. Sermon 229 J (= GUELF. App. VII) is an example. The beginning of it could not be clearer in order to show what it is trying to address: "Christ the Lord saw fit to persuade the truth and certainty of his resurrection with many and varied arguments to build faith, drive away perfidy from the heart and remove all kinds of doubts about his resurrection" (serm.229 J, l). He then explains the point of view of the Manicheans, according to which everything was appearance, to conclude: "What the Manichaeans now believe... is not different from that first thought that passed through the minds of the apostles." That is to say, the current position of the Manichaeans is identical to that of the apostles, who, "not believing that the flesh could be resurrected on the third day, believed they were seeing a spirit." "The error of the apostles is identified with what the Manichaean sect believes." In other words, the Saint has shown that the two "causes" are identical. It is the presupposition for being able to rightly apply to one case the sentence handed down in another, since the force of the praeiudicium is based, on the one hand, on the authority of those who previously judged and, on the other, on the similarity between the two cases, that of the past and that of the present. The Manichaeans, believing that Jesus was only spirit, but not flesh as well, denied the reality of the bodily resurrection. Agustín resorts to a previous judgment.

"If there is nothing wrong with that way of thinking (of the Manichaeans), Jesus should have left the disciples to their thoughts... Let them go like this, approve of what they rightly believed." Next, the Saint appeals to the "sentence" then pronounced by Jesus: "Listen to the evil that exists in believing what you believe... Do you believe that your danger is that of a small illness? [27] Transcend the soul.—In sermon 241,2, Augustine presents us with a process of ascension to God based on creation and under the key of mutability-immutability, which we find in many other of his texts: Confessions X 6,9-10; Comments on Psalms 145.5; Treatises on the gospel of Saint John 15; 20:11-12. The Augustinian method consists of passing through, transcending everything created that is mutable to reach the immutable creator. The stages of the process are always identical: from the exterior to the interior, and from the interior to the superior. From the external world of creatures one passes to the interior of the soul; Once one has reached one's own soul, a new jump is given to reach God. This is how he explains it in the Treatises on the Gospel of Saint John (20:12): «Think of your body: it is mortal, earthly, fragile and corruptible; despise it. Meat is a temporary and passing thing. Think about other bodies, the celestial ones: they are bigger, better and more brilliant. See how they turn from east to west; They are not immobile... It also flies above them... With flight not of the flesh, but of the mind. Don't appreciate them either... You say: 'Where am I going to go beyond the celestial bodies and what am I going to soar over with the flight of my mind?... With what have you reflected on those wonders? Let the same examiner appear. For he who scrutinizes, discerns and distinguishes all these wonders and weighs them in the scales of wisdom is the soul. Undoubtedly, the soul with which you think all those wonders is better than those wonders that you think.

This soul is spirit, not body. Elevate your flight also above this spirit... The soul is a great wonder. But how dare I say 'it'? Soar your flight over it too; Although in quality it surpasses all bodies, it is mutable. Now he knows, now he doesn't know; now he doubts, now he remembers; now he wants, now he doesn't want; now she sins, now she is just. Take flight over everything that changes; not only about everything visible, but also about everything changeable. You have already taken flight over the visible flesh; about the sky, the sun, the moon and the stars, which are visible; also rise above all that is changeable. Everything visible has already been pierced; You reached your soul, and in it you have found mutability. God is not mutable. So, take flight over your soul. Pour out your soul upon yourself to come into contact with God, about whom you are asked incessantly: Where is your God? Each of the steps, then, is caused by mutability. It is evident that bodies, even celestial ones, even if they are beautiful, are mutable, and transcending them is essential. Superior to any kind of bodies is the soul, the highest part of man; although invisible, she too

It is mutable. It is therefore necessary to transcend it as well in the search for the immutable. The immutable is God. The entire process that he develops at length in the aforementioned texts is condensed in the famous lapidary phrase: «Do not go outside; The truth lives inside man. And if you find yourself mutable, transcend yourself too” (True Religion 39,72). If we would like to emphasize something, it is precisely that step required by one's own interiority, by one's own soul to reach God. [28] Infant Baptism.—The practice of infant baptism was common in the fourth century, particularly in Africa. Augustine himself confirms it (Confessions I 11,17-18; The Acts of Pelagius II 4). But at the same time we must note the custom of delaying it as long as possible for various reasons: some, the lukewarm, to obtain a more global forgiveness, since by prolonging the wait they deferred their Christian responsibility; and others, the fervent, for fear of missing the baptismal grace, aware that the sin of a baptized person is greater than that of an unbaptized person (Confessions I 11,17). On the other hand, there was a tendency to bring forward baptism for girls before boys. The case of Saint Ambrose and his sister Marcelina is an example. Augustine, who notes the fact, reflects on it from the early days of his conversion. In The Dimension of the Soul (36.80) he indicates that the usefulness of baptism for children is an obscure problem, but he believes it exists. In Free Will (III 227) he answers those who ask again about its usefulness for children who die without being able to become aware of it, relying on the faith of those who present it to receive the sacrament. It is, according to him, a pious and reasonable belief. In the Confessions (I 11,17-18) he presents baptism as a healing of a wound, with the emphasis placed on personal sin, and as a safeguard for the future. In Baptism against the Donatists (IV 23,30-25,32) he unites the fruit of baptism with interior penance, but both things are separable, as in the case of the good thief and the baptism of children. The practice is not in vain; This is what the Church has unanimously believed, and Scripture is in accordance with tradition, he thinks. Faced with Donatism, a new element now appears: the conditions required for the reception of the sacrament.

In letter 98 to Boniface he addresses the issue of the baptism of children explicitly, showing how it is possible for them to participate in the faith of their parents or godparents, because there is a community of spiritual order: communion in the Holy Spirit; how, although it cannot be denied that the godparents have their own function, the main agent of sanctification that takes place in the sacrament is the Holy Spirit, and, according to that, it is not necessary for the carnal parents to present it, and how baptism is the sacrament of faith that survives until it is extinguished. With Pelagianism a new stage in his reflection begins. The new doctrine clashed with two firm convictions of the Church: the need for prayer and the baptism of children (cta.176,3; 178,3; 179,1). Augustine soon focuses on the fact of baptism, "which the universal Church multiplies in her maternal goodness" (The Consequences and Forgiveness of Sins III 1; cta. 166,24). He defends it with scriptural arguments, tradition and the rite of the sacrament itself (The consequences... I 34,64). In truth, the Pelagians did not deny either the fact or the necessity of infant baptism, but they provided other reasons. According to them, it was administered not so that they could achieve eternal life, but rather the kingdom of heaven (serm.294,2; The consequences... I 20,26; 30,58; act.175,6). That is, the baptism of children did not forgive

no sin in them—because they did not have it—but it obtained for them divine adoption and the kingdom of heaven. Eternal life and the kingdom of heaven were, therefore, two different things. Augustine justified the baptism of children based on original sin; From this perspective, denying baptism in the sense in which Augustine understood it meant putting into play the dogma of universal redemption, because if they do not have sin, they have no need of Christ (serm.176; 293,10; act.175,6; The consequences... I 23; II 48; III 7). If baptism always involves the forgiveness of sins, this sin in children cannot be other than original sin. In this way, the Church's custom of baptizing them is proof of the existence of original sin, certainly conceived in a different way than Origen conceived it, that is, as a guilt contracted before coming to this world, in a previous existence (The City of God XI 23). Augustine, who has always admitted the baptism of children, only before Pelagius and his followers explicitly affirms its absolute necessity; only before them does he justify the fact and consider it through the prism of original sin. Only then does he also seek support in tradition: Saint Cyprian, Saint Ambrose and Saint John Chrysostom. See J. C. DIDIER, S. Augustin et le baptéme des enfants: Revue des études augustiniennes 1 (1956) 109-129; also E. R. FAIRWEATHER, St. Augustine's Interpretation of Infant Baptism: Augustinus Magister II 897-903. [29] The outline of the sermon.—Shortly before concluding the long sermon 361 on the resurrection of the dead, Augustine summarizes the arguments adduced. It goes like this: «If you remember well, I have said everything God has suggested to me that was necessary; I have taken evidence from the nature of things and from everyday examples; I have also taken them from the omnipotence of God, for whom nothing is difficult...; and, finally, of the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ himself, of whom it is known that he rose again” (serm.361,18). We have, then, three kinds of arguments: 1) similarities taken from nature; 2) recourse to the person responsible for the act, and 3) historical examples. These are the three types of arguments that Augustine will use to prove the possibility of the facts that are preached about Jesus. In sermon 247, Augustine uses all three together, being in this sense a copy of 361, although applied to another specific fact: that Jesus could enter when the doors were closed.

Which shows that it is already an authentic scheme of Augustine's thought, which, without a doubt, was given by rhetoric. Let's look at the sermon more closely. In number 2 we find the presentation of the topic that will be discussed, the propositio: "The same reading invites us... to say something about how the Lord, who was resurrected in the solidity of his body, so that he was not only seen by his disciples, but also touched, was able to appear to them while the doors were closed." The problem, the controversy, has arisen because some deny the fact based on what Augustine calls the prejudices of his own reasoning, and which he exposes in the same sermon. The evidence adduced by the Saint are those presented above, although in a different order: 1) recourse to other examples; 2) to resemblances of nature, and 3) to the person to whom the fact is attributed. 1) Examples. Augustine presents other wonderful facts about Jesus: conception and virgin birth, which are similar to the case he is trying to prove, in that both involve passing through a closed path; walking on the sea, which serves as an example of how, when applied to Jesus, certain characteristics or properties of bodies are not completely valid.

2) Similarities. Augustine resorts to ordinary things for which no one asks for an explanation: the fig tree, which is a large tree, gives a small seed, and the small pumpkin gives a large one. In the same way that the event narrated in the gospel causes admiration and surprise, these too should cause it, but their frequency has made them normal in the eyes of men. 3) The omnipotence of God. As a final proof, Augustine turns to the author of the act, considering him in his divine condition, to which omnipotence is associated. Things that are impossible for man are easy for God (Luke 18:25-27). He can even make the corpulence of a camel pass through the depths of a needle. How much more can he make the smallest magnitude of a man pass through the hole in a door! (n.3). More fully developed, and with references to classical rhetoric and all Augustinian preaching, the Saint's actions can be seen in P. by Luis VIZCAÍNO, The Acts of Jesus in the Preaching of Saint Augustine. Classical rhetoric at the service of patristic exegesis. Augustinian study (Valladolid 1983) c.3 p.71-89. [30] The symbolism of the number 153.—Augustine has exposed the symbolism of the number 153 countless times, as he himself confesses (serm248 4- 249,3; 259,2; etc.). We preserve at least nine of these exhibitions (serm.229 M,3 [ = GUELF. 15]; 248.4; 249.3; 250.5; 251.5-6; 252.8; 252 A [=WILMART 13]; 259; cta.55,17,31). A constant fact of its interpretation consists of seeing symbolized in that number the thousands of saints and faithful who will form the blessed Church. What varies, however, is the derivation of the number. In this regard we know two interpretations of his that follow one another. In sermons 252.8; 259.2 and account 55,17,31 propose the following: from the number 153 the 3 must be subtracted, because it has the function of indicating that the remainder — 150 — must be divided precisely by 3; in the same way that, if there were 152, it would be necessary to divide by 2. The number 150, divided by 3, gives 50, a figure with a mystical meaning, which is equivalent to the future Church. The Saint presents two derivations. The first would be: 50 = (7 X 7) + 1, where 7 means the seven ages of the world, and 1 the return to unity.

The second takes as its starting point the number 40, a symbol of this mortal life (see complementary note 10: The symbolism of the number 40 p.788), to which must be added the 10, that is, the denarius given to the workers who have worked in the vineyard (Mt 20). We have, therefore, that 50 = 40 -f 10. The 153, consequently, results from the following equation: 50 X 3 + 3, the latter 3 being a symbol of the Trinity. In all the other sermons, Augustine explains the number 153 from 17, since it is the result of the sum of all numbers up to and including 17 (1 + 2 + 3 + 4...+ 17 = 153). In this way, 17 is like the root, and 153 like the tree. We must therefore decipher the mystery of this smaller number (serm.252 A,6). The 17 is formed from the sum of 10 + 7. The 10 is a symbol of the law, since the decalogue is the most important part of it, and the 7 is a symbol of the gifts of the Holy Spirit (Is 11:2). From here, it is no longer difficult to discover the mysterious meaning of the number 17: it symbolizes those who fulfill God's commandments with the help of the Spirit. The 153 captured fish symbolize, therefore, all the saints, who cannot be any more than those who fulfilled the law with divine help. The Augustinian commentary, which can seem so bizarre to us men today, had its charm and fully responded to the tastes of that time, especially when the Saint entertained them with his juggling.

[31] Faith as purification.—Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God (Mt 5:8). Purifying their hearts through faith (Acts 15:9). If you do not believe, you will not understand (Is 7,9, according to the LXX). The thought, repeatedly expressed by Augustine, of the necessity of faith, understood as purification, is built on these three biblical texts. It is evident, he says, that every man wants to be happy, a happiness that will only be achieved in the contemplation of God (The Trinity XIII 20,25). It is also evident that a person who is stained cannot see and adhere to the pure, authentic and unshakable truth. Consequently, “purification was necessary, since we were not capable of taking possession of the eternal; Our soul was burdened by the filth of sin, contracted with the love of temporal things and embedded in our nature with the filth of mortality. Only through the temporal, bait for our senses, was this purification possible, necessary to temper ourselves with eternal realities... Thus, if the rational mind, when it is purified, must apply itself to the contemplation of the eternal, when it still needs to be purified it must cling to faith, making use of temporal things" (The Trinity IV 13,24). We must, therefore, take hold of faith; Before our mind is purified, we must believe what we cannot yet understand and whose intelligence we aspire to. The proof is given by the prophet Isaiah: If you do not believe, you will not understand (The Christian Combat 13,14). Faith is what purifies the hearts of those who make a pilgrimage to the vision of God (Treatise on the Gospel of Saint John 68,3; Confessions VI 4,6; The Trinity VIII 4,6). In this context, the incarnation and faith in it is the eyewash that, applied to our stained eyes, allows us vision. «We are enlightened now if we have the eye salve of faith.

He therefore preceded the mixing of his saliva with the earth, with which he was to anoint the eyes of the one who was born blind. We are born from Adam blind too, and we need Christ to enlighten us. He made a mixture of saliva and earth: The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (Treatise on the Gospel of Saint John 34,9; also 2,16; 18,11; 35,6). We have a synthesis of Augustinian thought in this regard in The Trinity (I 8,17): «The vision (1 Jn 3,2) is the reward of faith; To obtain that reward, hearts are purified through faith, as it is written: Purifying their hearts through faith (Acts 15:9). That hearts must be purified to achieve this vision is proven, above all, by that phrase: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God (Mt 5:8)." [32] The Donatists, schismatics and heretics.—To address the Donatists, Augustine sometimes uses the term "schismatic"; sometimes, "heretic", and sometimes both (serm.269,2). Within this freedom, it should be noted that in the first period more of the first was used and in the second the use of the other increased. The change may be due to several factors, mainly one: from the year 405, imperial legislation began to recognize them as heretics, and, therefore, all the punishments fell on them.

penalties issued against heresy. The Donatists then began a campaign to prove that they were not. We have a good example in Cresconius, who denies that they can be called heretics with reason, since heresy is a sect composed of those who separate themselves along the doctrinal line, while schism is a break between those who maintain the same doctrine, a difference that does not exist between Catholics and them (Reply to Cresconius II 3,4). Augustine will respond, not without difficulty, that a schism is a recent break with the Church, a break caused by some divergence of opinion. Heresy is an inveterate schism (ibid., II 7,9). According to this thesis, the schism would become heresy with the mere passage of time. He expresses himself about the idea again, at the end of his life, in the work Las heresías (69). There he states that Donatism, initially a schism, later became a heresy. "After their case had been examined and sentenced, having been declared guilty of falsehood, strengthened by persistent dissension, they converted the schism into heresy" (see also cta.87,4). The reasons on which Augustine bases his power to call Donatists heretics, always according to the work The Heresies, are the following: affirming that the Church identifies with Donatus's party; that the alleged fault of Cecilian has contaminated it everywhere and that the Catholics must be rebaptized. Undoubtedly important points, which called into question Cresconio's assertion that there were no doctrinal differences between Donatists and Catholics. See P.
